title: Yolo County recognizes Bracero legacy
author: Monica Stark
description: Descendants of Yolo County Braceros, family and friends gathered at the Supervisors' chambers on Dec. 3 for special recognition and remembrance of those farmworkers whose hard work led to boosting the state and local economies and building up UC Davis' reputation as a leading research institution. The vast majority of Latinos, Mexican Americans and Chicanos in this community have extended family members who came through the Bracero program and still live and reside here in Yolo County, explained r etired Yolo County Office of Education Superintendent Dr. Jesse Ortiz. Whereas Yolo County received the largest number of Bracero workers that resided in California, whereas Braceros contributed to the development of large-scale ag in California, making it the fifth-largest economy in the world and a vital factor of Yolo County's economy; and whereas, while the Bracero Program provided opportunities, hope, and determination in the face of daily injustice and hardship, it also shortcomings and inequities; and whereas the Bracero Program separated families and created distress to mothers, wives, and children, and whereas Yolo County lead...
content:
Descendants of Yolo County Braceros, family and friends gathered at the Supervisors' chambers on Dec. 3 for special recognition and remembrance of those farmworkers whose hard work led to boosting the state and local economies and building up UC Davis' reputation as a leading research institution.
With the financial successes of the historical guest-worker program, supervisors also recognized their daily injustices, hardships and family separation. Many of those men came back with their families to live here, and their descendants were elected officials, educational leaders, labor leaders and agricultural leaders.
The vast majority of Latinos, Mexican Americans and Chicanos in this community have extended family members who came through the Bracero program and still live and reside here in Yolo County, explained r etired Yolo County Office of Education Superintendent Dr. Jesse Ortiz.
Supervisors adopted a resolution recognizing Yolo County Braceros and their descendants while outside the chambers, an exhibit featuring photos, items, stories, newspaper articles, and information to raise awareness about this historical legacy. The Ethnic Studies YOLO Academy organized the one-day exhibit with Supervisors Lucas Frerichs and Angel Barajas, the Mexican Yolo Concilio, and the Yolo County Archives.
Supervisor Angel Barajas, who had bracero family members himself, highlighted some areas of the proclamation:
Whereas Yolo County received the largest number of Bracero workers that resided in California, whereas Braceros contributed to the development of large-scale ag in California, making it the fifth-largest economy in the world and a vital factor of Yolo County's economy; and whereas, while the Bracero Program provided opportunities, hope, and determination in the face of daily injustice and hardship, it also shortcomings and inequities; and whereas the Bracero Program separated families and created distress to mothers, wives, and children, and whereas Yolo County leaders, educators, and community members, our sons and daughters, grandsons and grandsons – those (descendants) who are civically engaged and making a difference for schools and society.
The Bracero program began as part of the war effort in 1942. It continued to 1964, bringing more than 4 million Mexican nationals to the United States, with Yolo County hosting over 10,000 — the largest in California.
"The soldiers wouldn't have eaten, nor would the people in the communities if it wasn't for the sacrifices of the thousands of Mexican young men that came to this community and stayed here, and many of them remained in this community," said Cirenio Rodriguez, a retired professor (Sacramento State, UC Davis, UC Santa Barbara, Woodland Community College, and for 30 years an elected board member of the Woodland Unified School District and Yolo County Office of Education).
"Sundays, they would take the day off, and the merchants in downtown Woodland relied on them. Imagine 10,000 young men between 18 and 25 years old walking through the streets of downtown Woodland. Many of them remained and stayed in the community here," Rodriguez said.
Initially, Braceros came from Mexico City and later from rural areas like Michoacán. Braceros were sprayed with DDT and sent to a distribution center in Stockton, where they worked in agriculture, food processing, and railroads. Yolo County hosted many Braceros, contributing to large-scale agriculture while UC Davis expanded its agricultural research.
The Bracero program offered economic opportunities but caused significant family separation, with many workers away from their families for extended periods. Due to labor surpluses, Braceros faced unfair pay, mistreatment, and conflicts with U.S.-born workers. In addition, some employers withheld wages.
One of the displays at the exhibit spoke to a class action law for Braceros to receive the money that had been deducted from their pay and never received. Lalo Acevedo wrote about his father, Yolo County Bracero Crescencio Acevedo Soriano, who, in 2001, while supporting his family, advocated and won this lawsuit.
But only some Braceros with proof of Bracero I.D. were able to receive back payment, Lalo Acevedo wrote. Soriano was born in 1922 and lived to be 101 in Woodland until early this year. He was from Mexico City and worked in Seligman, Arizona, and Santa Fe, New Mexico. After his Bracero term ended he relocated to Woodland.
"Deeply grateful" for the resolution that recognizes the sacrifices and contributions of the workers who participated in the Bracero program, Antonio De Loera-Brust, whose grandfather, Jesus De Loera-Lopez, came as a Bracero from 1945 to 1949, said his family history is "like many others," in that it's "intertwined with the legacy of these courageous individuals who left their home in search of a better life, only to face challenges and hardships."
In his tribute to his grandfather, Antonio De Loera-Lopez explained that Jose De Loera-Lopez was born in Coahuila, Mexico, in the 1920s and raised in poverty in the aftermath of the Mexican Revolution. Jesus, a child of a tenant peasant, sought a better opportunity by enlisting as a bracero.
While a bracero, Jesus worked in Arizona and Minnesota in the agriculture and railroad industries. Like most braceros, he was sprayed with DDT. He recalled being assigned the task of unloading coffins of deceased U.S. servicemen being returned from the war.
After his time as a Bracero, Jesus returned home and became part of an "ejido" collective farmland in Coahuila. He became an advocate for Choahuila's ejidos and peasants. He was ultimately elected to represent his home district in the Mexican Congress as a federal deputy for Coahuila, where he prioritized issues of land reform and fair ag commodity prices for ejidos.
His descendants in Yolo County are his son Jesus De Loera-Herrera, Professor of Mathematics at UC Davis and advocate for Latino STEM education, and his grandson Antonio, a 2013 DHS alumni and a former staffer in the U.S. Department of State (which initially authorized the Bracero program) and now the communications director for the United Farm Workers. His other grandson, Andres De Loera-Brust, is a 2026 DHS alumni and a Harvard University Ph.D. Economics student.
Mariko Yamada, the former Democratic assemblywoman from California's 4th Assembly district, emphasized the country's long history "of agricultural labor exploitation" and warned of history repeating. "From the appropriation of native lands to slavery, sharecropping, and up into the present time, we have waves of immigrant workers who frankly have been taken advantage of throughout our nation's history … We should all be vigilant and prepare ourselves so that history hopefully does not repeat itself."
The reference to when the Bracero Program was established by executive order in 1942, she said, has "a bitter relationship" to what happened to Japanese Americans. California's agricultural economy was controlled by about 30% byJapanese American farmers, who produced about 40% of the truck crops in the state. She said, then "lo and behold, when 120,000 Japanese Americans were rounded up and interned, incarcerated, magically, the Bracero Program was established."
These events, she said, "inform us" of history repeating.
Writer David Bacon, a writer for Nation argues in Reviving the Bracero Program Is the Wrong Answer for Workers, that more than 50 years after the Bracero program, "little has changed": the bracero program is not dead. To channel migration from Mexico, Central America, and the Caribbean to halt "the dangerous and unlawful ways people are migrating," Biden had planned to "help American farmers bring in seasonal agricultural workers from northern Central America[n] countries under the H-2A visa program to improve conditions for all workers."
The H-2A program allows U.S. employers or U.S. agents who meet specific regulatory requirements to bring foreign nationals to the United States to fill temporary agricultural jobs.
De Loera-Brust said H-2A workers can come here legally but don't have many rights. "They're excluded from all sorts of basic protections. It's a non immigrant visa. No matter how many years you come here in a row to work, you're not able to ever get a green card or put down roots. You can't bring your family, of course, right?"
That was another issue with the Bracero program.
Still worst of all, De Loera-Brust said the visa depends on your employer. If your employer doesn't like you for any reason, they don't even have to give a reason, and they can send you back. "Not only are you losing your job, but you're losing your visa."
According to De Loera-Brust, nearly 50% of farmworkers in Yolo County are food insecure. "We have almost 20,000 people who are part of a farmworker household. 50% of those folks are food insecure, and these are the very workers who put food on our tables, but they too often can't afford to put food on their family's table."
He said the reason is not complicated: Their wages are too low for the cost of living in a place like this. "I think we need to raise wages, and we also need to find ways to lower the cost of living for working people across the board."
Exhibit organizer Dr. Melissa Moreno told supervisors to consider finding a physical space to showcase this history soon. "I'd like us to consider sometime in the near future, the importance of representing land, labor, the hearts and spirits of all the generations."
A retired high school counselor from Tracy and a Vietnam Veteran, Richard Soto, whose father was a Bracero, founded the Chicano Research Center at 2182 E. Main St. in Stockton, where he showcases more than 20,000 books, journals, and artifacts highlighting Chicano history. Seeing the one-day exhibit was testament to the preservation of the Bracero legacy.
As the descendant of the bracero, Elizabeth Esquivel, Area 1 Trustee-Yolo County Board of Education, also expressed her gratitude for the resolution's recognition of the sacrifices and contributions of the braceros. "For my family's story, like many others, is intertwined with the legacy of these courageous individuals who left their home in search of a better life, only to face challenges and hardships. This acknowledgment brings dignity to their struggles and honors their resilience. It's a reminder of the role farmworkers had in his area."
To Esquivel, the resolution also pointed to the "great impact" that the Bracero program had on children and their ability to obtain higher education.
It is also a historical event that schools have recently begun to teach with the encouragement of Ethnic Studies programs.
Being in the chambers watching her colleagues and community leaders who are descendants of Braceros recognize the legacy, work ethic and community leadership that has been passed on from generation to generation. "Here we are today, and just standing in the same room, and it was just so beautiful to see," Esquivel said.

title: Improving Health Equity in Tribal Communities
description: (StatePoint) Heart disease is the number one killer of new moms in the United States, and American Indian and Alaska Native (AI/AN) women have even more risk factors for poor
content:
(StatePoint) Heart disease is the number one killer of new moms in the United States, and American Indian and Alaska Native (AI/AN) women have even more risk factors for poor heart health than the general population, such as high rates of Type 2 diabetes, obesity and smoking, as well as increased exposure to trauma and violence. In fact, recent research reports that more than 60% of AI/AN women have suboptimal heart health when they enter pregnancy, which is strongly related to the development of heart disease later in life.
According to the American Heart Association and the National Collaborative for Infants and Toddlers, addressing heart disease risks in AI/AN women requires not only attention to traditional cardiovascular disease risk factors, but also an understanding of how the legacy of colonization, exploitation, racism and discrimination shape the health of members of these communities. That's why a new policy agenda identifies the most impactful ways to protect Tribal women during the vulnerable period of pregnancy, while honoring Tribal sovereignty.

content:
Yolo County is proud to announce its participation as the first pilot jurisdiction in the Bridge initiative, a new program launched by the Institute for Local Government (ILG). This initiative aims to strengthen California's local government workforce by creating Registered Apprenticeship Programs (RAPs) in non-traditional fields, including human resources, accounting, information technology (IT), health and human services and more.
'I'm thrilled that Yolo County will serve as an inaugural participant in ILG's Bridge Public Sector Registered Apprenticeship program,' said Yolo County Board of Supervisors Chair Lucas Frerichs. 'Apprenticeships have a long history of success in the construction trades, and I'm excited to bring this innovative model to support our broader local government workforce in Yolo County.'

title: What to Know Now to Help Protect Your Newborn from RSV
author: Rebecca Norwick
description: By Rebecca Norwick,
content:
By Rebecca Norwick,
National Association of Nurse
Practitioners in Women's Health
(NAPSI)—When I first started my career as a nurse practitioner, I saw pediatric wards fill each winter with children suffering from common infections that cause rotavirus diarrhea and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV). Since then and following the introduction of the rotavirus vaccine nearly two decades ago, hospital visits for rotavirus have notably decreased.
Protecting Newborns Now
Today, we are in a similar position to help prevent RSV through a maternal vaccine given to protect infants at birth. Getting vaccinated while pregnant helps your body create protective antibodies that you can pass on to your baby. These antibodies can help protect your baby from diseases such as RSV during the first few months of life when they are most vulnerable.
While RSV can cause cold-like symptoms most of the time, it can be dangerous in infants and young children—and is the leading cause of infant hospitalization in the United States. RSV season usually starts in the fall and peaks in the winter in most regions, which is why the vaccine is typically given from September through January. Because the RSV vaccine is administered seasonally, the protection passed to the baby will last for their first RSV season.
The good news is that if you or a loved one is pregnant, the maternal RSV vaccine is available now at no out-of-pocket cost to you through almost all insurance plans, including Medicaid and employer-sponsored plans. You should receive the maternal RSV vaccine during weeks 32 through 36 of pregnancy if you are pregnant between September and January.
Vaccines have been recommended during pregnancy for decades and are our most effective tool against preventable respiratory diseases. They are also a critical part of routine prenatal care, adding an important line of defense against severe respiratory diseases that can leave pregnant people and their babies at an increased risk of complications. The maternal RSV vaccine can be administered during the same visit that you may receive other vaccines during pregnancy, including Tdap, flu, or COVID-19 vaccines.
All recommended vaccines are held to the highest standards of safety—meaning they are carefully studied and monitored for side effects. Having worked for 20 years in community health centers in underserved areas, I have witnessed firsthand the protection that maternal vaccinations provide. At one clinic, we even implemented a 'cocooning' approach, vaccinating the entire family against flu to help protect newborns who are too young for vaccines. By ensuring the pregnant mother, father, siblings, and grandparents received their flu shots, we worked to minimize the risk of influenza spreading within families.
These days we can go a step further by providing early RSV protection to newborns during their first months of life. If you or a loved one is pregnant, ask your healthcare provider about the maternal RSV vaccine, along with other recommended maternal vaccines. Maternal vaccination is a powerful way to help strengthen your baby's immunity and share protection before they are even born.
Learn More
For more information on maternal vaccines and their importance, visit www.cdc.gov/vaccines/pregnancy.

title: Crowds come out for holidays
author: Special to The Enterprise
description: New research has revealed which tourist attractions in the U.S. and abroad are the most overcrowded over the winter months, with Universal Studios Hollywood ranking top. Universal Studios Hollywood is
content:
New research has revealed which tourist attractions in the U.S. and abroad are the most overcrowded over the winter months, with Universal Studios Hollywood ranking top.
Universal Studios Hollywood is the most overcrowded tourist attraction to visit over winter, according to visitors, with 40% of reviews complaining of crowds. Experts analyzed Tripadvisor reviews complaining of overcrowding and long waits at over 900 tourist destinations.
Rockefeller Center ranks second as the most likely to see congestion over the festive period, with Silverwood Theme Park in third.
The study, conducted by student travel company Rustic Pathways, looked at more than 900 tourist attractions across the U.S. and the rest of the world, analyzing complaints on Tripadvisor to see which has the most reviews related to busyness.
Terms analyzed were those related to overcrowding and waiting in line, such as 'overcrowded,' 'completely packed,' and 'long wait.' These mentions were scaled to per 1,000 reviews to see which attractions prove the most congested over Christmas.
Universal Studios Hollywood ranks as the most overcrowdedtourist attraction with 40% of reviewsmentioning crowding or long waits. One December review stated that the theme park was 'grossly overcrowded', while in January a user said, '[kids] would have lost their minds in lines that long'.
Ranking second is the Rockefeller Center Christmas Tree with more than one-third (34.9%) of Tripadvisor reviews complaining of crowds. Located in New York City, the tree is an iconic Christmas staple that draws in crowds from all over the world.
However, this popularity has a downside. One review complained of 'chaos' with the crowds being 'seriously dangerous'and another stated there was '0 crowd control.'
In third is Silverwood Theme Park, based in Idaho, with 31.3% of reviews featuring overcrowding complaints. One review stated it was 'very busy' with many others complaining of long queues.
Another theme park, Busch Gardens in Florida, ranked fourth, with 31.2% of visitor reviews complaining of busyness. Susceptible to large crowds and long queues for rides, theme parks are prone to congestion, while those in year-round warm climates are more vulnerable to overcrowding over the festive period as people seek winter sun.
The first non-American tourist attraction on the list is the Nuremberg Christmas Market. Based in Germany, the festive attraction sees 29.8% of Tripadvisor reviews complaining of overcrowding.
The market is regarded as one of the best Christmas markets in the world so it's no surprise the crowds can get a bit much.One review remarked it was 'packed shoulder to shoulder', while another said it was 'so busy you can barely walk through it.'
Back to theme parks, Six Flags Great Adventure ranked sixth with 28.2%of reviewers disappointed by the crowds. Located in New Jersey, one park-goer took to Tripadvisor to complain that 'the park is entirely too overcrowded'
Angel's Landing ranked as the seventh most overcrowded, with 27.2% of reviews complaining. Located in Zion National Park in Utah, this renowned trail has a reputation for being dangerous — but this doesn't stop people from hiking it for canyon views. One review called it'a very busy trail' while another said it was 'too crowded.'
Ranking eighth is Top of the Rock with 27.2% of Tripadvisor reviews mentioning crowding and long waits. Another New York staple, this observation deck allows tourists to see stunning views over the city skyline; if people don't get in your way. Users wrote it was 'rammed' and commented on the long waits for photos.
In ninth, also with 27.2% of reviews mentioning large crowds, is the second non-American location, the Christmas market on Rathausplatz.

title: Commentary: Make mountain meadows a priority
author: Ryan Burnett
description: When I stepped into a Sierra Nevada meadow over 25 years ago, I was struck by the diversity of life, the hub of biological activity — full of birds, frogs,
content:
When I stepped into a Sierra Nevada meadow over 25 years ago, I was struck by the diversity of life, the hub of biological activity — full of birds, frogs, fish and plants. As a wildlife ecologist, I was in love. That infatuation has endured, growing into one of the great passions in my life.
As a lifelong Californian, I've always been enamored with the natural wonders our state contains, and meadows are no exception.
Californians have a lot to be proud of. In addition to the highest GDP of any state, we have a proven track record as the country's climate and environmental leader. Since voters recently approved Proposition 4, we can be proud that California will deepen its commitment to large-scale action to address the state's water, wildfire and climate challenges.
The $10 billion bond measure will flow to environmental projects large and small, including $1.2 billion for land conservation and habitat restoration, which will benefit communities and wildlife around the state. But one question looms: What might these investments to increase climate resilience look like on the ground?
Some of the most important — and often overlooked — natural resources the state has are the verdant high elevation wetlands we call mountain meadows. These meadows lie at the headwaters of the rivers that flow out of the Sierra Nevada, Cascade and Klamath mountains, supplying the majority of water we rely on for agriculture and drinking, and supporting diverse ecosystems from the Sierra to the sea, from Yreka to San Diego.
They serve an important role in improving water quality and increasing water storage, acting as giant sponges that soak up snow melt and slowly release it through the dry summer months. And mountain meadows are superstars at carbon sequestration, pulling carbon out of the atmosphere as fast as tropical rainforests.
Mountain meadows provide important wildlife habitat for a broad suite of species, including many that are threatened with extinction, such as Willow Flycatchers and Yosemite Toads.
For a millennia, mountain meadows have also held a deep cultural significance for the many tribes that have stewarded these ecosystems.
Unfortunately, over 50% of Sierra meadows have been heavily degraded or lost over the past 150 years, due to road-building, overgrazing, fire suppression, mining, water diversions and more. These meadows no longer provide the wealth of important services they once did.
The Sierra Meadows Partnership has sought to protect and restore these crown jewels of the Sierra Nevada and Cascades mountains. Comprised of NGOs, government agencies, universities, conservation districts and restoration practitioners, we have restored more than 8,000 acres and protected 10,000 since 2016. The goal is to restore and conserve 30,000 acres by 2030.
Prop. 4 has the potential to dramatically scale up the meadow restoration and conservation work taking place, which will pay dividends to the people and wildlife statewide that rely on the many natural benefits of healthy mountain meadows. The billions designated for water projects, forest health and nature-based climate solutions could increase funding possibilities to restore meadows, amplify Indigenous voices and improve the resilience of our watersheds.
Recently, I had the privilege of engaging local elementary students from the small town of Chester to assist us in the restoration of Child's Meadow, near Lassen Volcanic National Park. Witnessing their sense of purpose and accomplishment as they took an active role in restoring their watershed reminded me once again of why California invests in the restoration of our incredible natural resources.
— Ryan Burnett leads the Sierra Nevada Group at Point Blue Conservation Science and is the chair of the Sierra Meadows Partnership. He wrote this for CalMatters, a public interest journalism venture committed to explaining how California's Capitol works and why it matters.

title: View From the Sideline: My No. 1 moment of the year
author: Mike Trask
description: Last week, I counted down my favorite sports moments of 2024. As promised, I will unveil my top moment of the year now.
content:
Last week, I counted down my favorite sports moments of 2024. As promised, I will unveil my top moment of the year now.
This is not the story of an athlete who has trained for years and was at the top of their sport. In fact, this athlete had never competed in any sport before this wrestling season. Additionally, they had lost every time they stepped on the wrestling mat.
Izabelle Mascorella competed on the Sheldon High Girls' wrestling team. Entering her junior year, she said, "One of my goals was to join a sport before my high school years were over. My best friend said wrestling was fun and we should do it together."
Girls' wrestling is relatively new; few schools have enough girls to form a team. But Sheldon had enough to compete in the Delta League with Davis and Pleasant Grove this year. There were no cuts, so Mascorella and her friend were welcomed to the team.
In the early part of the season, Mascorella would struggle on the mat, losing every match, most by being pinned. "I was not very good, but I enjoyed the competition and making friends. Everyone was really nice."
The Delta League held its first-ever girls wrestling championship in late January. Three teams — Davis, Pleasant Grove and Sheldon — would compete for the title.
In their first match, Sheldon faced Pleasant Grove. There was little drama, and Sheldon posted a dominant win, 54-18. Unfortunately for Mascorella, she found herself in a familiar position — on her back, getting pinned — another defeat.
A few minutes after her match, she came over to the bleachers, where I had set up my camera gear. She was getting water from her friend's mom, still a bit out of breath but smiling. She asked about my camera, and we talked about photography and school for a minute. She told me she was new to wrestling and not very good at it, but math and science were her thing.
She immediately struck me as someone to root for. She seemed out of place in such a demanding sport, yet had such a joyful spirit. It seemed so easy for her to shrug off that she lost minutes ago. Between matches, she was with her friends, laughing, joking and having fun, in a great mood. All this, knowing she would shortly be on the mat again and likely get beat. Which, by the way, hurts; getting tossed around and pinned does not feel great, no matter your spirit.
Davis High beat Pleasant Grove as well and would face Sheldon next for the League Title. The teams battled back-and-forth. Sheldon would win four matches by forfeit, which is common. It's still difficult to fill all the weight classes in girls wrestling.
However, Mascorella was not the beneficiary of one of the forfeits; she had an opponent and would need to wrestle. She stopped by the bleachers one more time. This time, she was not nervous or smiling. She was worried. Her best friend had just lost her match and had reinjured her ankle in the process. Mascorella's first instinct was to stay with her friend, even if it meant forfeiting her match.
Her friend encouraged her to go out there and try. Mascorella decided to wrestle. She was unaware that her match would decide Sheldon's fate. They were trailing Davis 30-31.
"I went out there not knowing my opponent or the score. I was distracted and was thinking about my friend."
Mascorella got ahead on points early in the match. By the third and final period, she was in the unfamiliar position of leading 8-3.
"It was a good matchup for me style-wise. I didn't even know I was ahead in points. Everything was a blur. I just told myself, don't get pinned."
The whole gym started to buzz. Mascorella's teammates were on their feet, cheering her on. Davis' wrestler would get Mascorella on her back in a precarious position. The Davis team leaped to their feet, sensing a big moment, knowing a pin would give them the Title.
With only 30 seconds left, time seemed to stop. Mascorella would strain to keep her shoulder off the mat. You could see the determination on her sweat-covered face. Then, in one swift movement, she escaped, got to her knees and lay in exhaustion on her opponent just as time ran out and the whistle blew. She had won.
While Mascorella and her opponent were still on their knees, she embraced her opponent. They helped each other up and hugged again. It was an incredible moment of respect, humility, sportsmanship and friendship.
Her teammates watched as her hand was raised for the first time. Then, the celebration started in earnest. She was mobbed by her teammates and coaches.
When things settled down and most had left, Mascorella approached the trainer's table to help her friend get her injured ankle taped. They were cracking up over inside jokes about school. Mascorella's wrestling triumph had already left her mind, just as easily as the losses had. She was back to being a humble, supportive friend.
Sports give us so many wonderful moments and lessons. Wins and losses rarely tell the whole story. The lesson Mascorella teaches may even have been diminished by her winning. Competing for a team, making friends, and having joy despite losing are powerful. But winning will definitely make a better movie. Thanks, Lizzy.
Mascorella, now a senior, has been too busy with school to get back to wrestling practice. She received one of the highest scores in the country on the ASVAB test and, with the confidence she gained from wrestling, will join the Navy's Nuclear Program in June.

title: Explorit: Ida Noddack, working with the elements
author: Sara Thompson
description: Born in the Rhine region of Germany in 1896, Ida Tacke knew as she grew up she did not want to be a schoolteacher, and instead focused on being a
content:
Born in the Rhine region of Germany in 1896, Ida Tacke knew as she grew up she did not want to be a schoolteacher, and instead focused on being a researcher.

title: The Week that helps parents find the right school fit for their kids
author: News USA
description: (NewsUSA) - Fifteen years ago, when National School Choice Week began, the world of education looked very different. In some places, school choice options were slim, and many families wished
content:
(NewsUSA) - Fifteen years ago, when National School Choice Week began, the world of education looked very different. In some places, school choice options were slim, and many families wished there was more to explore as the festivities took place. Today, the school choice landscape is far more open, but with this growth comes complexity. This year from January 26 to February 1, the national celebration is more necessary than ever: families need help navigating a K-12 education system that is evolving rapidly.
The demand for school choice has surged in recent years. In the last 12 months, 6 in 10 parents considered new schools for their children, reflecting the growing awareness of school choice policies. Parents are talking about school choice more than ever and more likely to consider education options like microschooling, homeschooling, or private schools. No matter what type of school they choose - neighborhood public, charter, magnet, private, online, or micro - families increasingly believe that education is not one-size-fits-all.

content:

Monday's plea deal and felony conviction ends a criminal case that has dragged through the court system since 2017.

title: Commentary: Prioritize community needs
author: Margaret Cooney
description: We've all been Californians these last few weeks. I was born and raised there. My experiences as a firefighter reached from the coastal redwoods of Humboldt County to the Santa
content:
We've all been Californians these last few weeks. I was born and raised there. My experiences as a firefighter reached from the coastal redwoods of Humboldt County to the Santa Ana Fire Academy and Los Angeles County. My family and friends in Pasadena recently experienced one of the worst fires in California's history.
I've learned from my share of run-ins with extreme weather events that these disasters don't honor state borders or party lines. Political distractions won't help the people trying to rebuild their lives or safeguard their communities from the next disaster. We need to come together to protect as many people as possible — and that requires leadership that supports recovery efforts based on Americans' needs, not scoring political points.

In response to the growing call for energy solutions that prioritize both efficiency and sustainability, LG has established the ES Company, a new business division that leverages LG's HVAC expertise to deliver innovative solutions for a better future.

content:

title: Commentary: Make playgrounds for everyone
author: Tilly Griffiths
description: Growing up, playtime was my least favorite part of the school day.
content:

They hopped, skipped and chased one another across the playground, while I watched from the sidelines. The kingdom they built atop the plastic jungle gym was one I could never enter in my powered wheelchair.

title: Yolo County launches Community Climate Action Fund to support local sustainability projects
author: Special to the Enterprise
description: The Yolo County Sustainability Division is excited to announce the launch of the Yolo County Community Climate Action Fund, a new funding program designed to support local organizations in implementing
content:
The Yolo County Sustainability Division is excited to announce the launch of the Yolo County Community Climate Action Fund, a new funding program designed to support local organizations in implementing sustainability initiatives. This program is a key step in advancing the county's 2030 Climate Action and Adaptation Plan (CAAP), which was adopted by the Board of Supervisors in December 2024. The CAAP outlines a framework for achieving a countywide carbon-negative footprint by 2030 while ensuring an equitable and just transition for all communities.
The Community Climate Action Fund will provide $171,270 in funding to projects that advance Phase I CAAP actions, priority actions scheduled for implementation between 2025 and 2027. Eligible applicants, including Community-Based Organizations (CBOs), schools, tribal governments, and special districts based in and/or serving Yolo County can apply for funds ranging from $5,000 to $30,000 per project. Funded projects must advance the CAAP's goals by reducing greenhouse gas emissions, enhancing climate resilience, and/or fostering environmental sustainability throughout Yolo County communities. Preference will be given to projects serving communities in the unincorporated area.

title: Cabaldon introduces legislation to automatically admit high school seniors to CSUs
author: Special to the Enterprise
description: State Senator Christopher Cabaldon (D-Yolo) has introduced Senate Bill 640, to automatically admit qualified graduating high school seniors—without an application—to California State University campuses with enrollment capacity.
content:
State Senator Christopher Cabaldon (D-Yolo) has introduced Senate Bill 640, to automatically admit qualified graduating high school seniors—without an application—to California State University campuses with enrollment capacity.
The bill, co-authored by Assembly Majority Leader Cecilia Aguiar-Curry and Assemblymembers Damon Connolly and Chris Rogers, is modeled after the West Sacramento Home Run Program, which was featured as an exemplar in Nudge, the NYT bestseller by Nobel Prize winner Richard Thaler and Cass Sunstein, the nation's most-cited legal scholar, and discussed in both Bloomberg and Harvard publications. SB 640 also builds upon a successful local direct admissions pilot by CSU, making the pilot permanent and statewide, and extending it to eligible community college students as well.

title: Pence Gallery: Springing forward with social commentary
author: Natalie Nelson
description: Ronald Peetz is an artist who views art as a form of social engagement and is not shy about expressing his opinion. 'Work in Progress,' his first exhibit at the
content:
Ronald Peetz is an artist who views art as a form of social engagement and is not shy about expressing his opinion. 'Work in Progress,' his first exhibit at the Pence, offers commentary on everything from art making and creativity to environmental degradation and gun violence. His exhibit, sponsored by Helen Richardson, is on display through April 2 at the Pence.
In the exhibit, Peetz's work buzzes with references to other makers, such as René Magritte, a Belgian painter known for his surrealist compositions. Ronald's 'Self-portrait Wearing Magritte's Hat and Coat' is a ceramic depiction of him facing away from the viewer, looking into a round mirror. A rock has smashed the mirror and fractured his reflection into pieces.

title: Commentary: LLCs can hide shady business practices
author: Suzanne Dershowitz
description: In 2018, when I was a lawyer in the Oakland City Attorney's Office, a code enforcement inspector walked into my office and said, 'I have to tell you about something
content:
In 2018, when I was a lawyer in the Oakland City Attorney's Office, a code enforcement inspector walked into my office and said, 'I have to tell you about something that keeps me up at night.'

The city of Davis announced today that it recently purchased an agricultural conservation easement on 120 acres of farmland located about a half-mile from the city limits, northeast of the Mace Boulevard curve, as a permanent preserve for farmland and open space. The property is currently planted with almond trees.
The city will co-own the $960,000 agricultural conservation easement with the Yolo Land Trust that will monitor the easement in perpetuity on behalf of the city. The city and the Yolo Land Trust were both interested in protecting this land because of its proximity to the city limits, its location near other protected farmland and its prime agricultural soils. This is the second collaboration with the property owner, the Gill family, who previously sold an agricultural conservation easement on 124 acres northeast of Wildhorse to the city and the Yolo Land Trust in May of 2022.

title: 4 tips to ensure improved in-home water quality
author: Brandpoint
description: (BPT) - A new Global World Water Day Report from Culligan International found that 67% of North Americans are somewhat to significantly concerned about the impact of increasing pollution on
content:
(BPT) - A new Global World Water Day Report from Culligan International found that 67% of North Americans are somewhat to significantly concerned about the impact of increasing pollution on drinking water.* The report, focused on global water habits, found North Americans' concern about pollution is significantly higher than those residing in Australia (45%) and Europe, the Middle East and Africa (42%). Given that 72% of water consumption happens at home in North America, the world leader in water treatment is sharing four important steps homeowners can take to ensure the water in their home is cleaner, safer and fresher to drink:
1. Know where water contamination can occur. Water impurities are not limited to water sources; distribution systems can contaminate water after it has been treated by local municipalities and private wells. While many naturally occurring chemicals and impurities can be filtered at the source, additional contamination can occur in service pipes. These are commonly found in homes built prior to 1986 when lead pipes, fixtures and solder were regularly used.

title: What Families With College-Bound Students Need to Know This Spring
description: (StatePoint) Perhaps even more nerve-wracking than waiting for your child's college acceptance letters is learning whether they've been awarded financial aid. Recent changes to the Free Application for Federal Student
content:
(StatePoint) Perhaps even more nerve-wracking than waiting for your child's college acceptance letters is learning whether they've been awarded financial aid. Recent changes to the Free Application for Federal Student Aid (FAFSA) designed to simplify the process have led to unforeseen hiccups and technical glitches, causing academic institutions to delay sending out financial aid award letters. However, once you finally get the results, it can give your family a better idea of what to do next.
'Our research shows that for a majority of parents, figuring out how to pay for college was the ‘road to college' activity that caused them the most stress. By making a financial plan and prioritizing it, you can be well prepared to avoid the most common bumps in the road,' explains Angela Colatriano, chief marketing officer, College Ave.

title: Help Keep Kids Safe From Lithium Coin Batteries
description: (StatePoint) About 7,000 children in the United States visit emergency rooms for battery-related injuries each year, according to the National Electronic Injury Surveillance System. Lithium coin batteries, those small, disc-shaped
content:
(StatePoint) About 7,000 children in the United States visit emergency rooms for battery-related injuries each year, according to the National Electronic Injury Surveillance System. Lithium coin batteries, those small, disc-shaped batteries about the size of a nickel, are particularly dangerous. The exact right size to get lodged in a child's throat if accidentally swallowed, they can turn deadly, burning a hole in an esophagus in as little as two hours. And, they're everywhere – in key fobs, key finders, flameless candles, remote controls, thermometers and many common home devices.
Despite parents' thirst for knowledge on how to keep their children safe, the potential dangers of lithium coin batteries are not widely discussed. It's no surprise then that 55% of parents with children ages 6 and under don't realize that lithium coin batteries are more dangerous than button batteries – in fact 45% think there is no difference. That's according to a 2023 Duracell survey conducted by Wakefield Research. This is why the brand is reminding parents that when it comes to lithium coin batteries, #BitterIsBetter.

title: Pediatricians Can Help Teens Quit Vaping and Using Tobacco
description: (StatePoint) Tobacco use is the leading cause of preventable death and disease in the United States and it almost always begins during adolescence. According to leading medical advocates, pediatricians have
content:
(StatePoint) Tobacco use is the leading cause of preventable death and disease in the United States and it almost always begins during adolescence. According to leading medical advocates, pediatricians have a role to play in getting kids to quit vaping electronic cigarettes and using other tobacco products.
Ten percent of American students report using tobacco products, according to the FDA. And while there have been declines in the use of cigarettes among adolescents, the popularity of e-cigarettes and other smokeless tobacco and nicotine products is on the rise. Smoking and vaping are both harmful to health, particularly to youth, whose brains are still developing and who are uniquely vulnerable to nicotine dependence.

title: UCD researchers identify microbes that help plants thwart parasite
author: Liana Wait
description: Bacteria that could help one of Africa's staple crops resist a major pest have been identified by researchers at UC Davis. Their findings, published March 26 in Cell Reports, could
content:
Bacteria that could help one of Africa's staple crops resist a major pest have been identified by researchers at UC Davis. Their findings, published March 26 in Cell Reports, could improve yields of sorghum, a mainstay of food and drink in West and East African countries.
About 20 percent of Africa's sorghum crop is lost due to witchweed (Striga hermonthica), a parasitic plant that steals nutrients and water by latching onto the plant's roots.
In the new study, UC Davis researchers show that soil microbes induce changes in sorghum roots that make the plant more resistant to infection by witchweed. They identified specific strains of bacteria that trigger these resistance traits and could be applied as a soil 'probiotic' to improve sorghum yields in future.
'These microbes have great promise as soil additives that can help farmers grow sorghum successfully in sub-Saharan Africa,' said Siobhan Brady, a professor in the Department of Plant Biology and Genome Center and a senior author on the paper.
A witchy weed
Witchweed is a major issue for smallholder farmers in sub-Saharan Africa. The parasitic plants produce thousands of tiny seeds that can remain dormant in the soil for up to 20 years, making them extremely difficult to eradicate. Current control methods — which include applying chemical agents, crop rotation and breeding resistant sorghum — have achieved only partial control, and many are inaccessible to the farmers who need them most.
Postdoctoral scholar Dorota Kawa worked alongside Brady and collaborators in the Netherlands and Ethiopia to show that soil microbes can mitigate witchweed infections in sorghum.
'This is the first example showing how microbes can induce changes in host root cells that are associated with the suppression of witchweed,' said Brady.
Hijacking a plant signal
When sorghum plants find themselves in low-phosphate soil, they release chemicals from their roots to attract fungi that help them acquire phosphate. Unfortunately for sorghum, witchweed has evolved to respond to this same signal.
'This parasitic plant has hijacked the signaling so that its seeds germinate when they perceive that same signal from the root,' said Brady.
After germinating, witchweed responds to additional chemical cues from sorghum that trigger the parasite to grow appendages called 'haustoria' that enable it to latch on and penetrate the sorghum roots.
'Once it has made this connection with the sorghum vasculature, it's like a superhighway of nutrients to the parasitic plant,' said Brady.
Brady and Kawa wanted to know whether soil microbes could interrupt this hijacking. Previous studies have shown that a species of soil fungus, Fusarium, suppresses witchweed germination, and thus infection of sorghum, but little is known about whether soil bacteria or fungi suppress witchweed infections by changing the sorghum root.
As a first test, the researchers compared the susceptibility of sorghum seedlings that had been sprouted in 'natural' soil to seedlings grown in sterilized soil. They found that plants grown in natural soil had fewer witchweed hangers-on than those grown in sterilized soil, suggesting that bacteria play an important role in the plants' ability to resist infection.
Microbial mechanisms
Next, the team wanted to investigate the mechanisms behind this resistance. Using a combination of genetics, microscopy and in vitro experiments, they showed that microbes degrade the chemical cues that help witchweed attach to its host and also alter the sorghum's root anatomy to make it harder for witchweed to latch on. They observed that when sorghum plants are grown in natural, microbe-laden soil, the bacteria induce genes that result in a thicker layer of suberin, a waxy substance that may act as a barrier to witchweed, and more air-filled gaps or 'aerenchymas' that may also impede witchweed's attachment to sorghum.
Using genetic sequencing, Brady and her collaborators identified over 100 bacteria taxa that were associated with witchweed resistance. When they tested the functions of eight of these bacterial strains in vitro, they identified a strain of Pseudomonas bacteria that degrades chemical cues in the soil and a strain of Arthrobacter that increased root suberization in sorghum.
'It's exciting that we were able to identify individual microbes because typically you have a whole suite of microbes within the soil and it's possible that they're acting together,' said Brady.
Another tool in the toolkit
'The ultimate goal is to identify microbial solutions that farmers can treat the soil or seeds with to help prevent Striga infection,' Brady said. 'The intention is that this should be part of an integrated package of solutions to farmers—another tool in the toolkit.'
Now, the researchers are searching for microbes responsible for conferring other resistance traits. They're also characterizing soil microbes from other regions, beginning with Ethiopia, and investigating whether these same microbes can confer witchweed resistance to other crop species that are also impacted by the parasite.
'We need to make sure that we're using microbes that come from the country in which those microbes will be applied so that we maintain biodiversity,' said Brady. 'We also want to prioritize microbes that are able to work well in other crop species, like pearl millet and rice.'
Additional authors on the study are: Tamera Taylor, Hannah Vahldick, Zayan Musa, Alexander Chen and Jiregna Daksa, UC Davis; Desalegn Etalo, Utrecht University; Benjamin Thiombiano, Aimee Walmsley, Harro Bouwmeester, and Mario Schilder, Swammerdam Institute for Life; Mahdere Shimels, Dominika Rybka, Marcio Leite, Francisco Dini-Andreote, Eiko Kuramae and Jos Raaijmakers, Netherlands Institute of Ecology; Alexander Bucksch, University of Georgia; and Taye Tessema, Ethiopian Institute of Agricultural Research. Kawa is now an assistant professor at Utrecht University.
The work was supported by the Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation, the Howard Hughes Medical Institute, the Advanced Research Projects Agency–Energy and the National Science Foundation.

title: Doing this during your pregnancy can help protect both you AND your baby
author: Brandpoint
description: (BPT) - Many pregnant people are focused on protecting the health of themselves and their babies by seeking out trusted healthcare providers and activating support networks of friends and family.
content:
(BPT) - Many pregnant people are focused on protecting the health of themselves and their babies by seeking out trusted healthcare providers and activating support networks of friends and family. One important protection pregnant people can consider for themselves and their little ones is getting recommended vaccinations. Getting recommended vaccinations during pregnancy can be an important — and empowering — way to help protect the health of both pregnant people and their babies. It is important for pregnant people and their support networks to revisit the benefits of vaccination during pregnancy. Here are three reasons to consider:
About two weeks after a pregnant person gets a vaccination, their body creates antibodies (proteins that fight off diseases), and those antibodies can be passed on to babies. These antibodies increase protection, for both the pregnant person and their baby, against severe illness and complications caused by some infectious diseases, like whooping cough.
Pregnant people are at higher risk for having severe complications from infectious diseases (like flu) than people who are not pregnant. This may be due to changes in pregnant people's immune system and heart and lung functions. Vaccination helps increase protection for pregnant people.
Newborns do not have fully developed immune systems when they are born. Vaccination during pregnancy increases protection for newborns until they are old enough to receive their own vaccinations.

title: First 5 Yolo's Welcome Baby program celebrates successful first year

content:
First 5 Yolo is delighted to share the remarkable achievements of its "Welcome Baby" program in its inaugural year. This initiative, offered free of charge and on a voluntary basis, has received support for three years with funding from Yolo County's American Rescue Plan Act funds.

title: Letter: Unequal treatment
author: Letter to the Editor
description: I read that a majority of Davis City Council continues to support the I-80 freeway widening with a toll lane.
content:
I read that a majority of Davis City Council continues to support the I-80 freeway widening with a toll lane.
I thought Davis values were about treating everyone the same regardless of income. But new lane will be viable toll lane. Thought it will be paid equally by everyone's gas tax money, it is being designed to gives the rich preference by auctioning off the new road capacity to the highest bidder as a so called 'managed lane.'

title: Police warn of ‘skimmer' credit-card thievery
author: Lauren Keene
description: Law-enforcement officials in Yolo County are warning residents to be aware of an increase in use of credit-card skimmers — oftentimes undetectable devices that thieves use to steal credit-card information.
content:
Law-enforcement officials in Yolo County are warning residents to be aware of an increase in use of credit-card skimmers — oftentimes undetectable devices that thieves use to steal credit-card information.
How it works: The skimmers, placed directly over card readers at locations such as ATMs and gas pumps, scan and store credit card data from the magnetic stripe.

title: UCD celebrates iconic eggheads
author: Monica Stark
description: The eggs that never spoil and crack or that are hard to find — the Eggheads on the UC Davis campus — have captured the hearts of the campus community
content:
The eggs that never spoil and crack or that are hard to find — the Eggheads on the UC Davis campus — have captured the hearts of the campus community for 30 years, the same amount of time their creator taught at UC Davis.
Since 1991, the bronze sculpted Eggheads have piqued curiosity and set the stage for photo ops and campus tour stops. There's Bookhead at Shields Library, Stargazer at Dutton Hall, Eye on Mrak (Fatal Laff) just north of the chancellor's office and See No Evil/Hear No Evil, just south of it, while Yin & Yang sit near the art building and Wright Hall.

title: Commentary: Fairfield tree tragedy
author: Richard L. Wood
description: OK, in the scope of current events, 'tragedy' is an exaggeration, but I couldn't resist the alliteration. I wish to discuss something locally tragic that we are better able to
content:
OK, in the scope of current events, 'tragedy' is an exaggeration, but I couldn't resist the alliteration. I wish to discuss something locally tragic that we are better able to do something about: City beautification. And street trees are a big part of that.
City beautification is the responsibility of our Public Works Department. They keep the city 'clean, green, and safe' by eradicating graffiti, picking up litter, controlling weeds, cleaning up illegal encampments, maintaining public buildings, streets, parks and landscaping, and more. If you care about city beautification and livability, support Public Works.

title: California salmon fishing banned for second year in row
author: Rachel Becker
description: In a devastating blow to California's fishing industry, federal fishery managers unanimously voted today to cancel all commercial and recreational salmon fishing off the coast of California for the second
content:
In a devastating blow to California's fishing industry, federal fishery managers unanimously voted today to cancel all commercial and recreational salmon fishing off the coast of California for the second year in a row.
The decision is designed to protect California's dwindling salmon populations after drought and water diversions left river flows too warm and sluggish for the state's iconic Chinook salmon to thrive.
Salmon abundance forecasts for the year 'are just too low,' Marci Yaremko, the California Department of Fish and Wildlife's appointee to the Pacific Fishery Management Council, said last week. 'While the rainfall and the snowpacks have improved, the stocks and their habitats just need another year to recover.'
State and federal agencies are now expected to implement the closures for ocean fishing. Had the season not been in question again this year, recreational boats would likelyalready be fishing off the coast of California, while the commercial season typically runs from May through October.
In addition, the California Fish and Game Commission will decide next month whether to cancel inland salmon fishing in California rivers this summer and fall.
The closure means that California restaurants and consumers will have to look elsewhere for salmon, in a major blow to an industry estimated in previous years to be worth roughly half a billion dollars.
'It's catastrophic,' said Tommy 'TF' Graham, a commercial fisherman based in Bodega Bay who now drives a truck delivering frozen and farmed salmon and other fish. 'It means another summer of being forced to do something you don't want to do, instead of doing something you love.'
About 213,600 Sacramento River fall-run salmon — a mainstay of the fishery — are estimated to be swimming off the coast. Though that's an improvement over last year, the forecast remains the second-lowest on record since the fishery was closed in 2008 and 2009, Yaremko told the Pacific fishery council.
The numbers this year, plus the fact that the forecasts for salmon returning to spawn are routinely overestimated, 'add concern,' Yaremko said.
Many in the fishing industry say they support the closure, but urged state and federal officials to do more to improve conditions in the rivers salmon rely on. Fishing advocates and environmentalists have lambasted Gov. Gavin Newsom's administration for failing to prioritize water quality and flows to protect salmon in the vital Bay-Delta watershed.
'Our fishing fleets and coastal communities can not be the only ones making sacrifices to save these fish,' said Sarah Bates, who owns a commercial fishing boat called the Bounty, berthed at Fisherman's Wharf in San Francisco. 'Water policy needs to take the health of our river ecosystems seriously.'
The closure comes as the fishing industry still awaits disaster aid promised from last year's salmon fishery closures, which state officials estimated to have cost about $45 million. The fishing industry says that's a vast underestimate.
'Some fishermen have already lost their businesses and many will in the coming months,' said RJ Waldron, who runs a charter fishing business out of the East Bay. Last year's closure dried up his customers, and he put his sportfishing boat up for sale months ago.
'My dream of being a charter boat owner is very much a nightmare now.'

title: Pat Tillman. 20 Years. One Legacy.
author: Pat Tillman Foundation
description: Nearly 30,000 People Ran or Walked 4.2 Miles to Honor Pat Tillman
content:
Nearly 30,000 People Ran or Walked 4.2 Miles to Honor Pat Tillman
TEMPE, Ariz., April 13, 2024 /PRNewswire/ -- Jake Plummer, former Arizona State University and Cardinals quarterback, joined by the 1996 - 1997 Rose Bowl team and the Pat's Run co-founders, kicked off the 20th Pat's Run this morning, presented by TEKsystems. Nearly 30,000 runners and walkers came together to honor the legacy of Pat Tillman. Hosted at Mountain America Stadium, home of the ASU Sun Devils in Tempe, the annual run extends globally through national ASU Alumni-hosted Honor Runs, overseas troop runs, and virtual runners. It has become more than a run for participants; it is viewed as an annual family reunion for some, a physical challenge for others, and a way to give back for all. Proceeds from the event are invested in the nearly 900 Tillman Scholars who are inspired to make an impact. To date, the Pat Tillman Foundation has raised $34M to support the Tillman Scholars. To learn more and support, visit www.ptf.org.

title: Tri-City Cardiology's Ambulatory Surgical Center (ASC) Leads the Way in Revolutionizing Heart Failure Management
author: Tri-City Cardiology
description: MESA, Ariz., April 12, 2024 /PRNewswire/ -- In the ongoing battle against heart failure, continuous monitoring stands as a beacon of hope. Among the array of innovative solutions, the CardioMEMS™
content: MESA, Ariz., April 12, 2024 /PRNewswire/ -- In the ongoing battle against heart failure, continuous monitoring stands as a beacon of hope. Among the array of innovative solutions, the CardioMEMS™ HF System shines brightly, offering a groundbreaking approach to managing this debilitating condition. Imagine a world where patients can receive crucial heart failure management in the comfort of an outpatient setting, such as an Ambulatory Surgical Center (ASC). This vision is now a reality, with Tri-City Cardiology's ASC at the forefront of this medical revolution. Access to cutting-edge technology is key in reshaping the landscape of heart failure management. The CardioMEMS HF System embodies this shift, offering a minimally invasive procedure that provides real-time monitoring of pulmonary artery pressure—a vital metric in tracking heart failure progression.

title: Pneumococcal Pneumonia Vaccination Can Save Your Life
description: (StatePoint) Pneumococcal pneumonia is a potentially serious bacterial lung disease that can disrupt a person's life for weeks. When severe, it can result in hospitalization and even be life threatening.
content:
(StatePoint) Pneumococcal pneumonia is a potentially serious bacterial lung disease that can disrupt a person's life for weeks. When severe, it can result in hospitalization and even be life threatening. Each year, pneumococcal pneumonia results in an estimated 150,000 hospitalizations in the United States, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). But it doesn't have to be this way.
The American Lung Association and Pfizer are partnering to raise awareness about pneumococcal pneumonia and encourage adults to get vaccinated if they are eligible. During World Immunization Week -- April 24 to 30 -- they are highlighting the collective action needed to reduce the burden of pneumococcal pneumonia.

content:

Whether you're renovating your current property, planning a complete transformation, or starting fresh with a custom build, use these tips and design elements to get started.
• Embrace Seamless Indoor-Outdoor Living: Create a seamless transition between indoor and outdoor spaces by incorporating features like bi-fold doors or expansive sliding glass doors that open onto a patio or courtyard. This continuous flow enhances your living experience and sets the stage for a resort-like ambiance.

title: Spring Home and Garden: Outdoor living for health and happiness
author: Penny Lorain
description: Davis and our surrounding communities are ideal for outdoor living this time of year. The mild weather and longer days beckon us to spend time outdoors nearly every day, whether
content:
Davis and our surrounding communities are ideal for outdoor living this time of year. The mild weather and longer days beckon us to spend time outdoors nearly every day, whether relaxing, cooking or enjoying a meal.

title: YoloCares: The Perfect Visit
author: Craig Dresang
description: In the pursuit of YoloCares' mission, to provide the highest quality of care to every patient, every family, every time, the agency underwent a re-evaluation of clinical practices in 2022.
content:
In the pursuit of YoloCares' mission, to provide the highest quality of care to every patient, every family, every time, the agency underwent a re-evaluation of clinical practices in 2022.
With each patient's experience at the heart of the reassessment, YoloCares collaborated with high-quality hospice providers across the country to perfect the structure and character of patient visits. By leaning on expertise of the best, most highly rated, hospice and palliative care providers from coast to coast, YoloCares developed a training strategy for clinicians that focused on human connection, respect, and compassion.

title: Chancell-ing: A town-gown partnership like no other
author: Chancellor Gary S. May
description: This month, I've invited a special guest to join me in writing this column. Josh Chapman was appointed as the mayor of Davis in January 2024, but I've known him
content:
This month, I've invited a special guest to join me in writing this column. Josh Chapman was appointed as the mayor of Davis in January 2024, but I've known him for years through his service on the Davis City Council. In the spirit of partnership, we wanted to express our commitment to maintaining the strongest possible town-gown relationship between UC Davis and the City, along with sharing what you can expect in the upcoming months.
Davis is California's ultimate college town and known for many things, including bikes and Eggheads. But it's our shared commitment to a strong partnership, along with our shared belief in the strength of community, especially in the face of adversity, which truly sets us apart. We are proud that for more than a century, the City of Davis and UC Davis remain so well connected. Today, we reflect on recent milestones and prospective possibilities.

title: Bexi Lobo: How to read an ingredient list and why it matters

content:
A skincare product's ingredient list enables you to read between the marketing lines and gauge whether you can trust a brand. It also helps you get the biggest bang for your buck.
The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) requires that the ingredient list be prominent, conspicuous, and easy to read and understand by ordinary people ([§ 701.3(d)], [§ 701.3(f)(2)]). The ingredients have to be listed in descending order of predominance.

title: Mercury Insurance Expert Offers Tips to Avoid Becoming a Victim of Insurance Fraud
author: Brandpoint
description: (BPT) - While inflation continues to drive up home and auto insurance costs, fraud is a hidden culprit contributing to the hikes. Whether you're an actual victim of insurance fraud
content:
(BPT) - While inflation continues to drive up home and auto insurance costs, fraud is a hidden culprit contributing to the hikes. Whether you're an actual victim of insurance fraud or simply an active policyholder, the reality is that insurance fraud impacts everyone. And as the frequency and complexity of fraudulent activities increase, so does the cost of insurance for all policyholders.
What exactly is insurance fraud? It's a deliberately deceptive act with the goal of receiving a wrongful payout from an insurance process. It can be committed by applicants, policyholders, third parties or even the insurance providers themselves — and it affects virtually every type of insurance including auto and homeowners.

content:
In the relentless battle against wildfires in California, it's clear that agencies and landowners must prioritize and implement wildfire prevention measures while continuing to build and maintain firefighting resources.

If strategically placed, these areas of reduced vegetation can slow the spread of wildfires, buying wildland firefighters more time to get ahead of rapidly developing wildfires.

title: Commentary: City piles insult on injury
author: Elaine Roberts Musser
description: I want to thank the Davis Enterprise for its excellent coverage in regard to the issue of merging city commissions. Had the reporter Rebecca Wasik not thoroughly covered this matter,
content:
I want to thank the Davis Enterprise for its excellent coverage in regard to the issue of merging city commissions. Had the reporter Rebecca Wasik not thoroughly covered this matter, it would have flown under the radar screen.
I am sorry to say the City Council made the decision to approve the mergers. (Councilwoman Donna Neville was unable to attend the City Council meeting, so took no part in the decision.)
What problem exactly was the City Council trying to solve? Never were City Council members specific about what allegedly 'wasn't working' in commissions, so commissioners could try to correct any perceived difficulties. Instead the Subcommittee on Commissions (Mayor Josh Chapmand and Vice Mayor Bapu Vaitla) kept the accusations purposely vague, so there was no way for commissioners to defend themselves.
In law, there is something known as the 'vagueness doctrine', which rests on the due process clauses of the 5th and 14th Amendments of the U.S. Constitution. 'By requiring fair notice of what is punishable and what is not, the vagueness doctrine helps prevent arbitrary enforcement of the laws.' Arbitrary enforcement is precisely what the City Council engaged in when approving the merging of commissions.
Because of this questionable process by the Subcommittee on Commissions, a petition was circulated, in which 159 citizens (21 of them current or former commissioners/City Council members) asked the City Council to immediately reverse moving forward with merging commissions.
Instead, Vaitla and Chapman doubled down, refusing to appoint any applicants to vacancies for more than a year, causing quorum problems. As a result, it appears the Finance & Budget Commission had been unable to meet for 9 months, the Senior Citizens Commission folded, and 6 commission meetings were cancelled in May.
Because of the FBC being put out of commission (pardon the pun), the city budget has had no citizen oversight for almost a year. Nor has the city had a financial audit for three years. City budget reserves have plummeted from $21 million to a mere $6 million in the last two years, according to the latest staff report.
How much confidence will taxpayers have to approve any tax measure proposed by this City Council, after the wanton destruction of the Finance & Budget Commission? Or was the purpose of destroying this particular commission to cut down on citizen oversight of the dire circumstances actually going on with city finances? (Citizen oversight can be a pesky nuisance when things aren't going well.)
So I have resigned my position as a commissioner on the Utilities Commission in disgust. I want no part of the newly formed Fiscal Commission (a merger between the Utilities Commission and the Finance & Budget Commission). Why would I want to remain after being told by Vaitla that commissions are dysfunctional, don't give information the City Council wants, and commissioners are somehow 'privileged'? The vote in favor of the merged commissions in effect says the City Council that approved the mergers agreed with this disparaging viewpoint.
That is incredibly disrespectful and disappointing. And I would remind the City Council it was they who appointed those supposedly 'privileged and useless' commissioners, and it is Vaitla and Chapman who made a number of commissions dysfunctional and severely restricted their missions.
And why should I be part of a merged commission requiring me to start all over the lengthy process of getting the commission up to speed, accompanied with: a heavier workload; twice as much ground to cover in subject matter I am not familiar with; longer meetings; and far less attention to critical matters?
I already went through that grueling process with the Utilities Commission, which took 10 years to become the well-oiled machine it was. I have devoted more than 20 years and thousands of volunteer hours to this city (I was voted Davis Citizen of the Year in 2014), as have many other commissioners, and this is the thanks we are to receive?
Apparently at least one commissioner was told he had suddenly 'termed out' of his former position as a commissioner, so could not be on the newly merged commission. How does one 'term out' of a newly formed commission before it even starts?
At least four other commissioners I know have also resigned. That is a lot of institutional knowledge walking out the door. And while the current members of the City Council who approved the merger pay lip service to supposedly wanting to 'improve' commissions and increase citizen participation, instead their actions have done the exact opposite.
By cutting out several commissions, they have eliminated a number of positions for citizens to take part in local governance. So how the heck has their 'solution' been a change for the better? A great quote by the writer Charlton Ogburn Jr. sums up the the current state of affairs nicely: '...we tend ... to meet any situation by reorganizing; and a wonderful method it can be for creating the illusion of progress while producing confusion, inefficiency, and demoralization.'

title: Almost Two-Thirds of Home Fires Are Due to Human Error. Here's How to Prepare

content:
(StatePoint) The threat of a home fire is greater than most people think. In fact, 40% of people believe they are more likely to win the lottery or get struck by lightning than experience a home fire, yet residential fires are the most common disaster people face in the United States, according to the American Red Cross. Here's how to help prevent fires, and how to prepare for the worst:
Be Informed: The National Fire Protection Association reports that 60% of home fires are due to human error. It's important to realize that humans are flawed. We forget things, we mess up, and we're often distracted. Accepting the fact that a house fire is a real possibility is an important step in the right direction. There are simple actions you can take to help prevent accidents. For starters, cooking is the leading cause of house fires. Never leave cooking unattended. Keep the cooking area free of flammable items such as potholders, towels and packaging, and always maintain a 3-foot safety zone free of pets and kids.

title: Little League all-stars begin tournament play
author: Alessandra Trask
description: VACAVILLE — The Davis Little League American 12s team played their first game in the District 64 All Stars tournament on Monday. In only three innings Davis quickly shut down
content:
VACAVILLE — The Davis Little League American 12s team played their first game in the District 64 All Stars tournament on Monday. In only three innings Davis quickly shut down the Woodland American All Stars to run-rule them 15-0.
Davis was the home team, Logan Wallace started on the mound. Throwing only 10 pitches in the first inning Wallace struck out the side in order.
By rule, if a pitcher throws more than 20 pitches in a game, they require one day of rest, if over 35 pitches two days rest and so on. In a double- elimination tournament with games nearly every day, that leaves the coaches to make strategic decisions on who to pitch, when and how long.
The Davis offense forced four walks and with singles from Wallace and Charlie Teague they rallied to score four runs in the home half of the first to take the lead. Under pressure, Woodland changed their pitcher, as his pitch count began to go into the 30s.
Three up and three down for Davis again in the second inning. Wallace struck out two more batters, finishing the last batter right on the number leaving their ace available for the next game.
With two outs and the bases empty, Davis would rally again in the second inning, scoring eight runs. The big blows were home runs by Wallace and Sam Adams to make the score 12-0. Singles by Reid Forward, Pete Prussel and a double by Teague would contribute to the big inning.
Alexander Ewers gets put in to close the game for Davis. With three consecutive strikeouts he successfully helps Davis shut Woodland out.
With hits by Milo Zicari, Evan Abrams and Forward, combined with two walks, and one hit by pitch Davis scored their 15th run to end the game by run rule. Beating Woodland 15-0 Davis will continue their path in the winners bracket.
It was clear that their offensive game was on but what was just as important was their defense. 'As great as our bats were, our battery was even better,' head coach Kermit Kruse told The Enterprise.
Both Wallace and Ewers pitched efficiently, leaving them open to pitch in the next game for Davis without restriction.
The game was short and sweet and Davis got a lot done. 'We had 10 hits tonight and seven walks in only three innings, we smashed,' Kruse told The Enterprise.

title: Per Capita: How we got to where we are

content:
My friend Michael gifted me a copy of 'Hothouse Earth', a small, short, succinct book that walks the reader through what the author, Bill McGuire, considers where we are now in terms of the climate crisis and where we are, in his view, likely to be in the near future.
So, two things to begin with. First, terminology. McGuire substitutes the term 'global heating' for the more comforting but less accurate term 'global warming.' Similarly, he argues that the term 'climate change' does not adequately express the 'rapidly increasing incidences of extreme weather'. He instead adopts the term 'climate breakdown' and indicates that both replacement terms better reflect reality and are coming into general usage.

title: Supreme Court gives cities more power to crack down on homeless camps
author: Marisa Kendall
description: The U.S. Supreme Court today granted cities more power to arrest, cite and fine people who sleep outside in public places — overturning six years of legal protections for homeless
content:
The U.S. Supreme Court today granted cities more power to arrest, cite and fine people who sleep outside in public places — overturning six years of legal protections for homeless residents in California and other western states.
In Grants Pass v. Johnson, the court sided with Grants Pass in a 6-3 decision, ruling that an ordinance passed by the Oregon city that essentially made it illegal for homeless residents to camp on all public property was not unconstitutional. Justices Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan and Ketanji Brown Jackson — all Democratic appointees — dissented.

title: Commentary: Credit cards can cope with reform
