description: A recent analysis of the 500 U.S. corporations generating the most profit per employee found investment firms, energy companies and Big Tech dominating the list — reporting extraordinary profits with
content:
A recent analysis of the 500 U.S. corporations generating the most profit per employee found investment firms, energy companies and Big Tech dominating the list — reporting extraordinary profits with relatively small workforces. Also high on the list: banks and financial institutions, which is particularly timely given that companies like Visa and Mastercard have been pleading poverty in response to recent legislation in Congress that would curb their ability to raise junk fees on retailers and consumers.
According to the research compiled by 24-7 Wall Street, Visa is the 21st-most profitable company per employee, recording $600,000 in profit for every worker. Mastercard, meanwhile, came in at No. 41, generating nearly $355,000 in profit per employee.

title: Padilla announces funding for zero-emission buses
author: Enterprise staff
description: WASHINGTON — Sen. Alex Padilla, D-Calif., on Tuesday announced that the Department of Transportation awarded more than $233.9 million to 16 California projects to help transition to low- and zero-emission
content:
WASHINGTON — Sen. Alex Padilla, D-Calif., on Tuesday announced that the Department of Transportation awarded more than $233.9 million to 16 California projects to help transition to low- and zero-emission bus models across the state.
The funding comes through the Federal Transit Agency's Low or No Emission (Low-No) grant program and Grants for Buses and Bus Facilities program. Padilla supported the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law's substantial increase in funding for these programs.
The Low-No program helps transit agencies buy or lease U.S.-made low- or no-emission buses and make critical facility, station, and charging upgrades to facilitate this transition. The Grants for Buses and Bus Facilities program provides federal funding for transit agencies to buy and rehabilitate buses and vans and build and modernize bus facilities.
'For too long, communities along busy transit corridors — especially lower income communities — have felt the impact of poor air quality,' said Senator Padilla. 'This substantial investment in the transition to low- and zero-emission buses will protect public health and promote a cleaner commute for millions of Californians. The Bipartisan Infrastructure Law is not only building a more sustainable, dependable transportation system, but also building the workforce needed to deploy modern technology.'
Recipients of funding from the Low-No and Grants for Buses and Bus Facilities programs include the city of Davis, which will receive $1.6 million to build infrastructure and buy charging equipment to support Unitrans' battery-electric bus fleet.
'Due to the funds being from the Federal Transit Administration, we had to apply on behalf of Unitrans,' Jenny Tan, the city's director of community engagement, said. 'We will act as a passthrough for the funds."
The equipment will allow the agency to continue to maintain safe and reliable public transit service to UC Davis and throughout the community.
The Sacramento Regional Transit District will receive $76.85 million. This funding will help SacRT buy new hydrogen fuel cell buses to replace older buses, modernize a maintenance facility and initiate a workforce development program. The project will create jobs and improve service, reliability, and air quality as SacRT works to convert its fleet to entirely zero emission by 2028.
The full list of awards for California is available here.

title: CalMatters Commentary: Prison workers excluded from heat rules
author: Anastasia Christman
description: California's workplace safety board recently approved an indoor heat protection standard and urged Cal/OSHA to put it into full effect as quickly as possible. Nearly two decades after the state's
content:
California's workplace safety board recently approved an indoor heat protection standard and urged Cal/OSHA to put it into full effect as quickly as possible. Nearly two decades after the state's outdoor workers won heat protections, millions of California's indoor workers will finally also be protected.
Tragically, this victory for workers must be tempered by the callous decision to cut out more than 100,000 workers from its scope. Corrections workers and detainees who labor in California's hundreds of jails and prisons, often enduring brutal and suffocating heat, must continue to wait.

description: The Winters Friends of the Library 2023 Summer Concerts at the Gazebo conclude with Welcome West (formerly Mandolin Manny) playing modern bluegrass on Thursday, July 25, from 7 to 8:30
content:
The Winters Friends of the Library 2023 Summer Concerts at the Gazebo conclude with Welcome West (formerly Mandolin Manny) playing modern bluegrass on Thursday, July 25, from 7 to 8:30 p.m. at Rotary Park, Main Street at Railroad Avenue in downtown Winters.
Their sound is steeped in tradition while pushing the boundaries of the string band format and dipping into the many influences of their eclectic collective of musicians. They play originals, traditional standards, and classic favorites re-imagined through a bluegrass lens, all with high energy, tight vocal harmonies, and with a virtuosic instrumental prowess. Learn more at welcomewestband.com.

title: Police Accountability Commission explores Facial Recognition Technology ban
author: Rebecca Wasik
description: According to the United States Department of Homeland Security, Facial Recognition Technology is 'a contemporary security solution that automatically identifies and verifies the identity of an individual from a digital
content:
According to the United States Department of Homeland Security, Facial Recognition Technology is 'a contemporary security solution that automatically identifies and verifies the identity of an individual from a digital image or video frame.'
While an increasing number of law enforcement agencies across the country are implementing this technology, the Davis Police Accountability Commission has passed a proposed draft ordinance asking the City Council to ban the use of FRT by the city.

title: Give your aging wood deck a composite makeover
author: Brandpoint
description: (BPT) - Of the more than 60 million decks in the U.S., it is estimated that 50% are 'past their useful life' and in need of repair or replacement, according
content:
(BPT) - Of the more than 60 million decks in the U.S., it is estimated that 50% are 'past their useful life' and in need of repair or replacement, according to a report by the North American Decking and Railing Association (NADRA). If yours is among them, consider this. As long as your substructure is in good shape, resurfacing the walking surface with high-performance composite can be a simple way to breathe new life into your deck, requiring about the same amount of time and energy as resurfacing with wood. And, you'll never have to stain your deck again.
Composite decking, like Trex ®, has gained popularity among today's homeowners who relish not having to sand, stain or seal the surface every year and who appreciate the eco-friendly nature of the material, which is made from mostly recycled and reclaimed materials. Better yet, with a little know-how and a few standard tools, even a novice DIYer can install it.

There are 39 nations with populations over a million that are high-income income according to the World Bank and free according to Freedom House. If we count the years that each nation has qualified as both free and high-income and add each nation's years, we get a total of between one and two thousand years.

author: Letter to The Editor
description: At Burning Man, we have a term for people who ride bikes in total darkness without lights, wearing dark clothing: "Darkwads."
content:
At Burning Man, we have a term for people who ride bikes in total darkness without lights, wearing dark clothing: "Darkwads."
I may have to stop driving downtown, on Russell, or on Sycamore after sunset. Too many Darkwads on bikes and scooters. Last night I only noticed a moving cyclist on Sycamore from the glow of their smartphone screen, which lit up their face as they gazed into it.

title: Novel vaccine offers hope for cancer
author: Monica Stark
description: Fighting Stage 4 breast cancer, a Davis mother of three and a literature and social justice professor at Cosumnes River Community College, Danielle Heard Mollel, recently qualified for a clinical
content:
Fighting Stage 4 breast cancer, a Davis mother of three and a literature and social justice professor at Cosumnes River Community College, Danielle Heard Mollel, recently qualified for a clinical trial with Orbis Health Solutions for a vaccine that uses a person's tumor cells to stimulate their immune system and fight the cancer itself like an infection.
Diagnosed in spring 2023, and despite a double mastectomy, chemotherapy, and hormone therapy, recent tests show the cancer is progressing, and she will need a novel treatment plan to beat it, explains her friend Allison Pedrazzi, who has known Heard Mollel since their kids were in kindergarten together, about four years ago.

title: City of Davis offers predesigned ADU plans
author: Special to the Enterprise
description: The city of Davis announced Wednesday that predesigned accessory dwelling unit (ADU) plans, that have already been pre-approved by the city's Building Department, are available for free to help speed
content:
The city of Davis announced Wednesday that predesigned accessory dwelling unit (ADU) plans, that have already been pre-approved by the city's Building Department, are available for free to help speed up the building approval process and lower costs to Davis homeowners who are looking to build ADUs on their property.
Three ADU size plans are available: a 300-square-foot studio, a 565-square-foot, one-bedroom unit and a 740-square-foot two-bedroom unit. Each ADU size is available in three different architectural styles: Adobe (Pueblo-style housing), Agrarian (farmhouse style) and Mid-Mod (mid-century modern style), creating nine different plans in total. The plans also provide some customizable features like lighting and window and door types. After a consultation with the City's Planning Department and starting the building permit process, homeowners will receive the plans for their preferred options, free of charge. Property owners (or contractors hired by the property owner) are responsible for the final preparation of the plans and paying for a building permit.

title: Manetti Shrem Museum kicks off fall season with new commissions
author: Laura Compton
description: Exhibitions featuring new sculpture and installation commissions, paintings from world-renowned artists, and large-scale ceramics debut this fall at the Jan Shrem and Maria Manetti Shrem Museum of Art at UC
content:
Exhibitions featuring new sculpture and installation commissions, paintings from world-renowned artists, and large-scale ceramics debut this fall at the Jan Shrem and Maria Manetti Shrem Museum of Art at UC Davis.
'Phillip Byrne, Beatriz Cortez, Kang Seung Lee, Candice Lin: Entangled Writing' opens Aug. 8. Four California artists working in sculpture and installation each present a new installation — the largest group of works the Manetti Shrem Museum has commissioned to date. The exhibition explores the way that people and objects move across time and space, allowing for multiple potentialities to exist. The exhibition ends Dec. 29.
'' Entangled Writing' grew out of early conversations between Beatriz Cortez and Phillip Byrne, and builds upon existing relationships between Cortez, Lee and Lin,' said Susie Kantor, associate curator and exhibitions department head. 'The resulting exhibition opens a portal to new and imagined worlds, allowing us to envision different futures and shine a light in difficult times.'
In the planning stages since 2022, Entangled Writing features artists making a splash on the international arts scene: Cortez, a UC Davis faculty member whose works are in the current Venice Biennale, along with those of Lee, and Lin, who was in 2022's biennale.
'Entangled Writing': About the artists
Phillip Byrne was raised in California's Central Valley and lives and works in Los Angeles. He views life as built upon multispecies collaborations and relationships between different types of matter. His project began with telecommunication cables found in a scrapyard in the Loire Valley, France.
Byrne envisions the past and future lives of the cast-aside cables as portals to other worlds. From underwater symbiosis between animals and cables to birds nesting in telecommunication wires above the ground, he explores the many possibilities these cables engender. He holds a B.A. in Studio Art from California State University, Stanislaus, and an M.F.A. from UC Davis in Studio Art (2022).
Beatriz Cortez is a multidisciplinary artist and sculptor who lives and works in Los Angeles and Davis. She joined the UC Davis faculty as associate professor of art in fall 2023. Her work explores life in different times and states of being as a way to imagine possible different futures. ' Adrift In A Mirrored Sea (Hansbukta)' brings together research on the history of whaling, the self-organizing architecture of icebergs, and the volcanic eruption of Ilopango in what is now El Salvador.
These interconnected constellations speak to global histories and worlds beyond the human scale. Ilopango, a work from her recent solo show ' Beatriz Cortez: The Volcano that Left' at Storm King Art Center, New York (2023), is currently on view through Nov. 10 in ' Future Dreaming … A Path Forward' at Montalvo Arts Center in Saratoga. She received an M.F.A. in art from the California Institute of the Arts and a Ph.D. in Literature and Cultural Studies from Arizona State University.
Kang Seung Lee is a multidisciplinary artist who was born in South Korea and now lives and works in Los Angeles. His work frequently engages the legacy of transnational queer histories, particularly as they intersect with art history. Skin focuses on 80-year-old queer dancer and performer Meg Harper. Through muscle memory, gestures and a magnified view of their skin, Lee honors Harper's own long-lived practice as well as the many artists and activists in Harper's extended queer community, linking those who may not have overlapped in life but are able to do so in the space of his work. Lee has also been included in ' Made in LA' at Hammer Museum, Los Angeles (2023); and in several recent solo exhibitions and projects, including National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art, Seoul (2023), Vincent Price Art Museum, Los Angeles (2023) and Gallery Hyundai, Seoul (2021). He received an M.F.A. from California Institute of the Arts (2015).
Candice Lin is based in Los Angeles and is an assistant professor of art at the University of California, Los Angeles. She works with installation, drawing, video and living materials and processes. Her work deals with the politics of representation and issues of race, gender and sexuality through histories of colonialism and diaspora. Lin's work in ' Entangled Writing' begins with the loss of a dear friend and mentor processed through a dream and a parable and takes the form of a round, rotating sculpture filled with ceramic, wood and metal objects reflecting loss, desire and the disintegration of the body. Lin's recent solo exhibitions include ' Candice Lin: The Sex Life of Stone,' at Monash University Museum of Art, Australia, through Sept. 7, and ' Seeping, Rotting, Resting, Weeping,' which started Walker Art Center, Minneapolis (2021), then traveled to Carpenter Center for the Visual Arts, Harvard, and Berkeley Art Museum and Pacific Film Archive, Berkeley (2022). Lin received her B.A. in visual arts and semiotics from Brown University (2001) and M.F.A. in New Genres from San Francisco Art Institute (2004).
Two more exhibitions open in September
Rounding out the fall season, ' Light into Density: Abstract Encounters 1920s–1960s | From the Collection of Jan Shrem and Maria Manetti Shrem,' and 'Ritual Clay: Cathy Lu, Paz G, Maryam Yousif' both open on Sept. 19. An official public opening day featuring artists and curators takes place at the museum Sunday, Sept. 29. More event details and exhibition information will be announced soon.
'Light into Density: Abstract Encounters 1920s–1960s' is the museum's first student-curated and student-designed exhibition. Most of the 15 paintings — including profound and exhilarating works by Francis Bacon, Salvador Dalí, Vassily Kandinsky and Joan Miró — are shown together for the first time. The works come from the collection of art lovers and philanthropists Jan Shrem and Maria Manetti Shrem, and are a shared gift between the Manetti Shrem Museum and SFMOMA. (On view Sept. 19, 2024–May 5, 2025)
'Ritual Clay: Cathy Lu, Paz G, Maryam Yousif' features three contemporary Bay Area ceramicists with a shared interest in clay who explore how their identities and experiences intersect with themes of immigration, ethnicity, race and gender in 21st century America. For Cathy Lu, Paz G and Maryam Yousif, clay is a link to the past and a conduit of cultural knowledge. (On view Sept. 19–Dec. 29)
New public hours
The Manetti Shrem Museum reopens Thursday, Aug. 8, with new hours. The public hours are 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday and Monday. The museum is closed to the public Tuesday and Wednesday but open for UC Davis classes by appointment.
Art Wide Open
The Jan Shrem and Maria Manetti Shrem Museum of Art at UC Davis is a contemporary art museum for today, committed to honoring the past and shaping the future while making art accessible and approachable to all. It builds on UC Davis' legacy of exceptional teaching and practice of the arts to offer engaging experiences, rotating exhibitions and vibrant programs that reflect and serve the community. The museum shares the university's core values of innovative research, interdisciplinary experimentation and a commitment to educational programming.
One-third of the museum's 50,000-square-foot space is devoted to instruction. An architectural masterpiece that stands as a testament to innovation, creativity and the power of philanthropy, the museum was designed by renowned architects SO-IL and Bohlin Cywinski Jackson.
Opened in November 2016, the museum has won numerous awards for its distinctive design including being named as one of the top 25 museum buildings of the past 100 years by ARTnews. 254 Old Davis Road, Davis, 95616; manettishrem.org.

content:
Davis School Board trustees approved a Declaration of Need for Qualified Educators for the upcoming school year at Thursday's 29-minute meeting.
The Declaration of Need for Qualified Educators is an annual process guided by state Code of Regulations, which requires all school districts that may need to use emergency-permit teachers to estimate the number of emergency permits that may be needed in the upcoming school year.

title: Yolo County announces nut-buying period
author: Enterprise staff
description: Yolo County Agricultural Commissioner Humberto Izquierdo announced that the nut buying period would begin Aug. 1, run through April 1, 2025, in accordance with the county's nut-theft ordinance.
content:
Yolo County Agricultural Commissioner Humberto Izquierdo announced that the nut buying period would begin Aug. 1, run through April 1, 2025, in accordance with the county's nut-theft ordinance.
On May 13, 2014, the Yolo County Board of Supervisors adopted a nut theft ordinance to address the issue of nuts being stolen from orchards and sold illegally. The declaration of the nut buying period, and related proof-of-ownership requirements, assists the department in enforcing the ordinance through compliance checks at places where nuts are sold.

content:
Empower Yolo has always prioritized the health and safety of children. The agency receives a Cal OES grant to fund the Youth Empowerment program, which provides advocacy and support to unserved/underserved youth who are victims of crime living in rural communities and foster youths.
Through this grant Empower Yolo partners with Yolo County CASA (Court Appointed Special Advocates), whose advocates provide crucial support for children in foster care, ensuring they have a voice in navigating support systems. By collaborating with Yolo CASA advocates aim to expand efforts to support vulnerable youths in the community.

title: Smart Starts for a Healthy Heart

content:

(Family Features) How you start your morning can impact the rest of your day. If you're looking to incorporate healthier choices into your morning routine, try a concept known as 'habit stacking.' Building tiny, healthier habits into routines you already have, like enjoying a morning beverage or breakfast before you check your email instead of jumping right into the day's tasks, can make it easier to stick to a new habit when it's built into an existing routine.

title: Letter: Personal touch
author: Letter to the Editor
description: I was in the grocery store the other day, Safeway on West Covell to be exact. I was looking for a specific cleansing agent that I thought might help remove
content:
I was in the grocery store the other day, Safeway on West Covell to be exact. I was looking for a specific cleansing agent that I thought might help remove the ring around my toilet, a particular nemesis because of the hard water in Davis. I asked a helpful clerk where I could find this particular cleanser, and the reason why I was seeking it out.
I want this clerk to know how grateful I am for her recommendation. She said her grandmother swore by pumice, and advised me to try it. Believe me, I have attempted to use just about every cleanser I could think of to clean that awful ring around the toilet. I tried the cleanser I had been looking for, but it didn't do a thing. Then I used the pumice as suggested - and it worked like a charm!

title: How Subaru is helping classrooms across the country get essential school supplies
author: Brandpoint
description: (BPT) - As summer winds down and thoughts turn to back-to-school, many teachers around the country know that not all of their students will come to school equipped with a
content:
(BPT) - As summer winds down and thoughts turn to back-to-school, many teachers around the country know that not all of their students will come to school equipped with a backpack full of school supplies. An alarmingly high number of teachers, 92% nationwide, have students whose families cannot afford the necessary school supplies, according to AdoptAClassroom.org. For families that may be struggling economically, those crayons, folders and No. 2 pencils can add up to a hefty price tag when wondering if they can put food on the table and keep the electricity on.
So, what's the answer? All too often, teachers use their own funds to purchase supplies for the classroom — an average of $860 out of pocket per year. As most people know, these dedicated educators don't get paid enough as it is. There has to be a better solution than stretching their resources thinner.

title: Free tools and resources that can help make buying a home a reality
author: Brandpoint
description: (BPT) - Many of today's homebuyers and renters face affordability challenges. Higher mortgage rates and low housing supply have increased homeownership costs. Corresponding increases in rent have also made it
content:
(BPT) - Many of today's homebuyers and renters face affordability challenges. Higher mortgage rates and low housing supply have increased homeownership costs. Corresponding increases in rent have also made it more difficult for potential borrowers to save for a down payment.
However, just because affordability is a challenge doesn't mean that the dream of homeownership is unattainable. In fact, despite consumers' apprehension about the mortgage process, research shows that the aspiration to own a home is very much alive and there are a number of tools and resources that can help potential borrowers make their dreams of owning a home a reality.

title: 6 reasons why renters insurance is essential for college students
author: Brandpoint
description: (BPT) - For young people, college is full of new experiences: It's often the first time living away from home, giving a taste of independence with the first step into
content:
(BPT) - For young people, college is full of new experiences: It's often the first time living away from home, giving a taste of independence with the first step into adulthood and new responsibilities. One of those responsibilities is keeping their belongings safe and secure. It's something they probably haven't had to think about before.
When you consider everything a college student brings to school — a laptop, backpack, gaming console, bike or skateboard, mini-fridge, ear buds, smartphone, expensive sneakers-of-the-moment and other expensive clothes and accessories, even a TV and other technology, it adds up to a hefty price tag if any or all of it needs to be replaced.

title: Top Reasons to Consider a Steel Roof for Your Home
description: (StatePoint) Steel is increasingly becoming the go-to material used for residential roofing. According to industry experts, this is because steel offers both a range of design advantages, as well as
content:
(StatePoint) Steel is increasingly becoming the go-to material used for residential roofing. According to industry experts, this is because steel offers both a range of design advantages, as well as features that align with sustainable living. Here are some of steel roofing's biggest benefits and why you should consider it for your home:
Durability: Steel roofing is highly durable and can last for 50 years or more with proper maintenance. This longevity means that fewer roofing materials end up in landfills over time compared to shorter-lived roofing materials like asphalt shingles, which typically need replacement every 20-30 years.

title: How to improve your kids' experiences on social media
author: Brandpoint
description: (BPT) - As kids retreat back indoors after a long summer outside, back-to-school season provides a good opportunity for parents to revisit how their children are using social media to
content:
(BPT) - As kids retreat back indoors after a long summer outside, back-to-school season provides a good opportunity for parents to revisit how their children are using social media to stay connected with their friends.
If heading back-to-school wasn't already an emotional experience for kids, a new global survey commissioned by LG Electronics found social media can be a source of anxiety for young people. Almost half of the respondents (45%) reported their social media feeds consist of an equal or greater amount of negative rather than positive content. In fact, more than 1 in 4 (28%) claimed negative content on social media feeds has increased their anxiety, and 1 in 5 (20%) said it has made them unhappy.

UC Davis researcher killed by anti-government Ethiopian protesters
The UC Davis community is mourning the death of postdoctoral researcher Sharon Gray, 31, who lost her life Tuesday during a massive anti-government protest in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia. Gray, a plant biologist, and UCD associate professor Siobhan Brady, also a plant biologist, were in Ethiopia to start preliminary work on a project with a Netherlands-based organization, university officials said. Her death is a tragic loss for her close-knit department. The U.S. Embassy attributed Gray's death to head injuries from a rock thrown by 'unknown individuals,' as the vehicle she was riding in was stoned by protesters, The Associated Press reported Thursday.

content:

Some districts have already started; now the state wants every district to become a landlord.

content:

This year, ZEISS Vision Care commissioned a study that found only 47% of parents reported taking their children to an optometrist annually, but 78% saw their primary care doctor each year and 71% made a trip to the dentist. title: Letter: You are responsible for your vote
author: Letter to the Editor
description: Today, I want to address a critical issue about our nation's role in global affairs. Modern occupation isn't just about territorial control; it's about exerting financial, social, and economic influence
content:
Today, I want to address a critical issue about our nation's role in global affairs. Modern occupation isn't just about territorial control; it's about exerting financial, social, and economic influence over other countries. Our sense of independence is increasingly overshadowed by these external pressures.
The recent address by a controversial foreign leader to the United States Congress starkly highlighted this issue. Despite strong opposition from many Americans, Congress repeatedly applauded this figure, revealing a troubling disconnect between government actions and public sentiment. This moment underscored a significant failure in our democratic process.

title: Councilmember Will Arnold endorses Victor Lagunes for Davis City Council
author: Special to the Enterprise
description: Davis City Councilmember and former Mayor Will Arnold has officially endorsed Victor Lagunes to succeed him on the Davis City Council representing District 2, emphasizing Lagunes' deep commitment to the
content:
Davis City Councilmember and former Mayor Will Arnold has officially endorsed Victor Lagunes to succeed him on the Davis City Council representing District 2, emphasizing Lagunes' deep commitment to the community and his passion for public service.
'I've seen firsthand the impact that dedicated, compassionate leadership can have, especially during challenging times," said Arnold. "Victor embodies these qualities and more. He brings a fresh perspective, a relentless work ethic and a thoughtful approach to problem-solving that is exactly what we need on the council.'
Lagunes, who teaches history at Da Vinci Junior High, first came to the city as a student at UC Davis. His career in education began with classroom volunteering, where he quickly found his calling. Since then, he has dedicated himself to teaching and advocating for the well-being of all students.
'My mother taught high school and junior high in Davis for 40 years and I deeply appreciate the passion and understanding of our needs that a school teacher brings to the table," remarked Arnold. "Like our next Vice President, Governor Tim Walz, Victor's experience in the classroom and his connection to the youth of our community make him uniquely qualified to address the challenges we face and to help guide Davis into the future.'
Arnold has been a steadfast advocate for Davis since his election to the City Council in 2016, serving two terms and playing a pivotal role in numerous initiatives, including the formation of Healthy Davis Together and the creation of Valley Clean Energy. His leadership has been instrumental during difficult times, providing comfort and guidance to the community in the wake of tragedies and advancing key reforms in public safety and housing.
Lagunes' candidacy reflects a commitment to these same values, with a focus on creating a more inclusive, accessible and sustainable Davis. His vision aligns with the community's aspirations for a thriving city that serves all its residents.
'I am deeply honored to have Will's endorsement,' said Lagunes. 'His leadership has been crucial in making Davis a city where people feel connected and supported. As a teacher who found a true home in Davis, I am committed to continuing this legacy of service. I want to ensure that our city is a place where everyone can feel secure, included and proud of our community."
Arnold's endorsement highlights the importance of leadership rooted in community values and a deep understanding of the people of Davis. With Lagunes' background in education and his dedication to making Davis a better place for all, Arnold is confident that the city will continue to thrive under his leadership.

content:
(Family Features)In today's America, 1 in 5 children faces hunger or food insecurity – a reality reported by the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA). For Black, Indigenous and Hispanic youth, these numbers are even higher. With rising poverty and deepening income inequality, the number of children living in food-insecure households has increased by 45% since 2021.
One powerful solution to youth food insecurity begins in the nation's schools. Nearly 30 million students – more than 60% of all schoolchildren – rely on school meals for all or part of their daily nourishment, according to the USDA. For many, these meals are the only reliable source of nutrition they receive each day.

title: View from the Dugout: Players stick to their routines
author: Mike Trask
description: Baseball is full of traditions, superstitions and celebrations. These have been working for the High Wheelers for the past two weeks; they've been red-hot, going 11-2, and are in the
content:
Baseball is full of traditions, superstitions and celebrations. These have been working for the High Wheelers for the past two weeks; they've been red-hot, going 11-2, and are in the playoff hunt. I had a chance to talk to some players about these things.
Before the game, players follow their routines, each important to the player. Some of these routines border on superstition, especially when not followed, which can cause a sense of unease.
"We start with a game of catch right at 20 minutes before game time,' Kirkland Banks said. 'Braeden Blackford and Tanner Smith play catch with the football every day."
"I apply eye black and chew gum without fail," Blackford added.
Braylin Marine chimes in: "I play catch with Kirk every game."
One of the celebrations that has become a staple in every game is the 'flick of the wrist.' When a player reaches first base after a single, he will turn to the dugout, raise an arm and flick his wrist.
Marine, who started the trend, explains: "It is just a flick of the wrist, 'cause that's all you are doing when you are hitting, just a little flick of the wrist." Despite its origin, this simple gesture has evolved into more of a jump shot, and each player must take their shot.
Most guys will automatically give the dugout what they want, but if they are distracted or new, the dugout will get on them and won't stop until they get them to take their shot. Once the player flicks their wrist, the dugout will cheer with approval. On the rare occasion a player gives a half effort and comes up "short," he will get grief from the guys.
The fans have caught on and are looking forward to the celebration. It livens things up and often leads right into a big rally.
The end-of-the-game celebrations come in two forms. The first is the high-five line. It seems random, but it has a definite choreography and order. All the bench players, bullpen pitchers, and coaches line up on the infield facing the outfield and wait.
The three outfielders meet in center field, put their gloves on their heads, circle up, and hug it out. They jog in, first greeted by the infielders, then hit the full line with high fives. The infielders fold in next, and the rest follow as the coaches greet everyone at the end.
The second celebration is more dramatic and not choreographed at all. The walk-off hit, or walk-off home run in a tie-breaking "knock-out" round is pure chaos. The players sprint onto the field to mob their hero. It often includes the orange bucket of water or Gatorade getting dumped and usually a shirt torn. The players look for anyone to hug and eventually find the hero.
It took the High Wheelers 48 games to get their first walk-off win, and it was pandemonium. There was double-bucket dousing and lots of running around. Sometimes, a dejected opponent will say, "Act like you have been there."

title: Lawmakers say Newsom staff ‘inflated' cost of failed health care bills
author: Ryan Sabalow
description: Lawmakers and advocates say Gov. Gavin Newsom's administration is making inflated estimates about the cost of legislation, with some suggesting his subordinates have been trying to kill the bills without
content:
Lawmakers and advocates say Gov. Gavin Newsom's administration is making inflated estimates about the cost of legislation, with some suggesting his subordinates have been trying to kill the bills without making the governor politically accountable for the outcome.
'While people are dying on the streets from a lack of access to behavioral health care treatment, state agencies continue to fabricate exorbitant cost estimates,' Sen. Dave Cortese, a Democrat from Campbell, told CalMatters after one of his mental health proposals died recently in the Assembly Appropriations Committee.
Sen. Scott Wiener, a Democrat from San Francisco who authored another mental health bill that died recently, said in a public hearing last month that the administration's cost estimate of his bill was 'extreme and outrageous.'
The pointed accusations from Democratic lawmakers and health care advocates who tend to be friendly with the Democratic governor are extraordinary because such criticism is rarely made in public. The examples also stand out because they challenge the administration's response on one of the governor's top priorities, mental health.
The administration did not accept an interview request with CalMatters and would not provide more detail – to CalMatters or to lawmakers – to explain the cost estimates. By email, however, a spokesperson insisted the costs were accurate and rejected the idea that they were intentionally inflated.
'It's outrageous and inaccurate for anyone to suggest these numbers are fabricated or artificially inflated,' Rodger Butler, a spokesperson for Newsom's Health and Human Services Agency, said in an email. 'Legislative fiscal analyses from state government departments are informed by real-world, on-the-ground experience implementing legislative mandates.'
Whatever the motivations, four health care bills with controversial cost estimates died quietly earlier this month in the Senate and Assembly Appropriations committees even after each had advanced without a single no vote from a Democratic legislator.

title: UPDATED: Aggies hold off Lions to win home opener
author: Mike Bush
description: David Meyer saved the day for UC Davis football team. The 6-foot-1 linebacker returned an interception 60 yards for a touchdown with 46 seconds left in Saturday's home opener against
content:
David Meyer saved the day for UC Davis football team.
The 6-foot-1 linebacker returned an interception 60 yards for a touchdown with 46 seconds left in Saturday's home opener against Texas A&M-Commerce at UC Davis Health Stadium. That sealed UCD's 36-22 victory over the Lions in front of 8,743 fans.
The win evens the Aggies' record at 1-1 after the season opening road loss to Cal on Aug. 31.
'I just think David Meyer is a fantastic football player,' said UCD head coach Tim Plough, who picked up his first career win. 'Incredible instincts. We saw him flying around, playing every single snap on defense and on special teams.'
Meyer, a redshirt junior, eyed the pass that Texas quarterback Ron Peace threw in hopes of finding a Lions teammate. But Meyer intercepted the ball intended for a Lions receiver and raced to the end zone for the touchdown. Aggie kicker Ridley Hunter booted the extra point for the final score.
Texas had been marching down the field, from its own 24 to the Aggie 48, before Meyer's pick-6. The Lions used a mixture of passes, plus a pass interference call, to reach Aggie territory.
Texas A&M-Commerce had cut the Aggies' lead to 29-22 with 5:03 left in the game when Peace connected with wide receiver Brooks Rigney on a 17-yard touchdown pass.
The Lions went for the 2-point conversion, where tight end Sean Sallis caught the pass.
Commerce scored earlier in the quarter when Peace found another wide receiver in EJ Oakmon on a 62-yard touchdown strike with 7:36 left on the clock. The extra-point was good, but UCD was holding onto a 29-14 lead.
Aggie quarterback Miles Hastings and tight end Winston Williams pushed the team's lead to 29-7 lead when Williams hauled in a 14-yard pass and raced into the end zone. Hunter's extra-point sailed through the uprights with 9:02 left in the game.
Peace threw his first TD pass of the night at 4:51 in the third when he found teammate Sean Sallis for 32 yards. Aidan Martin's kick was good for a 22-7 score.
Miles threw his second touchdown pass of the game at the 11:34 mark in the third, this strike to wide receiver Samuel Gbatu Jr. of 54 yards. Hunter's boot made it 22-0.
The Aggies had a 15-0 score in the quarter when Hastings threw his first TD pass of the night to wide receiver Chaz Davis, a strike of 4-yards to finish off a 7-play, 75-yard drive at 12:07. The Aggies opted for the 2-point conversion, a pass, but fell incomplete.
Commerce scored its first touchdown of the game in the third quarter. Peace found Devin Matthews for 31 yards with 4:51 remaining. Andy Gallegos' extra-point kick was good.
The Aggies booted three field goals in the second quarter to lead 9-0 at halftime.
Hunter's third chance was a 29-yard field goal with 3 seconds left for the halftime score.
'I was also happy to see Hunter bounce back and make some kicks,' said Plough of his kicker, who missed two field goals in the Aggies' opener at Cal.
Aggie running back Lan Larison had rushed for what was originally a 1-yard touchdown run in the second quarter. But UCD was penalized for illegal formation, pushing the football further away from the end zone, and ultimately leading to Hunter kicking the 29-yard field goal.
'You have to give them a lot of credit,' Plough said of the Lions' defense. 'They had some different defensive structure in the red area we hadn't prepared for. We didn't execute properly down there… that allowed them to stay in the game, which is what good teams stick around like that, things are going to get a little scary. We, obviously, do a much better job finishing drives when we're down there to (score) a touchdown.'
His second field goal came 26 yards at 5:44 on the clock. That gave the Aggies a 6-0 lead.
Hunter's first field goal was from 28 yards at 7:23 for a 3-0 score.
The Aggies had the ball inside the Lions' red zone three times in the second quarter. But Texas' defense forced UCD into field goals that were helpful, but touchdowns would've been better.
UC Davis finished with 143 rushing yards. Larison had 28 carries for 127 yards.
The Aggies had 320 passing yards. Hastings completed 26-of-39 passes, plus his three touchdown passes.
Texas A&M-Commerce had 457 passing yards. Peace was 26-of-56.

content:
It was my honor to serve the Davis community for 27 years on the School Board, City Council and county Board of Supervisors. Over those years, I became acutely aware of the challenges faced by all local governments in responding to the needs of our people and places. Our community needs both sufficient resources and effective leadership. That is why I proudly support Measures Q and T and the election of Linda Deos and Lea Darrah.

title: RSV Vaccines: What older adults need to know
description: (Family Features) Even though cooler days may seem far off, now is the best time to plan ahead for a healthy winter. One common respiratory illness, respiratory syncytial virus, or
content:
(Family Features) Even though cooler days may seem far off, now is the best time to plan ahead for a healthy winter. One common respiratory illness, respiratory syncytial virus, or RSV, usually causes mild, cold-like symptoms, but it can be severe and even deadly for older people.
'As we grow older, our immune systems do not work as well and we are more likely to have chronic conditions, which means we are at increased risk of getting very sick from common viruses as we age,' said Alison Barkoff, who leads the Administration for Community Living within the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services. 'Getting vaccinated is the best protection against fall respiratory viruses like RSV. It can help keep symptoms mild and help keep people out of the hospital.'

title: Paws for Thought: Do dogs love us?
author: Evelyn Dale
description: The 17th-century philosopher Rene Descartes believed that animals did not have souls, but responded mechanically to outside stimuli and so were without feelings.
content:
The 17th-century philosopher Rene Descartes believed that animals did not have souls, but responded mechanically to outside stimuli and so were without feelings.
This, of course, made it easy to dismiss animals' cries of pain or expressions of love. In the 19th century, Pavlov added to this idea with his theory of conditioned response, where learning was reduced to associations between stimuli and responses. Fortunately, there were ordinary people who continued to love their dogs and knew that their dogs loved them.

title: Letter: Measure Q helps the city
author: Letter to the Editor
description: Meeting the fiscal needs of our city has been a challenge for many years. The city has tried to meet that challenge in various ways. In 2018, the measure to
content:
Meeting the fiscal needs of our city has been a challenge for many years. The city has tried to meet that challenge in various ways. In 2018, the measure to pass a tax to fix roads and bike paths garnered more than 57% of the vote, but failed because of the need to pass by two-thirds. The city has done a very good job of managing to deliver services with a lean staff and recently hired an economic director to help stimulate revenue.
The reason many people are drawn to Davis is the access to quality city services. We enjoy the green belts, recreation services and community connections. All of these are supported by taxes into our General Fund. We are now at a critical tipping point that will require us to make hard choices about what services we can offer.

Mercedes Ibáñez was born in Perú and has lived in Davis since 1976. title: 5 Things Everyone Should Know About Falls and Concussions
author: Brandpoint
description: (BPT) - Five million people go to the emergency department for a traumatic brain injury (TBI) in the U.S. each year, but more than half of people who suspect they
content:
(BPT) - Five million people go to the emergency department for a traumatic brain injury (TBI) in the U.S. each year, but more than half of people who suspect they have a concussion never get it checked. [1], [2] A main reason for this is that people aren't familiar with the common causes and symptoms of concussions, and unfortunately, there are a lot of myths out there. One especially dangerous myth is that concussions only happen to athletes. Most concussions occur when people fall while doing everyday activities — such as falling while taking a shower or tripping on a toy at home. These types of falls account for nearly half of all concussions in the U.S. [3] And while concussions can happen to anyone, rates of concussions increase significantly in older adults.
Abbott, the developer of a rapid test for the assessment of concussions, and the National Council on Aging (NCOA) want to share five things everyone should know about concussions and falls prevention.

title: Commentary: Emotions, from the outside in
author: Jessica Shaker
description: In my class, we do a feelings check in every day where we share how we are feeling in terms of the Zones of Regulation. For those who are unfamiliar,
content:
In my class, we do a feelings check in every day where we share how we are feeling in terms of the Zones of Regulation. For those who are unfamiliar, a very quick summary is that blue represents sad, green represents happy and calm, yellow represents nervous, and red represents angry and terrified. It is more nuanced than that, but that's a quick explanation.
Each day, we share what colors we are feeling like. We often feel like more than one color. Every day I remind students that all our feelings are valid and it is OK to be in any of the colored zones. We know we would like to be in the green zone because that is the happiest, most emotionally regulated, and calm zone, but we acknowledge that there is no human who is in the green zone all the time and if there's a human who thinks they are in the green zone all the time, chances are they're faking it and not being honest to themselves or others about what's truly inside.

title: 4 Ways to Help Protect Against Tick Bites This Fall
author: Brandpoint
description: (BPT) - Beautiful fall days captivate many people, offering a burst of color as the leaves change and cooler temperatures that encourage outdoor adventures. However, as you're outside enjoying the
content:
(BPT) - Beautiful fall days captivate many people, offering a burst of color as the leaves change and cooler temperatures that encourage outdoor adventures. However, as you're outside enjoying the splendor, it's important to be aware of a pest you may not be thinking of — ticks.
Despite popular belief that cooler weather takes care of outdoor pests, ticks actually have two active times of year — first in early spring and second in the fall — during warming temperatures and higher humidity. However, in some parts of the country, ticks can be active year-round if temperatures are warm enough, so check out the CDC's Tick Bite Tracker, which approximates tick activity based on emergency room visits.

content:

With 90% of Americans over 65 taking at least one prescription, and one in five skipping doses due to costs (Source: KFF), this plan could make a meaningful difference for millions, helping them afford the medications they need to stay healthy. Starting in 2025, Medicare drug plan members can spread out their prescription costs over time, avoiding the need to pay in full each time they fill a prescription.

title: What You Don't Know Can Hurt: 3 facts about updated COVID-19 vaccines

However, the virus that causes COVID-19 keeps changing, so it's still important to stay up to date on your vaccinations. Respiratory viruses, including COVID-19, are common during the fall and winter months. That's why now is a good time to take care of yourself and your loved ones by getting the facts on the updated COVID-19 vaccines.
'As the virus changes, we are learning more and more about how to protect people from COVID-19,' said Namandjé N. Bumpus, Ph.D., principal deputy commissioner at the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA). 'Getting the latest COVID-19 vaccine means your protection is as up to date as possible.'

content:
The social and cultural forces behind MAGA in the United States and those that led the British in 2016 to vote to leave the European Union — by a small margin of 51.9 percent to 48.1 percent — are closely linked. I know those forces, and I feel connected to them.

title: Democrats support 'Yes on Measure Q'
author: Special to the Enterprise
description: The Yolo County Democratic Party has formally endorsed Yes on Measure Q, recognizing it as a critical step to secure essential services for the City of Davis. This endorsement underscores
content:
The Yolo County Democratic Party has formally endorsed Yes on Measure Q, recognizing it as a critical step to secure essential services for the City of Davis. This endorsement underscores the party's commitment to equity, community well-being, and responsible governance—principles at the core of Measure Q.
'Measure Q will allow the City of Davis to provide essential services, including public safety and needed infrastructure investments. The Yolo County Democratic Party applauds the City of Davis for bringing this measure forward to assure the provision of local government services to the most vulnerable populations in the community,' said Jake Whitaker, Chair of the Yolo County Democratic Party.
In contrast, the Yolo County Taxpayers Association is listed on the ballot as leading the opposition to Measure Q. The conservative association opposes every local ballot measure, including Measure Q as well as Measure T, which supports Davis libraries. According to its website, the Yolo County Taxpayers Association believes in 'privatizing whenever possible.'
'The choice for Democrats is clear,' said Will Arnold, Davis City Council member and former mayor. 'Measure Q embodies our values—equity, opportunity, and a government that works for all. It's a direct investment in essential services that protect the most vulnerable in our city, improve parks and infrastructure, and keep our streets safe. This is what makes Davis livable and inclusive."
Measure Q has garnered strong support from top Democratic leaders, including Congressman Mike Thompson, former State Senator Lois Wolk, and former Assemblymember Mariko Yamada. With backing from Democratic leaders, small business owners, and the unanimous Davis City Council, Measure Q represents a collective effort to strengthen Davis.

content:
IRVINE — UC Davis women's soccer player, redshirt senior goalkeeper Caeley Goldstein, was named Big West Defensive Player of the Week, the conference announced Monday.
Goldstein received the honor after two standout performances in goal for the Aggies, helping UCD secure a 1-0 victory against UC Santa Barbara and a 2-0 win against Cal Poly.
With these pair of shutouts, Goldstein led the Aggies to their sixth and seventh clean sheets of the year.
After recording a career-high 12 saves against UC San Diego two weeks ago, Goldstein has continued to pace the Big West Conference, leading all goalkeepers during conference play with 48 saves.
She recorded 10 saves against the Gauchos on a foggy night and seven against Cal Poly, helping the Aggies clinch a berth in the Big West Championship.
This recognition is Goldstein's first of the 2024 season and her fourth career Big West Defensive Player of the Week award.
Goldstein and the Aggies will be back in action for the regular season finale against CSU Northridge on Thursday at 3 p.m.

title: DMTC youngsters present ‘James and the Giant Peach'
author: Special To The Enterprise
description: Davis Musical Theatre Company Young Performers' Theatre is excited to present 'James and the GIANT Peach, Jr.' (Underwritten by Betty J, Paro), opening Saturday, Nov. 16, through Sunday, Dec. 8,
content:
Davis Musical Theatre Company Young Performers' Theatre is excited to present 'James and the GIANT Peach, Jr.' (Underwritten by Betty J, Paro), opening Saturday, Nov. 16, through Sunday, Dec. 8, at the Jean Henderson Performing Arts Center, 607 Pena Drive, No. 10 in Davis.
Celebrate the holiday season with Roald Dahl's classic story brought to life on the stage by a peachy-keen group of young performers. When James is sent by his conniving aunts to chop down their old fruit tree, he discovers a magic potion that results in a tremendous peach and launches a journey of enormous proportions.
Suddenly, James finds himself in the center of the gigantic peach — among human-sized insects with equally oversized personalities — but, after it falls from the tree and rolls into the ocean, the group faces hunger, sharks and plenty of disagreements.
Thanks to James' quick wit and creative thinking, the residents learn to live and work together as a family. Featuring a wickedly tuneful score and a 'Plump and Juicy' story, this adventurous musical about courage and self-discovery will have you 'Floatin' Along' with a happy tune in your heart and 'On Your Way Home.'
Directed and Choreographed by Megan Richmond, with musical direction by Montana Monce, this talented young cast features Patrick Cobb as James, Sebastian Muench as Grasshopper, Emma Nason as Earthworm, Quincy Gibbs as Ladybug, Lola Bonneau as Spider, Amelia Teramoto as Centipede and Alex Richmond as Ladahlord.
'James and the GIANT Peach, Jr.,' plays on Saturdays at 2 p.m., Nov. 16, through Dec. 7; Friday, Dec. 6 at 7 p.m.; and Sunday, Dec. 8, at 2 p.m.

title: Commentary: Fix state government first
author: Bob Stonebrook
description: For a great many Americans, the November election results elicited an intense reaction. These responses, played out in real time on election newscasts and social media timelines, included everyday working
content:
For a great many Americans, the November election results elicited an intense reaction. These responses, played out in real time on election newscasts and social media timelines, included everyday working people, media celebrities, television and movie stars, and even past and present politicians, including our own Gov. Gavin Newsom, who very quickly announced his plans to 'Trump-proof' the state through all necessary legal and legislative means.
His plan would theoretically aim to shield California's progressive policies from any federal manipulation by bolstering resources for the Attorney General's office and other state agencies in preparation for long, drawn-out legal battles with the Trump administration. The problem is that this is an exclusively defensive approach to solving a grassroots problem that will outlast Trump's second term.

title: 7 Steps to Help Keep Your Small Business Cyber Safe This Holiday Season
author: Brandpoint
description: (BPT) - The holidays bring a whirlwind of excitement, sales, and unfortunately also scams. Black Friday, Small Business Saturday, and Cyber Week mean increased online transactions, e-commerce traffic, and a
content:
(BPT) - The holidays bring a whirlwind of excitement, sales, and unfortunately also scams. Black Friday, Small Business Saturday, and Cyber Week mean increased online transactions, e-commerce traffic, and a heightened focus on fulfilling customer orders — all of which make small businesses, especially micro-businesses, prime targets for cybercriminals.
According to Bank of America's Small Business Owner's Report, more than half of small business owners said cybersecurity threats have impacted their business. Unlike larger corporations with dedicated IT departments, many small and micro businesses lack proper security infrastructure, leaving them more vulnerable to and harmed by threats. A single scam or breach can be costly and can put a business behind during the busy holiday season.

content:

In August, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) issued a request for information to identify additional detention bed space in the state as other federal agencies intensified border enforcement. The effort began in the wake of the Biden administration's sweeping asylum ban, implemented in June, for migrants caught crossing the U.S.-Mexico border outside designated entry points. Under the ban, border agents can deport such migrants within hours or days without considering their asylum claims.

De Familia a Familia de NAMI is a comprehensive program that provides essential education, practical tools, and the opportunity to connect with others who understand the unique challenges of supporting a loved one with mental illness. Participants will gain insight into mental health conditions, learn about effective communication strategies, and explore ways to care for themselves while supporting their loved ones.

title: View From the Sideline: High Wheelers owners face the fans
author: Mike Trask
description: The (now Yuba-Sutter) High Wheelers' owners, Paul Freedman and Bryan Carmel, were in town last Tuesday, hosting a community outreach to explain the details of their departure and get feedback
content:
The (now Yuba-Sutter) High Wheelers' owners, Paul Freedman and Bryan Carmel, were in town last Tuesday, hosting a community outreach to explain the details of their departure and get feedback from fans on what went well and what failed.
They were ready for anything, even an angry mob. It was impressive to see nearly every fan show up to the meeting. Everyone is spread out in a large stadium, and the crowd looks sparse, but when you get them all in one place, eight people can really fill a picnic table.
One positive aspect of having the smallest fan base in professional sports is there are no mobs. Everyone was gracious and kind and had a turn to say their piece.
Carmel said, "I was impressed with the turnout and surprised at how nice everyone was to us."
After their meeting, I sat down with Paul and Bryan for more than an hour to help get some footage for a possible film project chronicling their journey with two new professional baseball teams this past season.
I was instructed to not hold back and really let them know where they screwed up. They are both great guys, but of course, mistakes were made in Davis, and they were eager to be accountable. I had thoughts.
At the top of the list was how poor they were at engaging the community and getting local involvement. Then I mentioned how they abandoned their Davis team. When things got hot, they retreated back to the comfort of the cool breeze in Oakland. They played in the gorgeous, sold-out stadium, making nightly rounds with adoring fans and investors.
That was a wrap on the 2024 season. Now, it's time for the sequel. The High Wheelers have made three considerable moves to give this iteration of the High Wheelers in Yuba-Sutter a fighting chance.
They found a great stadium with a storied history and a community that has supported baseball at many levels for years.
Most importantly, they found a way to involve the community. They welcomed a new owner, Lon Hatamiya, a third-generation member of the Yuba-Sutter community and a huge baseball fan.
Hatamiya grew up in Roseville and attended Roseville High, where he was recently inducted into the school's Hall of Fame. He played baseball many times on historic Bryant Field, the new home of the High Wheelers. In 1973, his Eagle Scout project consisted of refurbishing the bleachers at the stadium where Babe Ruth and Jackie Robinson had played.
Hatamiya moved to Davis in 1999 with his wife and two sons, Jon and George. He says, "We loved the quality of the public schools in Davis and that they were strong in the areas of academics, Music, and Baseball."
He definitely nailed the extracurriculars. Jon is a Faculty member at the USC Thornton School of Music and has had an illustrious career as one of the top jazz trombone players in the country. George played for the Davis High baseball team and played four years of college ball at Haverford University.
When asked about his interest in baseball, Hatamiya said, "Baseball has always been my passion. Baseball was huge in the Yuba-Sutter area growing up. I played as much as I could and loved it. As a father, I loved coaching Little League and watching George through High School and College."
The opportunity to join the High Wheelers ownership group came at the perfect time. He recalls," My wife, seeing my frustration with my golf game, gently hinted that I find a new hobby. So that's exactly what I did; I decided to buy a baseball team."
I have no doubt that his passion for the game and his roots in the Yuba-Sutter area will be just what the doctor ordered for the High Wheelers in try No. 2. Also, it can't hurt that he graduated from Harvard and has a couple of other degrees from UCLA.
I will give Freedman and Carmel props for getting Hatamiya involved this time. But I won't let them totally get off the hook. I mean, he was right here in Davis the whole time. Good Luck to all!

title: Learning from Voices of War: Honoring the 80th anniversary of World War II's final major battle
description: (Family Features) The Ardennes Offensive, commonly known as the 'Battle of the Bulge,' stands as the single bloodiest battle fought by the United States during World War II. Waged in
content:
(Family Features) The Ardennes Offensive, commonly known as the 'Battle of the Bulge,' stands as the single bloodiest battle fought by the United States during World War II. Waged in the bitter cold of mid-December 1944, it took the Allies a month to secure victory. The cost was staggering: nearly 20,000 Americans were killed in action, close to 50,000 wounded and another 20,000 captured.
In honor of the 80th anniversary of this pivotal battle, the Library of Congress Veterans History Project has launched an online exhibit to commemorate the milestone. While the battle itself is etched in the annals of history, the personal stories from those who endured it remain one of the most powerful testaments to its impact.

title: UCD baseball to play under the lights this season
author: Enterprise staff
description: The UC Davis baseball program on Wednesday officially announced its schedule for the 2025 season.Part of the 56-game slate for the regular season features 28 home contests at Phil Swimley
content:
The UC Davis baseball program on Wednesday officially announced its schedule for the 2025 season.
Part of the 56-game slate for the regular season features 28 home contests at Phil Swimley Field are seven straight for Aggie and baseball fans at heart.
As part of this early-season homestand, UCD will open on the weekend of Feb. 14-16 with a three-game set against Gonzaga, with action being played under lights for the first time in program history on the team's home field.
Weekend series times at Phil Swimley Field are tentatively set for 6 p.m. on Fridays, 2 p.m. on Saturdays and 1 p.m. on Sundays.
'The addition of lights to Phil Swimley Field is exciting for everyone in and around our program,' said UCD head coach Tommy Nicholson. 'Players, past and present, have envisioned playing night games in Davis for a long time. Thanks to Rocko and his staff, we are finally able to see this vision come to fruition. I think night games will give the community and student body a chance to come out and create one of the best college baseball atmospheres in the Big West (Conference) and a home field advantage for our team.'
Along with new state-of-the-art lights allowing for night games, the addition of a brand-new video board in right center field will enhance the game day experience for both players and fans alike.
The list of opponents UCD is scheduled to host under the lights includes Gonzaga, Santa Clara, San Francisco, UC Riverside, Nevada, Cal Poly, UC Irvine, Washington State, Cal State Fullerton, Utah Tech, Northridge and Causeway rival Sacramento State.
In addition to the team's home games, the Aggies will play two highly anticipated games against Stanford in Palo Alto on April 7 and April 21.
After the seven-game home stand to begin the season, the Aggies' first road test is a midweek matchup against Pacific in Stockton on Feb. 25.
The first road series for UCD will be at Utah Valley from Feb. 28 through March 2. This will be the third consecutive season in which the Aggies and Wolverines will face off, with UCD traveling to Utah for the first time after hosting the Wolverines for the past two years.
One of the most exciting trips for the Aggies will be their series against Creighton in Omaha, Neb. UCD will face the Bluejays from March 7 to March 9, with all action taking place at Charles Schwab Field Omaha, which annually hosts the College World Series in June.
Following this trip to the Midwest, UCD will host UC Riverside from March 14-16 at Phil Swimley Field for the first Big West series of the season.
The Aggies will then take their talents to the Aloha State to face Hawai'i in their first road Big West Conference series of the season, playing the Rainbow Warriors from March 22-24.
The Aggies' full slate of road Big West games will also feature series at UC Santa Barbara (April 4-6), Bakersfield (April 17-19), Long Beach State (May 2-5) and UC San Diego (May 9-11).
Along with hosting the Highlanders to begin conference play, the Aggies will welcome Cal Poly (March 28-30), UC Irvine (April 11-13), and Cal State Fullerton (April 25-27).
UCD will also honor its departing seniors during the weekend of May 15-17, when CSU Northridge comes to visit for the final home series of the year.
Following the regular season, Cal State Fullerton's Goodwin Field will play host to the 2025 Big West Baseball Championship from May 21-25. Five teams will qualify for the championship, which features a play-in game before the final four teams clash in a double-elimination tournament.
The winner of this postseason tournament will earn the conference's automatic berth in the 2025 NCAA Tournament.
The NCAA Tournament action will commence with regionals from May 30-June 2 and super regionals from June 6-8.

author: Kelli O’Neill
description: Congratulations to Joshua Greenfield, bird stroll leader for Friends of North Davis Ponds. He found 274 species in Yolo County in 2024.
content:
Congratulations to Joshua Greenfield, bird stroll leader for Friends of North Davis Ponds. He found 274 species in Yolo County in 2024.
Josh explains: ' I tied the previous Yolo county big year record of 274 species, which was set by Holly Coates in 2018. Second place was 272 by Emmett Iverson, also in 2018, and third place was Zane Pickus with 265 in 2020. The reason the record is so difficult to achieve is that the average total number of species observed in the county (by everyone) over the last eight years is 273.4, so it isn't even possible 50% of the time. To get the record you need to have either an exceptionally good year (2020 had 282 species total), or you need an above-average year (2018 had 278, and 2024 had 277) and you can't miss more than 3-4 birds.'

title: Briefly Educational: Schools, UCD focus on King's message
author: Monica Stark
description: Note: Briefly Educational is a local education roundup.
content:
Note: Briefly Educational is a local education roundup.
"Love is the greatest force in the universe. It's the heartbeat of the moral cosmos. He who loves is a participant in being of God."
"Intelligence plus character — that is the goal of true education"
'If you can't fly then run, if you can't run then walk, if you can't walk then crawl, but whatever you doyou have to keep moving forward.'
"The ultimate measure of a man is not where he stands in moments of convenience and comfort, but where he stands at times of challenge and controversy.'
Darkness cannot drive out darkness; only light can do that. Hate cannot drive out hate; only love can do that.'
'One day we will learn that the heart can never be totally right when the head is totally wrong.'
Reading the quotes above during public comment at Thursday's Davis Joint Unified School District Board of Education meeting, a local parent, Liam, told trustees, staff and the audience that as we celebrate Martin Luther King, Jr. on Monday, it's important to remember 'the good things,' 'the good people.'
————
Arianna Shaprow
Courtesy photo
Arianna Shaprow, 13, of Las Vegas wrote an inspiring poem, 'The Way It Should Be…,' for Martin Luther King Day and Black History Month that will be displayed at the Mosaic Museum in Woodland.
Her poem tells the story of her intriguing family narrative, the perseverance of her community, and celebrates the lives of key historical figures including Martin Luther King, Rosa Parks, Frederick Douglas, Muhammad Ali, Harriet Tubman, Maya Angelou, Ida B. Wells, and James Baldwin.
Shaprow did a Q and A with the Enterprise:
Q: Tell me about your journey as a poet and writer? When did you start writing?
A: I started writing in a journal when I was six years old. It was my way of processing everything that was going on in my life at the time. I would write a mixture of poetry and prose. Writing definitely helps me relieve stress.
Q: How do you feel about having your poem displayed at the Mosaic Museum during Black History Month?
A: It's very exciting for me! The Mosaic Museum is a place that celebrates inclusivity, imagination, creativity, art, and science.
I am so happy they believed in the power of my words to inspire visitors to think more deeply about these issues on Black History Month. My poem celebrates the lives of many influential Black leaders including Martin Luther King, Maya Angelou, Rosa Parks, and Frederick Douglas. It highlights the importance of remembering how beautiful, bold, daring, and courageous we are as a community.
Q: Tell me about poetry readings or displays you've done in the past?
A: The first exhibit I did was last year at the Natural History Museum in Las Vegas. I wrote a poem entitled "Resilience," honoring the strength of my ancestors. It was this time last year. Since then, a lot has happened. I have displayed my poetry in museums across the country. I'm really excited about what's next. I would love to write a book and be a voice for social change.
Q: What does it mean to you to be an activist?
A: An activist is anyone who strives to bring about social change. During the Civil Rights Movement, my ancestors fought to bring about social change. They were activists. I believe my ancestors would be proud of me if they could read my poetry. Words are a powerful thing. I definitely believe words are capable of bringing about social change.
Q: What does Black History Month mean to you? How does your upbringing shape your connection to Black history?
A: It is a time for me to celebrate the lives of my ancestors and focus on the impact Black people from all periods of history have had on society. I was raised by a Black single mom and my grandmother, who is also Black. Being raised by two strong Black women shaped me in many ways. I was taught how to embrace my differences, how to be fearless, the importance of community and leadership.
Q: Have you had any role models who have helped you along your journey that you would like to acknowledge?
A: I would like to acknowledge my ancestors who were enslaved, my mother, and my grandmother who was like a second mother to me. Without their love surrounding me, none of this would be possible.
Q: What are your dreams?
A: My dream is to always keep dreaming.

From 2012 to 2017, Ragini Shah, a clinical professor of law at Suffolk University, interviewed more than 70 former migrants, their families, and community organizers in Mexico for perspectives on U.S. immigration policies which formed the basis of her book, 'Constructed Movements, Extraction and Resistance in Mexican Migrant Communities.'
The UC Davis Labor and Community Center will host Shah at an Author Meets Reader talk on Tuesday, Jan. 21, from noon to 1:10 p.m. at King Hall, room 1001.
Per the announcement: 'Constructed Movements centers stories from communities in Mexico profoundly affected by emigration to the United States to show how migration extracts resources along racial lines. Ragini Shah chronicles how three interrelated dynamics — the maldistribution of public resources, the exploitation of migrant labor, and the U.S. immigration enforcement regime — entrench the necessity of migration as a strategy for survival in Mexico. Shah concludes with a forceful call for the U.S. and Mexican governments to make abolitionist investments and reparative compensation to directly counteract this legacy of extraction.'
————
Stanford University art professor Enrique Chagoya is a Mexican-born American painter, printmaker and educator who will hold an artist talk at the Manetti Shrem Museum at UC Davis on Thursday, Jan. 30, from 4:30 to 6 p.m. Doors open at 4 p.m.
According to the announcement, 'his prints, drawings, collages and multiples offer critical commentary on the global reach of the United States and its cultural, political and historical tensions with Latin America. Chagoya has received an honorary doctorate from the San Francisco Art Institute and awards and fellowships from the National Endowment of the Arts, National Academy of Arts and Letters, Louis Comfort Tiffany Foundation and Guggenheim Foundation. He also has received the Lifetime Achievement in Printmaking Award from the Southern Graphics Council International and was inducted into the National Academy of Design in 2021.'
Chagoya was born and raised in Mexico City. His father, a bank employee by day and artist by night, encouraged his interest in art by teaching Chagoya color theory and how to sketch at a very early age.
As a young adult, Chagoya enrolled in the Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México, where he studied political economy and contributed political cartoons to union newsletters. He relocated to Veracruz and directed a team focused on rural-development projects, a time he describes as 'an incredible growing experience … [that] made me form strong views on what was happening outside in the world.'
