title: Frerichs speaks to League of Women Voters
author: Special to The Enterprise
description: The League of Women Voters of Yolo County will host its annual State of the Community Luncheon on in late February, featuring guest speaker County Supervisor Lucas Frerichs addressing issues
content:
The League of Women Voters of Yolo County will host its annual State of the Community Luncheon on in late February, featuring guest speaker County Supervisor Lucas Frerichs addressing issues affecting all Yolo County residents.
The 2025 State of the Community Luncheon will take place from 11:30 a.m. to 1 p.m., Thursday, Feb. 27. Catered by Treasure Dragon Chinese Restaurant, it will be held at the California Agricultural Museum, 1958 Hays Lane, Woodland. Tickets will be $35 a person, and $250 for a table of eight. Sponsorships are also available.
The State of the Community is the LWVYC's primary fundraiser of the year, and a chance to brief the community on issues that will affect residents of Yolo County in the coming years. Frerichs will speak about the challenges and opportunities facing Yolo County in the areas of agriculture, business, immigration, housing and healthcare.
Frerichs began a four-year term on the Board of Supervisors in January 2023 and represents the central and western portions of Davis as well as Winters, the campus of UC Davis, and the rural areas of southwestern Yolo County.
As a supervisor, Frerichs said he is committed to advancing policy that promotes the ability of families, in all their forms, to have their basic needs met in safe, connected communities where there is opportunity for personal fulfillment, and access to protected natural resources.
'I'm so grateful for the opportunity to speak at the League of Women Voters of Yolo County's 2025 State of the Community Luncheon,' stated Frerichs.
'The League of Women Voters continues to play a valued role in keeping residents informed and engaged in our local democracy,' he continued. 'As we launch into 2025, we face a mix of opportunities and challenges. Yolo County will be hiring a new Chief Administrative Officer and preparing for a challenging budget cycle. At the State of the Community event, I look forward to providing an update on a variety of topics, including the County's actions to protect our most vulnerable community members.'
People who want to attend can make out their checks to: League of Women Voters of Woodland, P.O. Box 2463, Woodland, CA 95776; or go to https://my.lwv.org/california/woodland to pay online. Luncheon reservations must be received by Wednesday, Feb. 19.
The LWVYC is the result of efforts by the Leagues of Women Voters of Davis Area and Woodland to support all county residents The League is committed to informing voters on local politics and increasing access to voting and information. They are a non-partisan organization dedicated to voter education and empowering citizens to shape better communities worldwide.

title: Bird flu detected in Yolo County backyard poultry flock
author: Special to the Enterprise
description: Avian influenza, also known as bird flu and influenza A (H5N1), has been detected in a backyard poultry flock in Yolo County, according to the Yolo County Health and Human
content:
Avian influenza, also known as bird flu and influenza A (H5N1), has been detected in a backyard poultry flock in Yolo County, according to the Yolo County Health and Human Services Agency and the Yolo County Agricultural Commissioner.
While bird flu has been detected in wild birds in Yolo County since 2022, this is the first detection of bird flu in poultry in the county. Since 2022, bird flu has been detected in 100 commercial flocks and 37 backyard flocks in California, affecting over 23 million birds.

title: Biodiversity Museum Day is a 'super science day'
author: Kathy Keatley Garvey
description: Have you ever wished that you, your family and your friends could visit the UC Davis campus and chat with the scientists about their research and see their work?
content:
Have you ever wished that you, your family and your friends could visit the UC Davis campus and chat with the scientists about their research and see their work?
You can.
The 14th annual UC Davis Biodiversity Museum Day, also known as "Super Science Day," is set for Saturday, Feb. 8. It's an opportunity to see displays, engage in scores of activities, and chat with the scientists.
Visitors will see everything from a great-horned owl at the California Raptor Center, dog heartworm specimens at the nematology display, monarch butterfly specimens at the Bohart Museum, and a variety of plants at three places: the Arboretum and Public Garden, the Botanical Conservatory, and the Center for Plant Diversity.
And much, much more, including displays at the Museum of Wildlife and Fish Biology, the Paleontology Collection and the Phaff Yeast Culture Collection.
It's all free and family friendly. So is the parking.
Your hosts:
* Arboretum and Public Garden, Habitat Gardens in the Environmental GATEway, adjacent to the Arboretum Teaching Nursery on Garrod Drive. Hours: noon to 4 p.m.
* Bohart Museum of Entomology, Room 1124 and main hall of the Academic Surge Building, 455 Crocker Lane. Hours: 9 a.m. to 1 p.m.
* Botanical Conservatory, the greenhouses along Kleiber Hall Drive. Hours: 10 a.m. to 2 p.m.
* California Raptor Center, 1340 Equine Lane, off Old Davis Road (Located three miles south of the central campus.) Hours: 9 a.m. to 3 p.m.
* Center for Plant Diversity, Katherine Esau Science Hall off Kleiber Hall Drive. Hours: 10 a.m. to 2 p.m.
* Nematode Collection (part of the UC Davis Department of Entomology and Nematology), Katherine Esau Science Hall, off Kleiber Hall Drive. Hours: 10 a.m. to 2 p.m.
* Museum of Wildlife and Fish Biology, Room 1394, Academic Surge Building, 455 Crocker Lane. Hours: 10 a.m. to 2 p.m.
* Paleontology Collection, Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences, 1309 Earth and Physical Sciences Building, 434 LaRue Road. Hours: 10 a.m. to 2 p.m.
* Phaff Yeast Culture Collection, Robert Mondavi Institute Brewery and Food Processing facility, Old Davis Road. Hours: 10 a.m. to 2 p.m.
* Visual Journal Exhibit (new), Design Museum at Cruess Hall, Room 124, 375 California Ave. Hours: 1 to 5 p.m.
* Moth Documentary (new), Cruess Hall, Room 100, 375 California Ave. Hours: 2:45 to 5 p.m.
Committee chair Tabatha Yang, education and outreach coordinator and a co-founder of the Biodiversity Museum Day, points out that "Super Science Day" is an opportunity for youngsters to think about or learn more about scientific careers.

content:
The Donald Trump administration on Wednesday rescinded a memo issued on Monday intended to go into effect Tuesday that would have temporarily frozen federal aid and left state officials scrambling to decipher the scope of the order.
The Monday memo from the U.S. Office of Management and Budget directed federal agencies to suspend financial loans and grants that could be 'implicated' by any of the president's prior executive orders, including assistance for 'foreign aid, nongovernmental organizations, DEI, woke gender ideology, and the green new deal.'

The City of Davis Human Relations Commission announced today that the nomination period is now open for the Thong Hy Huynh Memorial Awards until March 17, 2025, at 5 p.m. The process to nominate is easy and can be completed in 15 minutes by filling out a simple form and statement.
Established in 1986, the Thong Hy Huynh Memorial Awards recognizes local individuals or organizations promoting civil rights, civic engagement or positive human relations and are helping improve the quality of life for Davis residents and visitors. The awards are in memory of Davis High School student Thong Hy Huynh, who was stabbed to death on May 4, 1983, and to help raise awareness for social justice and inclusion.

title: Local Roundup: UCD softball starts season on winning note
author: Enterprise staff
description: The UC Davis softball team started the 2025 season hosting its annual NorCal Kickoff at LaRue Field over the weekend.Wrapping up the kickoff in which two of its six games
content:
The UC Davis softball team started the 2025 season hosting its annual NorCal Kickoff at LaRue Field over the weekend.
Wrapping up the kickoff in which two of its six games were canceled due to rain. UCD still came out strong with a 3-1 record, ending on Sunday with beating Saint Mary's 2-1.
Ashley Sawai went the distance in the final game of the kickoff, striking out eight that is a career-high for her.
Alyssa Dethlefson, a freshman who is the younger sister of former Aggie standout Anna Dethlefson, went 2-for-3 in the game. She scored a run and had two stolen bases.
Clarie Shelton knocked in two runs for the Aggies. Alyssa Dethlefson and Vanessa Calvillo, a pinch-runner, were on the base paths when they scored.
In the first game on Sunday, Boise State proved to be too much for the Aggies, posting a 15-5 win that was called after five innings because of the run rule.
Mickey Buscemi went 2-for-3 with two RBIs and scored a run for the Aggies.
Former Davis High softball standout Naomi Kalanetra, one of nine freshmen on this year's team, was hit by a pitch and scored in the contest.
On Saturday, UCD knocked off San Jose State 3-0 and Utah Valley by the same score.
This Friday through Sunday, the Aggies will be taking part in the Cardinal Classic. On Friday, UCD plays Portland State at 10 a.m., then No. 22 Stanford at 3:30 p.m. Both games will be played in Palo Alto.
Then on Saturday, the Aggies face Big West Conference foe UC Riverside at 10 a.m. and play Portland State again at 12:30 p.m.
The Aggies wrap up the classic against Stanford again on Sunday at 1:30 p.m.
The last three games will also be played in Palo Alto.
UCD men's basketball
Guard Leo DeBruhl had a career night at both ends for UCD with 11 points and 10 assists. That led to the Aggies posting a 65-49 win over CSU Fullerton on Saturday. He also had six rebounds and six steals. The steals and assists are both career highs for DeBruhl.
Another UCD backcourt player in TY Johnson led UCD (8-5 in the Big West, 14-10) by scoring 20 points. He also had three 3-pointers, his third straight game making multiple shots behind the line.
Carl Daugherty Jr. continued to provide energy off the bench, scoring 10 points on an efficient 4-9 from the field.
Niko Rocak added four blocks. He is now the all-time Aggie single season leader in blocks with 52.
UCD forced 22 turnovers, which resulted in 27 points at the opposite end.
On Thursday, UCD returns to the University Credit Union Center hosting UC Riverside at 6 p.m.
Then the Aggies make another road trip this Saturday, this time to UC San Diego for a 4 p.m. Big West game.
DHS girls basketball
Lorelei Nachman and Sonia Clayton scored 11 points each for DHS (6-6 in the Sierra Foothill League, 15-11 overall) in Friday's game at Del Oro. The host Golden Eagles soared to a 49-34 win over the Blue Devils.
Clayton finished with a double-double for DHS, as she grabbed 10 of the team's 21 rebounds.
Del Oro only led 32-31 after three quarters. But the Golden Eagles held the Blue Devils to only three points to come out with the win.
On Tuesday, DHS hosted Rocklin.

description: The Woodland Camera Forum will present local photographer Bill Wagnon, who will share some of his travel and other favorite photography images, on Monday, Feb. 17, at 7 p.m. at
content:
The Woodland Camera Forum will present local photographer Bill Wagnon, who will share some of his travel and other favorite photography images, on Monday, Feb. 17, at 7 p.m. at the Living Hope Church, 240 N. West St. The presentation is free and open to the public.
Wagnon, a member of the Woodland Camera Forum for many years, will present some travel photos from Europe and some from the United States that he has taken over the past 40-plus years.
His love of photography began in 1981 when he was in chiropractic college. He had been given an old camera when he and his wife, Linda, took their two children (2 and 4 years old) to a park where he laid on the ground as his daughter lead her brother away from him holding hands and snapped a simple photo of them in black and white.
"I've been hooked on photography ever since,' Wagnon said. 'I have gone through several cameras during that time as I'm guessing you have also done. I would love to share some of my travel and other favorite photography with you. Friends and neighbors are always more than welcome to attend the Woodland Camera Forum. I hope to see you there."
In addition to Wagnon's images, members of the WCF will show some of their recent images for discussion and learning.

title: Tree-death trial looks at upkeep
author: Lauren Keene
description: City delayed maintenance recommendations, witness says
content:
City delayed maintenance recommendations, witness says
WOODLAND — The city of Davis failed to perform a series of recommended tree prunings and removals, even after a fallen branch killed a 44-year-old mother in Slide Hill Park, the city's former urban forest manager testified last week in Yolo Superior Court.
Rob Cain took the witness stand in a wrongful-death case filed by the family of Jennifer Comey, who sustained fatal injuries on Feb. 23, 2021, when a decaying shamel ash branch fell onto her in the park's sandbox, narrowly missing her daughter Margaret Pitts, then 3.
Margaret and her father, Ted Pitts, are the plaintiffs in the lawsuit, which seeks between $30-40 million in damages from the city of Davis and Davey Resource Group, the private firm that conducted an inventory of Davis' city-owned trees in 2018.
The city has admitted liability in Comey's death, but attorneys for the city's insurance carriers, YCPARMIA and CJPARMIA, dispute the amount of damages that should be awarded to the Pitts family, putting the figure at around $10 million.
(Davis City Attorney Inder Khalsa told The Enterprise on Friday that "the city has attempted to resolve this case outside of litigation, but we haven't been successful.")
It was Cain who spearheaded a formal inventory the city's 40,000 trees, the goal of which was to 'identify and document trees requiring risk management' so the city could allocate resources for their care, Cain testified during the civil trial's second week.
At the time, Davis had no routine or proactive pruning schedule for Slide Hill Park or any of the city's parks, Cain said, instead taking a reactive maintenance approach when citizens or park workers noticed hanging limbs — referred to as "hangers" — and other problems.
The city received four 'hanger' reports at Slide Hill Park between August 2019 and September 2020, according to documents presented in court.
Cain said he was not aware the arborist Davey Resource Group assigned to the inventory wasn't certified, as called for in the job contract. Attorneys for DRG, which has denied any liability in Comey's death, have said the arborist was highly trained and obtained certification shortly after the inventory's completion in August 2018.
The arborist deemed the shamel ash tree next to Slide Hill Park's playground in 'fair' condition at the time, with no noted pest or disease damage, and in need of 'priority 3' pruning — the lowest level possible.
But Cain testified the city hadn't taken action on any of DRG's maintenance recommendations as of his departure from the city 10 months after Comey's death.
When asked why, Cain said the city was in the process of removing about 8,500 privately-owned trees from the inventory, although he acknowledged that process didn't preclude the city from performing tree maintenance.
The city did order a risk assessment of 35 Slide Hill Park trees two weeks after Comey's death, Cain recalled, and the firm, Tree Associates, recommended the removal of 13 of them.
But again, nothing happened, according to Cain.
'Even after Jennifer Comey died, you didn't take them down?' DRG attorney Andrew Cox asked.
'No,' Cain replied.
In addition to wrongful death, the civil lawsuit seeks damages for the pain and suffering Comey endured in the hour and 17 minutes she survived following the impact, and the emotional distress that Margaret, now 6, experienced from witnessing the event.
Dr. Gregory Riber, a forensic pathologist who reviewed records of Comey's medical treatment at the park and UC Davis Medical Center, testified that Comey died of multiple blunt injuries and massive blood loss, having suffered fractures to her basal skull, pelvis and leg, 'all of which would be the sources of considerable pain.'
The injuries were consistent with a high-speed vehicle collision or fall from a multi-story building, Riber said. Although comatose, Comey still recorded a blood pressure, indicating her brain was still functioning during that time.
Clinical neuropsychologist Dr. Erin Bigler testified that "there was sufficient time for her to experience pain" before she died, noting her thalamus — the part of the brain that relays sensory and motor information to the cerebral cortex — continued to process information after her injury.
'He was broken'
A former neighbor of Jennifer Comey described her as a patient and affectionate mother, as well as a 'natural teacher' to her toddler daughter.
'She was constantly teaching and getting Margaret excited about anything,' said Alison Feliciano, who met Comey and her family when they moved next door in August 2019. Margaret 'was always engaged with Jen, just a cheerful little girl.'
Feliciano said Comey and Margaret were 'inseparable,' and even more so when Covid forced the family into lockdown in the spring of 2020.
'Even when it was hard to entertain a 2-year-old, (Comey) found a way,' Feliciano said. 'Margaret was always smiling, happy, dancing, interested in all sorts of things.'
Comey and her husband, Ted Pitts, 'reminded me of teammates, very much working together for their daughter,' Feliciano added. 'They were always supporting one another.'
That all changed after Comey's death, said Feliciano, who took care of a distraught Margaret following the park incident and later became her daycare provider when Pitts returned to work.
'Ted was struggling very much' with single parenting and full-time work, Feliciano recalled. 'He was just broken.' Margaret, meanwhile, spoke often of Comey and how she died, occasionally saying 'I want to be (dead) too.'
'Margaret was just a different child,' she said.
Ultimately, Pitts made the decision to move himself and Margaret back to their native Ohio to be near family and friends. Feliciano said she's kept in touch, and while Pitts is an attentive and capable father, she sometimes worries about the pair.
'Parenting is tough enough with two parents. The thought of being a single parent, that's what makes me worry,' she said. Without her mother, 'I feel like Margaret's missing out.'
Bigler, the clinical neuropsychologist, testified that he reviewed a deposition of Margaret and information from both her father and teacher about her current behaviors.
Although she enjoys a variety of activities and interests that help her cope, Bigler opined that the 6-year-old suffers from symptoms of post-traumatic stress disorder, including anxiety, nightmares, avoidance and adjustment challenges.
'At some point, these features will become more prominent,' particularly during 'triggering' events such as birthdays and other milestones her mother won't experience, Bigler said. 'They will need to be dealt with therapeutically throughout her lifespan."
Testimony resumes Tuesday in Judge Tim Fall's courtroom.
— Reach Lauren Keene at lkeene@davisenterprise.net

title: Nothing to sneeze at: Expert tips on coping with spring allergies

description: (BPT) - Spring is just around the corner — and so are those annoying spring allergy symptoms. If your first signs of spring aren't a robin or crocus in the
content:
(BPT) - Spring is just around the corner — and so are those annoying spring allergy symptoms. If your first signs of spring aren't a robin or crocus in the yard but itchy eyes, wheezing, sneezing and/or congestion, you'll want to learn the best ways to handle seasonal pollen allergies, which are a type of hay fever.

title: Living with narcolepsy: Lindsay and Matt's journey with a life-changing diagnosis
author: Brandpoint
description: (BPT) - Imagine you haven't slept in 72 hours and every step you take feels like you're walking through wet cement. Then imagine you experience this feeling every day. This
content:
(BPT) - Imagine you haven't slept in 72 hours and every step you take feels like you're walking through wet cement. Then imagine you experience this feeling every day. This is how excessive daytime sleepiness can feel for people living with narcolepsy, a rare neurological disorder that can affect all aspects of a person's daily life. Approximately 170,000 people in the United States are thought to be living with narcolepsy.
All people living with narcolepsy experience excessive daytime sleepiness, which means they struggle to stay awake and alert during the day, or they constantly feel sleepy. This can impact their daily lives at work or at home in many ways. They may have trouble staying awake while being sedentary or inactive, such as during meetings or while reading. Some may also experience difficulty with memory, concentration, and attention due to excessive daytime sleepiness. Their sleepiness may affect interactions and relationships with family and friends. Excessive daytime sleepiness can be mistaken for symptoms of other disorders, making a narcolepsy diagnosis challenging.

'This is a rare time, it's a different time, it's a difficult time,' said Rep. Mike Thompson, D-St. Helena. 'I know a lot of people are worried, a lot of people are mad as hell. I understand you, I agree, I'm worried and I'm mad as hell.'
On Thursday at the Woodland Community and Senior Center, Thompson, State Assembly Majority Leader Cecilia Aguiar-Curry and State Sen. Christopher Cabaldon gathered to lead a town hall meeting regarding the actions of the Trump Administration.

title: Show Your Love with a Special Sweet Dessert
description: Show Your Love with a Special Sweet Dessert
content:
Show Your Love with a Special Sweet Dessert
(Family Features) Going above and beyond for your loved ones, whether it's a special occasion or a regular night at home, can show just how much you care. Homemade desserts like these Cheesecake Cookie Cups offer a perfect way to make a delicious treat with love. Find more dessert ideas at Culinary.net.

title: Northridge rallies to top Aggie men on court
author: Mike Bush
description: For most of its Big West Conference home game on Saturday, the UC Davis men's basketball team looked like it was going post a win over CSU Northridge's squad.
content:
For most of its Big West Conference home game on Saturday, the UC Davis men's basketball team looked like it was going post a win over CSU Northridge's squad.
After all, the Aggies had a 12-point lead over the visiting Matadors.

title: New Harmony sets two shows for March
author: Special to The Enterprise
description: The New Harmony Jazz Band has a pair of performances lined up for March.
content:
The New Harmony Jazz Band has a pair of performances lined up for March.
First, for the 2nd Friday ArtAbout on March 14 in downtown Davis, New Harmony will present a free concert of big band, swing, and Latin jazz in the E Street Plaza from 6 to 9 p.m.

title: Emerson PTA sets final community shoe drive for March 1
author: Special to The Enterprise
description: The Emerson Jr. High PTA (www.emersonjrhighpta.com) is conducting a shoe drive fundraiser through March 6 to raise funds for teacher grants and a new marquee sign for the school.
content:
The Emerson Jr. High PTA (www.emersonjrhighpta.com) is conducting a shoe drive fundraiser through March 6 to raise funds for teacher grants and a new marquee sign for the school.
The PTA will earn funds based on the total weight of the pairs of gently worn, used and new shoes collected, as Funds2Orgs will issue a check for the collected shoes. Those dollars will benefit the PTA.

title: Tom Elias: Some Trump firings thwart his own aims
author: Tom Elias
description: It now clear that some moves President Trump has authorized his pal Elon Musk and the so-called Department of Government Efficiency to make will thwart at least a few of
content:
It now clear that some moves President Trump has authorized his pal Elon Musk and the so-called Department of Government Efficiency to make will thwart at least a few of Trump's own often-repeated priorities.
Among the actions figuring to affect California most are three, so far. One was the abrupt firing of 20 judges from immigration courts in San Diego, where they decided on the legitimacy of immigrant amnesty claims.

title: Recalls: Las medidas de seguridad que la gente no debe saltarse
description: (NAPSI)—Una reciente encuesta de opinión pública realizada por Stellantis, el fabricante de los vehículos Chrysler, Dodge, Jeep, y Ram, encontró que el 43% de los propietarios de vehículos no saben
content: (NAPSI)—Una reciente encuesta de opinión pública realizada por Stellantis, el fabricante de los vehículos Chrysler, Dodge, Jeep, y Ram, encontró que el 43% de los propietarios de vehículos no saben cómo verificar si sus vehículos tienen recalls de seguridad. Para los conductores que poseen autos y camionetas nuevas y que reciben actualizaciones regularmente de sus concesionarios, puede que esto no sea un problema. Sin embargo, para aquellos que poseen un vehículo viejo o usado, que se han mudado recientemente o que conducen un vehículo del que no son propietarios, es importante saber cómo verificarlo.

title: UC strike includes key lab workers
author: Monica Stark
description: As bird flu continues to soar, workers at the only lab in California with the authority to confirm high-risk cases are on strike. Employees at the California Animal Health and
content:
As bird flu continues to soar, workers at the only lab in California with the authority to confirm high-risk cases are on strike. Employees at the California Animal Health and Food Safety Laboratory join nearly 60,000 workers UC-wide from across the healthcare, research, and technical sectors.
Claiming unfair labor practices, the unions aligned their efforts with overlapping strike dates starting on Wednesday.

title: Planning Commission ok's CUP for rock climbing gym
author: Rebecca Wasik
description: On Wednesday, the Davis Planning Commission unanimously approved a Conditional Use Permit at 607 Pena Dr. to allow an indoor rock climbing gym and fitness center.
content:
On Wednesday, the Davis Planning Commission unanimously approved a Conditional Use Permit at 607 Pena Dr. to allow an indoor rock climbing gym and fitness center.
The center will consist of approximately 12,000 square feet in a 54,674 square foot multi-tenant industrial building. Commercial recreation is an allowed conditional use under the current zoning.

title: Commentary: The Trump way comes to The Washington Post
author: Llewellyn King
description: As Juliet might have said, 'O America, America, wherefore art thou America?'
content:
As Juliet might have said, 'O America, America, wherefore art thou America?'
What has become of us when the president, Donald Trump, who opposes big government, wants the government to have its hand in everything, from the operation of The Kennedy Center to the regulatory commissions, to gender identification, to traffic control in New York, to the composition of the White House press pool?

title: UCD men hoops' home finale airing nationally

content:
The Big West Conference has selected UC Davis men's basketball home game against UC San Diego on Saturday, March 8, as ESPN's final wildcard game.
The game has been rescheduled to broadcast at 8 p.m. It was scheduled for a 2 p.m. start.

author: Derrick Bang
description: A challenging field has become even more difficult
content:
A challenging field has become even more difficult
What a mess.

title: Doug Kelly: Stafford stays put in Los Angeles
author: Doug Kelly
description: One more week to daylight savings time, and is it ever necessary!
content:
One more week to daylight savings time, and is it ever necessary!
* The Los Angeles Rams made the right move Friday when they agreed on terms with quarterback Matthew Stafford on a restructured contract that keeps him in L.A. for the foreseeable future.

title: View from the Sideline: Keep the good times rolling
author: Mike Trask
description: The spring season is in full swing for the Davis High athletes. However, one winter squad made a long playoff push and extended its season by a couple of weeks.
content:
The spring season is in full swing for the Davis High athletes. However, one winter squad made a long playoff push and extended its season by a couple of weeks. The Blue Devil boys soccer team's Sac Joaquin Section playoff run has included blowouts, comebacks and controversial nail-biters.
The Blue Devils had a great regular season, going 11-3 to win a strong Sierra Foothill League. They were the No. 2 seed and would face Chavez of Stockton in the first round.

title: Human Relations Commission hit by hate-speech accusations
author: Rebecca Wasik
description: At the city of Davis Human Relations Commission's meeting last Thursday, Feb. 27, concerns were raised by members of the public regarding a comment made by a HRC commissioner about
content:
At the city of Davis Human Relations Commission's meeting last Thursday, Feb. 27, concerns were raised by members of the public regarding a comment made by a HRC commissioner about another HRC commissioner during the public comment period of the Feb. 18 Davis City Council meeting.
On Feb. 3, Commissioner Deema Tamimi, a Palestinian American, shared a photo of the book, 'They Called Me a Lioness: A Palestinian Girl's Fight for Freedom' on Instagram with the caption, 'An important and moving book, especially at this critical moment in history. This is one I recommend also for teens who are interested in learning more. Thank you to (authors) Ahed Tamimi and Dena Takruri for your bravery and your commitment to truth, justice and peace.'

title: UCD Vet Med hosts bilingual equine health symposium
author: Monica Stark
description: Horse owners, riders, equine professionals and students passionate about horses — anyone interested in the equine industry — can attend Saturday's Equine Health Symposium presented by the Veterinary Medical Teaching
content:
Horse owners, riders, equine professionals and students passionate about horses — anyone interested in the equine industry — can attend Saturday's Equine Health Symposium presented by the Veterinary Medical Teaching Hospital Large Animal Clinic in conjunction with the Equine Medicine Club.
Morning lectures from 9 a.m. to noon include emergency preparedness with Dr. Briana Hamamoto, assisted reproduction techniques and placentitis with Dr. Pouya Dini, wounds street nails and trauma injuries with Dr. Isabelle Kilcoyne, preventative medicine with Dr. Jennifer Cassano, colic with Dr. Sandra Valdez, and foals with Dr. Gary Magdesian.

title: On KDRT: The nonprofit freeze
author: Special to The Enterprise
description: The Trump administration is hammering away at the federal government by eliminating jobs, cancelling programs, freezing spending and generally creating confusion.
content:
The Trump administration is hammering away at the federal government by eliminating jobs, cancelling programs, freezing spending and generally creating confusion.
The current edition of 'Davisville' looks at one part of the fallout in Yolo County — the effect of the spending freeze on local nonprofits — by talking with Jessica Hubbard, executive director of the Yolo Community Foundation.

title: Burning question: How to save an old-growth forest in Tahoe
author: Kat Kerlin
description: Management key to conservation in seasonally dry West
content:
Management key to conservation in seasonally dry West
On the shores of Lake Tahoe at Emerald Bay State Park grows what some consider to be the most iconic old-growth forest in the Lake Tahoe Basin. Giant ponderosa pines — some of the last remaining in the area — share space with at least 13 other tree species.

title: Council approves license plate readers request from PD
author: Rebecca Wasik
description: On Tuesday, the Davis City Council unanimously approved the Davis Police Department's request to procure additional automated license plate readers and public safety cameras.
content:
On Tuesday, the Davis City Council unanimously approved the Davis Police Department's request to procure additional automated license plate readers and public safety cameras.
Council approved the use of public safety cameras and automated license plate readers (ALPR) back in 2018, which the police department does currently own and operate. This technology is used to investigate leads in criminal cases; it is not used for traffic enforcement.

title: Real People, Real Downtown: Upper Crust still rising
author: Special to The Enterprise
description: For more than 50 years, the Kalisky Family has been baking bread in Davis.
content:
For more than 50 years, the Kalisky Family has been baking bread in Davis.
It started as a hobby with Trudy and Mo Kalisky making bread as UC Davis graduate students. From there it turned into a successful baking enterprise that served farmer's markets throughout the Sacramento region. Now, with Trudy and Mo retired and their son Lorin at the helm, Upper Crust Baking has grown to include retail locations in Davis and Winters.

title: District renames DHS academic center for Ross
author: Monica Stark
description: The Bob Ross Academic Center is the new name for the Academic Center at Davis Senior High School, which Bob Ross proposed and advocated for during his 37-year teaching career
content: The Bob Ross Academic Center is the new name for the Academic Center at Davis Senior High School, which Bob Ross proposed and advocated for during his 37-year teaching career at the high school.

title: Aggie men lose to Anteaters
author: Mike Bush
description: Two days before playing its Big West Conference home finale, the UC Davis men's basketball team was looking to have a strong outing in front of a large number of
content:
Two days before playing its Big West Conference home finale, the UC Davis men's basketball team was looking to have a strong outing in front of a large number of local fans.
But the UC Irvine squad ruined the Aggies' plans.

title: School district not tracking immigration-related absences
author: Monica Stark
description: According to the California County Superintendent's 'Common Message' for the Second Interim Budget, 'absenteeism due to immigration concerns for families and potential federal policy and funding changes with a new
content:
According to the California County Superintendent's 'Common Message' for the Second Interim Budget, 'absenteeism due to immigration concerns for families and potential federal policy and funding changes with a new administration brings a risk of state budget shortfalls in future years.'
When asked to localize these impacts for DJUSD, spokesperson Maddie Shumway reiterated that the district does not track students/families' immigration status or any immigration-related documents. 'As a result, we have no data related to immigration status and any district data, including but not limited to attendance,' she said.

title: Three arrested on drug charges
author: Anne Ternus-Bellamy
description: Two Davis residents and a Dixon resident were arrested Wednesday on drug-related charges at a home on Chestnut Lane.
content:
Two Davis residents and a Dixon resident were arrested Wednesday on drug-related charges at a home on Chestnut Lane.
Davis police detectives had served a search warrant on the 1200 block of Chestnut shortly after noon and, during the search, arrested the three individuals and seized narcotics including Fentanyl and Methamphetamine, the police department reported.

title: Letter: Ukraine betrayed
author: Letter to The Enterprise
description: Three years ago without a legal or moral justification, Russia invaded Ukraine from three directions thinking that it would overthrow the Ukrainian government and force Ukraine into the Russian orbit.
content:
Three years ago without a legal or moral justification, Russia invaded Ukraine from three directions thinking that it would overthrow the Ukrainian government and force Ukraine into the Russian orbit. Ukraine has valiantly resisted the Russian aggression, but its people have suffered tremendously.
Russia, an enormous country with vast military resources, has committed war crimes in Ukraine, including genocide, torture, destruction of the grid, and abduction of Ukrainian children. The Kremlin leaders have become indicted war criminals and can't travel freely around the world. The United States and its NATO allies have stood with Ukraine by supplying it with weapons, but not troops.

title: Frerichs announces 2025 Party with a Purpose
author: Enterprise staff
description: Yolo County Supervisor Lucas Frerichs has announced the date, time and place for his annual Party with a Purpose to celebrate his birthday.
content:
Yolo County Supervisor Lucas Frerichs has announced the date, time and place for his annual Party with a Purpose to celebrate his birthday.
The party, on May 21 from 6 to 8 p.m., will benefit Winters Healthcare. Tickets include entry to Berryessa Brewing Co. in Winters, one drink ticket, dessert, live music and non-profit support. Additional food and drink will be available for purchase as well.

title: Citrus Circuits RoboCamps registration open
author: Special to The Enterprise
description: Registration is open for summer RoboCamps sessions by Citrus Circuits, the Davis High School robotics team.
content:
Registration is open for summer RoboCamps sessions by Citrus Circuits, the Davis High School robotics team.
RoboCamps are summer camps for incoming kindergarteners through eighth-graders interested in robotics and learning about STEM. Each week-long camp is immersive and hands-on, offering different levels of experience to teach students how to design, program, and operate with small robots. Visit www.citruscircuits.org/robocamps for more specific information and to register for RoboCamps.

title: Local Roundup: Aggie women win conference hoops finale
author: Enterprise staff
description: The UC Davis women's basketball team wrapped up Big West Conference action on Saturday with a 69-58 win over UC San Diego at LionTree Arena in La Jolla.
content:
The UC Davis women's basketball team wrapped up Big West Conference action on Saturday with a 69-58 win over UC San Diego at LionTree Arena in La Jolla.
This victory had UCD (13-7 in the Big West, 19-11 overall) take third place behind UC Irvine (15-5 in the Big West, 21-9) and Hawaii (16-4 in the Big West, 22-8).

title: View From the Sideline: Some things are still as we remember
author: Mike Trask
description: There are so many things that today's kids miss out on. I will spare everyone the back-in-my-day rant. However, when we called a friend's house, we would have to talk
content:
There are so many things that today's kids miss out on. I will spare everyone the back-in-my-day rant. However, when we called a friend's house, we would have to talk to their parents first.
But there are a few great traditions that remain to this day. One in particular has remained as wonderful as ever and continues to shine as a timeless reminder of community, joy, and hope: Opening Day.

title: Name Droppers: UCD researcher earns grant
author: Sarah Brickman
description: Sarah Brickman of Davis was selected as a 2025 recipient of a Graduate Research Grant by The Honor Society of Phi Kappa Phi-the nation's oldest and most selective collegiate honor
content:
of Davis was selected as a 2025 recipient of a Graduate Research Grant by The Honor Society of Phi Kappa Phi-the nation's oldest and most selective collegiate honor society for all academic disciplines.
The grants of up to $1,500 are designed to support graduate students who are active society members seeking funding for research in support of career development opportunities. Brickman is one of 20 recipients nationwide to receive the award.

title: Name Droppers: UCD emeritus professor earns Lifetime IPM Achievement Award
author: Enterprise staff
description: UC Davis distinguished professor emeritus Frank Zalom, an internationally recognized integrated pest management (IPM) specialist whose stellar career spans 45 years, has received a Lifetime IPM Achievement Award from the
content:
UC Davis distinguished professor emeritus Frank Zalom, an internationally recognized integrated pest management (IPM) specialist whose stellar career spans 45 years, has received a Lifetime IPM Achievement Award from the California Department of Pesticide Regulation (CDPR).
Zalom, a member of the UC Davis Department of Entomology and Nematology faculty, and formerly the 16-year director of the UC Statewide IPM Program, was honored at CDPR's IPM Achievement Awards virtual ceremony on Feb. 29.

title: Accused stabber pleads not guilty, awaits trial-setting date
author: Lauren Keene
description: WOODLAND — The former UC Davis student accused of committing a series of local stabbings last year returned to court Wednesday for arraignment.
content:
WOODLAND — The former UC Davis student accused of committing a series of local stabbings last year returned to court Wednesday for arraignment.
Carlos Reales Dominguez, 22, pleaded not guilty to murder, attempted murder and other charges listed in the information — the charging document filed by Yolo County prosecutors following a preliminary hearing in the case.

title: Supes briefed on department budgets in two-day workshop
author: Rebecca Wasik
description: A two-day budget workshop was the focus for the Yolo County Board of Supervisors on Monday and Tuesday.
content:
A two-day budget workshop was the focus for the Yolo County Board of Supervisors on Monday and Tuesday.
Each department in the county presented to the board on its past fiscal year to help launch the development process for the upcoming fiscal year. The goal was to help shape budget recommendations that will be presented for consideration at the upcoming fiscal year 2024-25 budget hearing on June 11.

title: Fire breaks out behind Woodland's Yolo Food Bank headquarters
author: Lauren Keene
description: WOODLAND — The Woodland Fire Department is investigating the cause of a fire that destroyed pallets, crates and other property Thursday behind the Yolo Food Bank facility in Woodland.
content:
WOODLAND — The Woodland Fire Department is investigating the cause of a fire that destroyed pallets, crates and other property Thursday behind the Yolo Food Bank facility in Woodland.
High winds had spread the flames to a neighboring field and pile of railroad ties by the time crews arrived to the scene at 233 Harter Avenue around 12:45 p.m.

title: Shambhala Center offers meditation classes
author: Enterprise staff
description: The Davis Shambhala Meditation Center will host a Dharma talk and discussion at 10:15 a.m. Sunday, March 17: 'How would the Buddha manage stress?'
content:
The Davis Shambhala Meditation Center will host a Dharma talk and discussion at 10:15 a.m. Sunday, March 17: 'How would the Buddha manage stress?'
When life feels difficult and challenging it is normal to try to avoid the feeling of discomfort through distraction and entertainment. The Buddha taught that looking directly at what makes us uncomfortable through meditation practice provides a path of non-resistance, and offers another approach to working with pain. On Sunday, Megan Murphy will discuss this teaching which is based on a book by Pema Chodron titled, 'The Wisdom of No Escape.'

title: DHS roundup: Lacrosse, baseball, tennis win
author: Enterprise staff
description: Nothing much has changed in a year between girls' lacrosse rivals Davis and Carondelet high schools.
content:
Nothing much has changed in a year between girls' lacrosse rivals Davis and Carondelet high schools.
The Blue Devils nipped the Cougars, 13-12, at Ron & Mary Brown Stadium on Friday night. It was the same winning DHS score from last March 17 in Concord.

title: Gibson House debuts two new exhibitions
author: Rebecca Wasik
description: The Gibson House in Woodland has a new exhibition on display: 'Pathways of Resistance — Women at the Turn of the 20th Century.'
content:
The Gibson House in Woodland has a new exhibition on display: 'Pathways of Resistance — Women at the Turn of the 20th Century.'
On Thursday evening, a reception was held by The Gibson House and Yolo Arts to celebrate the opening of this exhibition, which will be on display through June 1.

title: Bob Dunning: Congress stands up for journalism
author: Bob Dunning
description: Sometimes, I see newspaper headlines that make me jump for joy, and other times, frequently on the same day in the same paper, I see headlines that make me wonder
content:
Sometimes, I see newspaper headlines that make me jump for joy, and other times, frequently on the same day in the same paper, I see headlines that make me wonder what the world is coming to.
The former was the case earlier this year when I saw a headline in The Bee that declared "House passes PRESS Act to shield journalists from revealing sources."

title: DHS volleyball losing close ones
author: Sean Campbell
description: Down two sets to zero against the Oak Ridge Trojans, the Davis High boys volleyball team had control of the third set, 23-18.
content:
Down two sets to zero against the Oak Ridge Trojans, the Davis High boys volleyball team had control of the third set, 23-18.
A comeback felt possible against a team that handled the Devils in a March 9 tournament contest, 2-0 (25-18, 25-22).

title: Suspect arrested in trio of Woodland robberies
author: Lauren Keene
description: Woodland police, with help from a K-9, arrested a man suspected of robbing three people at knifepoint last week.
content:
Woodland police, with help from a K-9, arrested a man suspected of robbing three people at knifepoint last week.
Officers made contact with Jose Guerrero shortly after 9:30 p.m. March 8 after being dispatched to a robbery report in the 1200 block of East Gibson Road, Sgt. Richard Towle reported Thursday.

title: UCD men a win away from The Big Dance
author: Bob Dunning
description: HENDERSON, Nev. — UC Davis built a 17-point second-half lead, then held on at the end to take a tense 68-65 win over the University of Hawaii to move into
content:
HENDERSON, Nev. — UC Davis built a 17-point second-half lead, then held on at the end to take a tense 68-65 win over the University of Hawaii to move into the championship game of the Big West men's basketball tournament late Friday night at the Dollar Loan Center.
The Aggies (20-12) now will take on Long Beach State at 6:30 p.m. Saturday with a chance to advance to the NCAA's March Madness with a victory. The Beach, a No. 4 seed, shocked No. UC Irvine, 83-79, earlier in the day.

content:
The Yolo County Board of Supervisors is seeking applications for openings on its Community Services Action Board.
The Community Services Action Board's mission is to combat poverty by promoting the health, safety, stability and self-sufficiency of low-income persons residing in Yolo County. The board is advisory to the Board of Supervisors with the following primary functions:

title: Rich Rifkin: Remembering the Hamels in three historic properties
author: Rich Rifkin
description: After the Davis City Council appointed me to serve on the Historical Resources Management Commission in 2005, I was handed a roster of properties in town that had been officially
content:
After the Davis City Council appointed me to serve on the Historical Resources Management Commission in 2005, I was handed a roster of properties in town that had been officially designated as 'historic resources.'
At the suggestion of one of my fellow commissioners, I visited all 39 on the list. Most were simple enough to see. But one — the Werner-Hamel House, a city landmark at 1140 Los Robles Street in South Davis — was blocked by a thick growth of foliage.

title: Letter: More to this group
author: Letter to the Editor
description: The Enterprise 'Students for Justice in Palestine' article provided a one-sided glimpse of SJP's mission, but Davisites should know more about their long history of supporting terrorism and promoting anti-Israel
content:
The Enterprise 'Students for Justice in Palestine' article provided a one-sided glimpse of SJP's mission, but Davisites should know more about their long history of supporting terrorism and promoting anti-Israel activity in our town.
After the Oct. 7 massacre of 1,200 people by Hamas in Israel, the national chapter of SJP celebrated the barbaric act by proclaiming that "National liberation is near — glory to our resistance, to our martyrs, and to our steadfast people" and "Today, we witness a historic win for the Palestinian resistance." "Resistance" is the word Hamas and SJP use to describe terrorism against men, women and children.

title: Newsom backs Biden's cease-fire call
author: Sameea Kamal
description: Gov. Gavin Newsom said Thursday he supports President Biden's call for a cease fire in Gaza, citing the 'ongoing and horrific loss of innocent civilian life.'
content:
Gov. Gavin Newsom said Thursday he supports President Biden's call for a cease fire in Gaza, citing the 'ongoing and horrific loss of innocent civilian life.'
'I support President Biden's call for an immediate cease fire as part of a deal to secure desperately needed relief for Gazan civilians and the release of hostages,' he wrote in a letter addressed to California's Muslim, Palestinian American, and Arab American communities. 'I also unequivocally denounce Hamas's terrorist attack against Israel. It is time to work in earnest toward an enduring peace that will furnish the lasting security, autonomy, and freedom that the Palestinians and the Israeli people both deserve.'

title: Bob Dunning: Should March Madness expand?
author: Bob Dunning
description: The question keeps popping up. Should the NCAA expand the field of its post-season March Madness basketball tournament?
content:
The question keeps popping up. Should the NCAA expand the field of its post-season March Madness basketball tournament?
While the question concerns both the men's and women's tournaments, it seems most of the commentary and speculation surrounds the men and where that single-elimination playoff may be headed.

title: Mikuni donates $5K to Make It Happen
author: Enterprise staff
description: Mikuni Charitable Organization recently donated $5,000 to ensure local under-resourced transition-age youths can successfully live independently through services provided by nonprofit Make It Happen for Yolo County. The donation will
content:
Mikuni Charitable Organization recently donated $5,000 to ensure local under-resourced transition-age youths can successfully live independently through services provided by nonprofit Make It Happen for Yolo County. The donation will help Make It Happen provide furniture, appliances and other essential household items needed to establish a first home.
'Mikuni continues to be one of our most steadfast donors and ardent advocates for youth in Yolo County,' said Cathi Schmidt, executive director, Make It Happen for Yolo County. 'We are so thankful to Mikuni for using its important profile as one of our region's top restaurants to provide support for the youth in our community who need it most.'
Celebrating its 10th anniversary this year, Make It Happen for Yolo County provides local transition age youths ages 18-24, many of whom have been in foster care or experienced homelessness, with furniture, appliances and household items needed to move into their first apartments.

title: Wildhorse gunfire leads to man's arrest
author: Lauren Keene
description: Gunfire early Friday morning sent Davis police to the Wildhorse neighborhood, where they arrested a man who allegedly shot at a fleeing vehicle.
content:
Gunfire early Friday morning sent Davis police to the Wildhorse neighborhood, where they arrested a man who allegedly shot at a fleeing vehicle.
Deputy Police Chief Todd Henry said the incident unfolded around 12:30 a.m. with a conversation between two men in the 2400 block of Moore Boulevard.

title: Yolo Crisis Nursery: A shell-ebration of community, support
author: Heather Sleuter
description: The 12th Annual Yolo Crisis Nursery Crab Feed was a resounding success, proving to be an extraordinary gathering that reconnected our community in a powerful way. Almost 400 crab dinners,
content:
The 12th Annual Yolo Crisis Nursery Crab Feed was a resounding success, proving to be an extraordinary gathering that reconnected our community in a powerful way. Almost 400 crab dinners, both take-out and in-person, were enjoyed!
This incredible turnout made the crab feed sell-out faster than ever before, a true testament to the unmatched generosity of our community. All proceeds from the Crab Feed directly support the Yolo Crisis Nursery Respite Care Programs serving Yolo County children and families facing unimaginable crises.

title: Readers' Choice 2024: Marie Farver — Best Volunteer
author: Lauren Keene
description: Marie Farver maintains several tenets when it comes to her volunteer work.
content:
Marie Farver maintains several tenets when it comes to her volunteer work.
First is her commitment to her Christian faith. 'It's really the source for sacrificial service,' said Farver, a longtime member of Davis' Grace Valley Christian Center.

title: Readers' Choice 2024: Davis Glass & Screen — Best Glass Replacement
author: Special to The Enterprise
description: In Summer 2016, Johnny Rexroth became the new owner of Davis Glass and Screen (previously Anderson Glass), keeping the same crew but changing the name.
content:
In Summer 2016, Johnny Rexroth became the new owner of Davis Glass and Screen (previously Anderson Glass), keeping the same crew but changing the name.
Davis Glass and Screen is a state-certified contractor specializing in residential windows, sliding patio doors, beveled glass/mirrors, solar screens, screen repairs and replacements as well as shower/tub doors and enclosures.

title: Readers' Choice 2024: Bella Luna Jewelers — Best Jewelry Store
author: Special to The Enterprise
description: De Luna Jewelers, established in 1967 by Richard Luna, relocated to 207 F St. as the new entity of Bella Luna Jewelers in 2016. Under the continual mentorship of Richard
content:
De Luna Jewelers, established in 1967 by Richard Luna, relocated to 207 F St. as the new entity of Bella Luna Jewelers in 2016. Under the continual mentorship of Richard and Kyoko Luna, and new owner Stephanie Choi, Bella Luna Jewelers continues to serve the community as a family-owned business with generations of experience in the gem, jewelry and timepiece trade. For the past 53 years, it has established a reputation for quality craftsmanship, trend-setting designs, and superior restoration services.
'Our motto is to provide quality products and services and to inspire confidence while delivering the knowledge and skills necessary to keep clients' jewelry safe and long lasting,' Choi said. 'Bella Luna offers fine jewelry collections, professional jewelry and timepiece restoration, custom design, consignment, appraisals, and — in long standing tradition of de Luna — Southwest pottery and Oaxacan folk art.'

title: Expert Landscaping Tips for Choosing and Installing Plants
description: (StatePoint) The perfect landscape may start with a healthy, lush lawn, but for interest and depth, you'll also need to consider the plants that surround it.
content:
(StatePoint) The perfect landscape may start with a healthy, lush lawn, but for interest and depth, you'll also need to consider the plants that surround it.
Thankfully, it's easy to make considerable improvements to your backyard life using tips from professionals. Landscape designer Doug Scott has partnered with lawn care equipment manufacturer Exmark, to offer these tips for selecting and installing plants that will beautify your outdoor living areas.

title: Poetry night back on April 4
author: Special to The Enterprise
description: The Poetry Night Reading Series is excited to feature Davis Poet Laureate Julia B. Levine and Rebecca Foust at 7 p.m. Thursday, April 4, on the roof of the John
content:
The Poetry Night Reading Series is excited to feature Davis Poet Laureate Julia B. Levine and Rebecca Foust at 7 p.m. Thursday, April 4, on the roof of the John Natsoulas Gallery, 521 First St. in Davis. Dress warmly.
Levine's poetry has won many awards, including a 2021 Nautilus Award for her fifth poetry collection, Ordinary Psalms, (LSU press, 2021), as well as the 2015 Northern California Book Award in Poetry for her fourth collection, Small Disasters Seen in Sunlight, (LSU, 2014).
Recently, she has won the 2023 Oran Perry Burke Award from The Southern Review, the 2022 Steve Kowit Poetry Prize, the 2020 Bellevue Literary Review Poetry Award, as well as a 2022 American Academy of Poetry Poet Laureate Fellowship for her work in building resilience in teenagers related to climate change through poetry, science and technology.
She received a Ph.D. in clinical psychology from UC Berkeley and an MFA in poetry from Pacific University.
Rebecca Foust's fourth book, 'ONLY' (Four Way Books, 2022) earned a starred review in Publishers Weekly and was recently reviewed by Mark Jarmon in The Hudson Review. Her poems, in journals including Narrative, POETRY, Ploughshares, and Southern Review, won last year's New Ohio Review prize and were runner-up for the Missouri Review Editors Prize. Recognitions include the James Hearst, Pablo Neruda and Poetry International prizes, fellowships at Hedgebrook, MacDowell, and Sewanee Writers Conference, and a Marin County Poet Laureateship where Rebecca's program, 'Poetry as Sanctuary,' featured readings by local immigrant poets.
An open mic will follow the featured performers. Open mic performances will be limited to four minutes or two items, whichever is shorter. The open mic list typically fills by 6:50 p.m., so arrive early if you would like to perform something during the 8 o'clock hour.

title: Human brains are getting larger; good news for dementia risk
author: Special to The Enterprise
description: SACRAMENTO — A new study by researchers at UC Davis Health found human brains are getting larger. Study participants born in the 1970s had 6.6% larger brain volumes and almost
content:
SACRAMENTO — A new study by researchers at UC Davis Health found human brains are getting larger. Study participants born in the 1970s had 6.6% larger brain volumes and almost 15% larger brain surface area than those born in the 1930s.
The researchers hypothesize the increased brain size may lead to an increased brain reserve, potentially reducing the overall risk of age-related dementias.

title: How Volunteering Can Help Older Adults Combat Loneliness
description: (Family Features) The bonds found in friendships and other relationships are an important factor in health and wellness – even science says so.
content:
(Family Features) The bonds found in friendships and other relationships are an important factor in health and wellness – even science says so.
According to the American Psychological Association, forming and maintaining social connections at any age is one of the most reliable predictors of a healthy, happy and long life. Studies show having strong and supportive friendships can fend off depression and anxiety, lower blood pressure and heart rates in stressful situations and change the way people perceive daunting tasks.

title: Per Capita: Pieces of the puzzle
author: John Mott Smith
description: The climate crisis is complicated. It's impossible to keep track of all the positive, negative and neutral events taking place around the globe, in turn making it hard to figure
content:
The climate crisis is complicated. It's impossible to keep track of all the positive, negative and neutral events taking place around the globe, in turn making it hard to figure out if we are moving forward, backsliding, or stuck in the status quo. Here, for your amusement, or frustration, are a few items I plucked from recent news.
First, from a sustainability newsletter 'The Hill,' their 'big story' in the March 27 edition is titled, 'Record growth in renewables, with a long way to go.' Talk about a glass half full and half empty at the same time, it starts off with the good news from a recent report from the International Renewable Energy Agency.

title: Newsom, Legislature get a $17 billion jump on California budget deficit
author: Alexei Koseff
description: Not filling open positions in state government, cutting welfare programs that serve tens of thousands of families, delaying funding for public transit — these are some of the first steps
content:
Not filling open positions in state government, cutting welfare programs that serve tens of thousands of families, delaying funding for public transit — these are some of the first steps that California officials plan to take to deal with a looming multibillion-dollar budget deficit.
Facing a shortfall estimated at somewhere between $38 billion and $73 billion next year, Gov. Gavin Newsom and legislative leaders announced today an 'early action' plan to tackle part of that gap before the regular budget process later this spring.

title: Explorit: April showers and storms
author: Chris Vera Zelada
description: Did you know that in April several jet streams form in the Northern Hemisphere causing a lot of rain? This is called the April showers.
content:
Did you know that in April several jet streams form in the Northern Hemisphere causing a lot of rain? This is called the April showers.
Jet streams in the early spring start to rotate northward and pick up strong winds and rain from the Atlantic Ocean. One thing about April is that it can be all sunshine and rainbows one day, and then suddenly heavy downpour of rain occurs the next day. Some of these heavy rain showers can also cause lightning storms.

description: In April, Empower Yolo recognizes Sexual Assault Awareness Month (SAAM) and Child Abuse Prevention Month, campaigns to raise awareness about sexual violence, and support survivors.
content:
In April, Empower Yolo recognizes Sexual Assault Awareness Month (SAAM) and Child Abuse Prevention Month, campaigns to raise awareness about sexual violence, and support survivors.
Sexual violence is sexual activity when consent is not obtained or freely given; it includes any type of unwanted sexual contact including sexual assault, harassment, and abuse. It is a serious public health problem in the United States that profoundly impacts lifelong health, opportunity, and well-being. Sexual violence impacts every community and affects people of all genders, sexual orientations, and ages. See Fast Facts: Preventing Sexual Violence, Centers for Disease, Control and Prevention, June 22, 2022.

title: Explaining California college costs
author: Mikhail Zinshteyn
description: University tuition is free! No, wait, the full cost of college is tens of thousands of dollars annually. Hold up. There's enough financial aid to bring down the price tag
content:
University tuition is free! No, wait, the full cost of college is tens of thousands of dollars annually. Hold up. There's enough financial aid to bring down the price tag to just a few thousand dollars a year — tuition, food and housing included.
All of those statements are true, depending on where you attend and how much you or the parents who claim you on their taxes earn. For something as consequential — and at times more costly than a small condo — as affording a degree, understanding how much a family must shell out for a better shot at higher wages can be complicated.

content:

title: Tom Elias: Simpson trial destroyed our illusions
author: Tom Elias
description: The late OJ Simpson does not leave many personal legacies: the most meaningful are probably one Heisman Trophy, his children and grandchildren.
content:
The late OJ Simpson does not leave many personal legacies: the most meaningful are probably one Heisman Trophy, his children and grandchildren.
But his 1994-95 trial for the stabbing murders of his ex-wife Nicole Brown Simpson, mother of two of those children, and her friend Ron Goldman is another story. Its legacies include openness about using race as a prime factor in selecting jurors; making jury selection consultants key legal figures, and establishing Johnny L. Cochran as one of the pre-eminent defense lawyers of the last century.

title: Letter: It doesn't count

content:
Defacing a flag in someone's yard is a property crime, but certainly not a hate crime. That's been clarified in U.S. courts countless times. It's an act of protest, regardless of how distasteful you might find it. Davis politicians saying otherwise are just pandering to the electorate.
You have the right to fly a confederate flag, but would you be surprised if someone tore it down? You have the right to fly a nazi flag, but would you be surprised if someone tore it down?

title: Letter: Lay off the theater
author: Letter to the Editor
description: The same destructive components that contributed to the self-evisceration of the Former Republic of Yugoslavia in the 1990s — racial hatred, politicians intentionally fomenting hatred and fear, rampaging paramilitary organizations,
content:
The same destructive components that contributed to the self-evisceration of the Former Republic of Yugoslavia in the 1990s — racial hatred, politicians intentionally fomenting hatred and fear, rampaging paramilitary organizations, and national news agencies that act more like propaganda machines than agencies of solid journalism — are, unfortunately, part of the current cultural landscape of the U.S. today.
The civil war that took place in the Former Republic of Yugoslavia in the 1990s left millions traumatized, hundreds of thousands scarred for life, and over a hundred thousand killed. The parallels to what is currently happening in my own country right now are alarming. This is not the time for political kabuki theater — like what some politicians staged for over 28 months (longer than the JFK and 9/11 commissions put together) investigating the murder of our diplomatic team in Benghazi.

title: Citrus Circuits concludes 20th season at World Championship
author: Special to The Enterprise
description: Davis robotics team 1678 Citrus Circuits concluded its 20th season as third in the world after the FIRST World Championship. This is the 10th consecutive year it won its division
content:
Davis robotics team 1678 Citrus Circuits concluded its 20th season as third in the world after the FIRST World Championship. This is the 10th consecutive year it won its division and competed in the finals matches.
Citrus Circuits competed in the FIRST Robotics Competition (FRC) alongside nearly 600 teams from around the world. The exciting event drew 50,000 people from 58 countries to Houston, Texas, from April 17 to 21.
'This was a great conclusion to our 20th season and really shows the level of excellence our team is able to achieve,' said head coach Mike Corsetto. 'The team has come a long way since 2004 and we're excited to be among the best in the world.'
The 2024 game, Crescendo, presented by The Gene Haas Foundation, was based on the 2021 winning game design concept developed by Citrus Circuits named Storm Surge. Each match begins with a 15 second autonomous period where teams cannot manually control their robot and must instead run an autonomous program to score torus shaped game pieces called notes into the goal located at each end of the field.
After the first 15 seconds, teams gain control of their robots to continue scoring and in the last 30 seconds attempt to have up to three robots climb on hanging chains.
Founded in 2004, Citrus Circuits has slowly worked to become one of the top teams in FRC, gaining members, new sponsors, and numerous awards along the way. This season, the team won two regionals, the regional Impact Award, Excellence in Engineering Award, and Innovation in Control Award.
At the World Championship, the team received the Autonomous Award and were winners of the Archimedes Division. Statistically, the team is ranked number one in the world in terms of overall performance.
The team competed against 74 other teams in the Archimedes division, placing 2nd overall after Qualification matches. Citrus Circuits joined the 1st seeded alliance, lead 4613 Barker Redbacks from Sydney, Australia, and included 4206 Robo Vikes from Fort Worth, Texas, and 2178 Team OKC e'possums from Oklahoma City.
The alliance pushed through playoff matches and advanced to the Einstein field for the 10th year in a row, setting the game high-score twice and the world record.
The team consists of almost 100 students from high schools and junior high schools within the Davis Joint Unified School District. Major sponsors include UC Davis, DJUSD, TechnipFMC, Lockheed Martin, DMG Mori, and Cedaron.

content:
Maria Maea creates sculpture and installations, often of abstracted bodies. Through her practice, she deepens her connection to land, somatic memory and ancestry in work that celebrates her experience growing up in her family's Samoan Mexican American community in Southern California. She will give a public lecture at UC Davis on May 2 at 5 p.m. in 1003 Cruess Hall. The event is free and open to the public.
The palm features prominently in Maea's work, speaking to the resilience of those forced to uproot their lives in the wake of colonization and their ability to thrive in new, often hostile environments. She engages with these plants through a practice that that emphasizes collaborative making with family and friends. In addition to her public lecture, Maea will lead a weaving workshop at the Student Farm at UC Davis for current students and conduct graduate student critiques with Art Studio MFA students.

title: Historic Agreement Signed By Red Cross and Armed Forces
description: (NAPSI)—Good news for American military members and their families: A new program aims to provide emergency communications briefings to 100% of military recruits.
content:
(NAPSI)—Good news for American military members and their families: A new program aims to provide emergency communications briefings to 100% of military recruits.
The American Red Cross, alongside the United States Military Entrance Processing Command, signed a historic Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) to present the Red Cross Emergency Communication brief to all new military recruits.
What it Means
'For decades, the American Red Cross has provided services to applicants at Military Entrance Processing Stations throughout the nation,' said Colonel Megan B. Stallings, Commander, U.S. Military Entrance Processing Command. 'At our stations, volunteers provide information that could be critical to applicants and families in an emergency. It was a pleasure to meet with Dr. Jordan and discuss our Memorandum of Understanding.'
The Red Cross traditionally has volunteers who go to a Military Processing Entrance Station (MEPS) and meet with recruits who have recently taken the oath of enlistment. The recruits are preparing to ship to basic training, based on their branch, all over the country.
'The MEPS command is committed to setting the expectation with all 66 MEPS stations to present the Red Cross brief to 100% of shippers,' said Dr. Michael Jordan, Vice President of Service to the Armed Forces and International Services at the American Red Cross. 'It's a bold and extraordinary commitment that will benefit all new recruits.'
Through the Red Cross 'Get To Know Us Before You Need Us' program, new enlistees and their families are able to ask questions about military family life and learn how Red Cross services can help before, during and after deployment.
One of the many ways the American Red Cross supports U.S. service members is through the Hero Care Center. In times of emergency, the Red Cross helps military families communicate with their loved ones through the Hero Care Network, available 24 hours a day online, by phone and through the mobile app.
'We share information that basically says, ‘if your family has an emergency, or if you have an emergency, you both need to know how to call the Red Cross and initiate Emergency Communication,'' said Joshua Cain, Director of Service to the Armed Forces and International Services at the Red Cross and Army Veteran. 'The signing of the MOU gives us sustainability for this program for years to come and helps us get military families the support they need.'
Cain served in the Army as a medic, working alongside medical professionals and Red Cross volunteers at military hospitals. Before shipping to basic training, Cain received the Red Cross Emergency Communications brief at the MEPS site in Fort Meade, Maryland alongside his father who reenlisted after the 9/11 terrorist attacks.
'We went to Fort Jackson, South Carolina for basic training. It was intense,' Cain said. 'When we arrived to basic training, they gave us a 90-second call to our parents and said to tell them that if there's an emergency, to call the Red Cross.'
Along with Red Cross Emergency Communications briefings, Red Cross Service to the Armed Forces has initiated skill-building and wellness workshops at MEPS sites. The programs are designed to bring wellness to the staff at the sites, many of whom are veterans or family members of veterans.
'Recruits don't know what communication will look like while they are in basic training or while serving,' Cain said. 'The Red Cross bridges that gap that says, ‘It doesn't matter where you go, your family will be able to get in touch with you during an emergency because of the Red Cross.''
Learn More
To find out more about how the Red Cross helps members of the military, veterans and their families prepare for, cope with, and respond to, the challenges of military service visit www.redcross.org.
About the American Red Cross
The American Red Cross shelters, feeds and provides comfort to victims of disasters; supplies about 40% of the nation's blood; teaches skills that save lives; distributes international humanitarian aid; and supports veterans, military members and their families. The Red Cross is a nonprofit organization that depends on volunteers and the generosity of the American public to deliver its mission. For more information, visit redcross.org or CruzRojaAmericana.org, or follow it on social media.
"'For decades, the American Red Cross has provided services to applicants at Military Entrance Processing Stations throughout the nation,' said Colonel Megan B. Stallings, Commander, U.S. Military Entrance Processing Command."
