content: New Harmony Jazz Band will play two free sets of big band, swing, and Latin jazz standards amid the splendor of the Davis Craft & Vintage Fair on Sunday, April 21, 11 a.m. to 1 p.m. in Central Park.

title: Commentary: Protect consumers from AI
author: Justin Kloczko
description: Artificial intelligence may soon replace financial advisors, and that's just the start. While one algorithm predicts stock price, another decides what to disclose to regulators. Chat GPT-style language models could
content:
Artificial intelligence may soon replace financial advisors, and that's just the start. While one algorithm predicts stock price, another decides what to disclose to regulators. Chat GPT-style language models could soon hallucinate your mortgage application or life savings, and you won't even know it.
I spent several months combing through the U.S Patent and Trademark Office to see how the world's most powerful investment banks are incorporating artificial intelligence, and it's a scary glimpse into the future.

title: Tom Elias: In a rental surprise, Bay Area tenants do best
author: Tom Elias
description: Rents are higher in Silicon Valley and the rest of the San Francisco Bay area than anywhere else in California, but the generally higher salaries in that region nevertheless give
content:
Rents are higher in Silicon Valley and the rest of the San Francisco Bay area than anywhere else in California, but the generally higher salaries in that region nevertheless give tenants there more disposable income than anywhere else in this state, even the far lower-priced Central Valley.
That's the surprising conclusion of a study by the RentCafe website, which tracks income vs. expenses for renters everywhere in America.

title: Solid wins a harbinger for DHS lacrosse?
author: Bruce Gallaudet
description: Not a bad way to enter a layoff: both Davis High girls and boys lacrosse teams came away with resounding victories over Bella Vista last week. Now the meat of
content:
Not a bad way to enter a layoff: both Davis High girls and boys lacrosse teams came away with resounding victories over Bella Vista last week. Now the meat of the Delta League schedule looms.
This week is spring break and there's time for the Blue Devils to collect their thoughts about what needs to be done down the stretch as each DHS squad sits unbeaten in conference.

title: Comings & Goings: Bruxie to open first Northern California eatery
description: Bruxie – the chicken and waffles restaurant coming to Davis Commons – is set to begin its soft opening on Monday, April 8. The grand opening is Saturday, April 20.
content:
Bruxie – the chicken and waffles restaurant coming to Davis Commons – is set to begin its soft opening on Monday, April 8. The grand opening is Saturday, April 20.
The restaurant offers unconventional waffle sandwiches, chicken tenders and custard shakes. The brand began in 2010. The Davis store is Bruxie's first in Northern California. It has eight eateries in Southern California and two in Georgia.

title: Yolo CASA: Opportunities to help kids in foster care
author: Doni De Bolt
description: April is Child Abuse Prevention Month which is an issue near and dear to our hearts at Yolo County CASA. We know that prevention is key, and in light of
content:
April is Child Abuse Prevention Month which is an issue near and dear to our hearts at Yolo County CASA. We know that prevention is key, and in light of the challenges posed in the past years with the pandemic and the economy, it is more crucial than ever to remain vigilant in identifying and addressing instances of child abuse and neglect.
The stressors stemming from these difficult times have unfortunately exacerbated the risk factors for child abuse, underscoring the urgency for heightened awareness and action. Our collective efforts in recognizing and responding to the warning signs can make a significant difference in safeguarding the well-being of vulnerable children.

title: High stakes: Inside the multimillion-dollar battle for gambling rights in California
author: Ryan Sabalow
description: Powerful tribal casinos and their rivals in California's multi-billion dollar gambling industry are fighting an epic battle in the Legislature this year. Millions of dollars in tax revenues for local
content:
Powerful tribal casinos and their rivals in California's multi-billion dollar gambling industry are fighting an epic battle in the Legislature this year. Millions of dollars in tax revenues for local cities hang in the balance.
Pending legislation would let California's tribes sue their competitors, private card clubs, over their claim that card rooms are violating the tribes' exclusive rights to Las Vegas-style gambling.
Card rooms have responded with an enormous lobbying blitz. The Hawaiian Gardens Casino in Los Angeles County spent a staggering $9.1 million on lobbying last year, the second highest amount reported to state regulators. Only the international oil giant, Chevron Corp., spent more.
'If you're going to attack us and try to take away what we've had for decades, then we've got to fight back,' said Keith Sharp, the card room's general counsel. 'And so we're going to spend the money that we need to spend. I mean it's about survival at this point.'
Cities also have a lot at stake with the card rooms. San Jose officials told legislators they could hire 80 police officers if they could add 30 more tables to their local card rooms. Nearly two thirds of the budget for the city of Hawaiian Gardens and almost half for the city of Commerce, also in Los Angeles County, come from local card rooms.
'Those games, we're very dependent on here in the city,' said Commerce Mayor Hugo Argumedo. 'They provide many of the programs and services that we offer to the residents in our community.'
The legislation, Senate Bill 549, is backed primarily by a group of Native American tribes that run major casinos. The tribes are among the most influential and biggest spending lobbies in Sacramento. Since 2014, California's candidates for state office have received about $23.5 million from tribes. That's more than double what oil companies have given the state's politicians during the same years.
The state's card room industry, by comparison, has donated about $3.8 million during the same timeframe.
A group of tribes contend the 80 or so privately-owned gambling halls are illegally offering games such as blackjack, baccarat and pai gow poker, and by doing so, they've for years been stealing hundreds of millions of dollars of revenue from historically disenfranchised tribal communities across California.
'It's not about killing card rooms. It's not about killing cities. It's about protecting what's ours,' Tuari Bigknife, the attorney general for the Viejas Band of Kumeyaay Indians, told CalMatters. His tribe operates a large casino in San Diego County.
SB 549 is pending before the Assembly Governmental Organization Committee, which handles gambling legislation. A hearing hasn't been scheduled, but those following the bill say it will be heard later in April or in May.
Card rooms frame the issue as a David vs. Goliath fight, since their annual earnings are barely 10% of what tribal governments make from gambling at their 70 tribal casinos. The card rooms also have influential allies in local governments officials who say their cities could go bankrupt if their local gambling hall loses this legislative fight.
When the pandemic shut down gaming in Hawaiian Gardens, the city was forced to lay off much of its staff and cut services. Mayor Victor Farfan said it was a sign of what would happen if the card room was no longer able to play the disputed games.
'We're very, very limited in what we can do,' Farfan said in an interview with CalMatters at Hawaiian Gardens City Hall, the card room visible from the parking lot. 'And so we're fortunate enough to have a revenue source that we do today.'
Mayor Victor Farfan at Hawaiian Gardens City Hall in Hawaiian Gardens on March 14, 2024. Photo by Ted Soqui for CalMatters
Tribes, however, argue there are other ways for cities to raise money without infringing on tribes' gambling rights that California voters enshrined into the state's constitution.
'They can tax; they can issue bonds; they can do lots of things,' said Bigknife, the attorney general for the Viejas tribe. 'All this does is shut down illegal revenue.'
Gold Rush gambling rules fuel conflict
The gambling dispute has roots in the Gold Rush, a time when unscrupulous gambling halls were fleecing miners. In response, the young Legislature prohibited gambling halls from offering games like the kind in Las Vegas where casinos are the 'house' and take bets directly.
That prohibition lasted until 2000, when voters approved an initiative that and gave tribes the right to negotiate compacts with the state to host certain house-banked casino games.
No one disputes that the privately owned card rooms can offer poker, since players bet against each other. The dispute behind SB 549 involves traditionally house-banked card games, especially blackjack, the most lucrative of the disputed games.
Under the California constitution, the card rooms can't accept wagers from customers. The card clubs get around the prohibition by contracting with third-party companies that serve the role as the 'house' or the 'bank.' These third-party employees typically sit at card tables next to the card room employees who deal cards to players. The third-party employee plays no part of the game except to collect players' bets and pay out winnings. The dealers must periodically offer the opportunity for the players to act as the bank. Almost every customer declines. The card clubs collect fees from each game.
First: A blackjack training game demonstration at Gardens Casino. Last: The outside of the Gardens Casino. Hawaiian Gardens on March 14, 2024. Photos by Ted Soqui for CalMatters
A card room at Commerce Casino in Commerce on March 14, 2024. Photo by Ted Soqui for CalMatters
The gambling halls say their business model has been approved by state regulators.
'Every game that (the tribes are) saying is illegal right now, every single one of them has been explicitly approved individually in every card room in the state of California,' Ed Manning, a lobbyist for the card room industry, told lawmakers last summer at the bill's first hearing.
Tribal casinos, however, call the card room business model an illegal sham, and they have been pleading with state regulators, voters and now lawmakers to end it.
The tribes have repeatedly urged the California Justice Department to step in and prohibit the disputed games. The past three attorneys general have discussed various regulations, but so far none have resolved the politically fraught issue.
Current Attorney General Rob Bonta last year proposed a new set of rules that card rooms say could make it difficult to keep playing the disputed games and tribes say don't go far enough. The proposed regulations are pending at the department's Bureau of Gambling Control without a schedule for consideration.
Meanwhile, card rooms and tribal governments have been donating heavily to Bonta since he took office in 2021. Since then the card room industry has donated at least $287,000. Tribes have given at least $222,000, according to OpenSecrets. Bonta said he is considering a campaign for governor in 2026.
Tribes seek standing to sue competitors
Getting no satisfaction from regulators, the tribes tried to sue card rooms for unfair business practices. But California's courts have ruled that because the tribes are sovereign governments, they don't have standing to sue under that particular statute.
The tribes next turned to voters. In 2022, the tribes put Proposition 26 on the ballot. The initiative, mainly about sports betting, contained a provision that would have allowed anyone, including tribal members, to file a lawsuit if they believed state gambling laws were being violated and the Department of Justice declined to act.
Voters overwhelmingly rejected the measure after more than $170 million was spent trying to sway them.
Now, the tribes want lawmakers to give them a brief window to sue card rooms to settle their dispute. SB 549 explicitly prohibits the tribes from seeking monetary damages, penalties or attorney's fees from card rooms. It would only let a court decide whether the gambling halls' business model is legal.
The tribes contend that if the card rooms are operating legally, they have nothing to fear.
'The card rooms should relish the opportunity to defeat the tribes on this issue and to prove up the legality of what they're doing,' Bigknife, the Viejas attorney general, told lawmakers at the hearing last summer.
Sharp, the general counsel for the Hawaiian Gardens Casino, said the bigger worry is that if SB 549 passes, the courts would become the de facto gambling regulator. It could force card room operators to seek a court's permission for any new game they'd like to play or any time they'd want to modify the hundreds of games they already play, he said.
'We'll be tied up in court forever, so the lawyers will make money,' Sharp said. 'That may be the (tribes') other strategy: … Grind the card rooms down ultimately with legal fees.'
Plus, the card rooms argue that if the tribes are given standing to sue them, it wouldn't cut both ways. As sovereign governments, the tribes couldn't be sued by the card rooms.
Bipartisan support for bill
SB 549 is authored by Fullerton Democratic Sen. Josh Newman, and it has nine co-authors including prominent Democrats, Cecilia Aguiar-Curry, the Assembly's majority leader, and former Senate President Toni Atkins. The bill's Republican co-authors include Senator Scott Wilk and Assemblymember Marie Waldron, both former minority leaders in their chambers.
Despite the support for the tribes from some of the Legislature's most influential members, it's anyone's guess whether the bill ends up making it to the governor's desk. This gambling dispute doesn't break down along partisan, regional or ideological lines. How lawmakers vote will most likely depend on whether they have a major card room or a tribal casino in their district.
Meanwhile, both sides have been spending millions of dollars to influence lawmakers.
Atkins' campaign, for instance, has received at least $215,000 from tribes since 2014.
'SB 549 allows tribes to bring their concerns about possible infringement of their constitutional rights to the courts, where this issue can be addressed by an impartial judicial system,' Atkins told CalMatters in an emailed statement. 'After a history fraught with injustice, allowing tribes access to the courts to get an answer is a step worth taking.'
The tribes also have been major backers of causes important to prominent Democrats, including Gov. Gavin Newsom. For instance, the Federated Indians of Graton Rancheria contributed $1.5 million to the campaign for the Newsom-championed Proposition 1 mental health bond, which barely passed in the March primary election. That tribe also donated $750,000 to help Newsom defeat the 2021 campaign to recall him.
By comparison, card rooms and their affiliated businesses have only donated at least $229,250 to Newsom since 2014.
But money isn't the only way the gambling interests are trying to sway legislators.
Card rooms, unions pressure Sen. Newman
It was a sunny day in December when a bus stopped at Sen. Newman's Fullerton district office. Dozens of protestors stepped off, wearing small red and white stickers on their chests, made to look like nametags.
'Hi. My name is Newman,' they read. 'I support wealthy tribal casinos over my constituents' jobs.'
Shavon Moore-Cage, a member of AFSCME (American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees), a municipal employee union, was among the more than 100 people who attended the rally that day.
She said the protesters wanted to send a message to Newman about his 'job-killing' bill that would harm the local gambling hall whose tax revenues bankroll her employer, the city of Hawaiian Gardens.
'We ruined his day, hopefully,' she said as she grinned in a recent interview. Newman didn't respond to repeated requests for comment from CalMatters.
Shavon Moore-Cage, a member of AFSCME Local 36, at Hawaiian Gardens City Hall in Hawaiian Gardens on March 14, 2024. Photo by Ted Soqui for CalMatters
Newman is one of the state's most vulnerable Democrats. He was successfully recalled in 2018 before regaining his seat two years later. Newman just spent months fending off a primary challenge from four novice Democratic candidates with possible ties to the gambling dispute.
A local chapter of AFSCME gave more than $700,000 to the four challengers. The statewide union is an opponent of Newman's casino bill. Janice O'Malley, a lobbyist representing AFSCME's statewide political efforts in Sacramento, didn't respond to requests for comment.
But Moore-Cage said her union, AFSCME Local 36, didn't back the four candidates. Newman told Politico he believes the election challenge was payback over a separate fight about University of California workers.
Newman's colleagues have noticed the pressure he's been under, regardless of whether the card room dispute played a role in AFSCME's decision to back Newman's primary challengers.
'I feel sorry for Newman,' said Aguiar-Curry, the principal coauthor of SB 549. 'For God sakes.'
She said Newman's gambling bill has some of her colleagues 'worried about their campaigns.'
Still, she said it's time to pass SB 549 and move the dispute between the tribal casinos and the gambling halls to the courts. 'Let's just get this done,' Aguiar-Curry said, 'and, as they say, have a brass backbone, legislators.'
Aguiar-Curry's district, which stretches west of Sacramento to Napa and north to Lake County, is home to Cache Creek Casino Resort, run by the Yocha Dehe Wintun Nation, one of the anti-card room tribes.
'Illegal activities at card rooms in our region have led to annual losses of $13 million to our gaming operation, Cache Creek Casino Resort,' Anthony Roberts, chairman of the Yocha Dehe Wintun Nation, told CalMatters in a statement. 'These activities violate our rights and impact our ability to serve our people, employees and local governmental partners.'
The Yocha Dehe tribe is a prominent political spender, having donated at least $2.6 million to statewide political campaigns since 2014. Aguiar-Curry's reelection campaign has received $37,700 from the tribe.
The tribe recently attacked Democratic Sen. Bill Dodd of Napa, whose district overlaps Aguiar-Curry's, over his role in the card room dispute.
Tribe attacks Sen. Dodd
In 2022, Dodd cast a deciding 'no' vote that killed a bill the Yocha Dehe and other tribes wanted that would have temporarily extended an expiring moratorium that kept new card rooms from opening.
Dodd told his colleagues at the time that a longer-term card room moratorium was needed. He jokingly called the never-ending moratorium debates 'the Continuing Employment Act for Lobbyists.'
'I'm sorry to say that, but you know what? We shouldn't have to hear this every two or three years and be subject to these fights,' he told the committee.
The Yocha Dehe tribe was furious at Dodd, since without the moratorium in place, new competing card rooms could potentially enter the market. Plus, the tribe was still smarting over a failed constitutional amendment Dodd introduced in 2019, which would have legalized sports betting via computers and cell phones. The amendment also would have clarified that card rooms had a right to offer their disputed games.
Early last year, the tribe sent out mailers to Dodd's constituents, accusing him of being too friendly to card rooms. They also put up a billboard on J Street not far from the Capitol in Sacramento.
'After $94,000 in political contributions from card rooms, Bill Dodd made it easier for card rooms to expand and open in Napa,' the billboard read.
In response, Dodd sent a video to his colleagues in the Legislature. Standing in front of the billboard, he said the tribe 'impugned my character and misled the public on my positions.'
'This was put forward by special interests and sleazy lobbyists,' he said in the video. 'You know, I've never liked bullies, and I never let bullies win. Cache Creek Casino and their lobbyist, Kevin Sloat, don't respect legislators. They don't respect the facts or the rules.'
State Sen. Bill Dodd speaks during the first day of session at the state Capitol in Sacramento on Jan. 3, 2024. Photo by Fred Greaves for CalMatters
Sloat declined to comment, referring to the tribe's emailed statement to CalMatters. It didn't address the tribe's dispute with Dodd.
In the end, Dodd co-authored legislation last year that prohibits new card rooms from opening in California for another 20 years. It had support from most card rooms and tribes. The warring gambling factions may not agree on which games card rooms should be allowed to offer, but both sides can agree that they don't want any new gambling halls cutting into their revenues.
The Yocha Dehe tribe was a notable exception. The tribe testified that it opposed the bill because it allowed some smaller existing card rooms to expand the number of what it contends are illegal gaming tables. (Aguiar-Curry, the tribe's close ally, cast the lone 'no' vote in the Assembly.)
Dodd's fight with the tribe could play a critical role in deciding the fate of the pending bill that would give tribes standing to sue card rooms, should SB 549 pass the Assembly.

title: UCD hoops star Johnson enters transfer portal
author: Bob Dunning
description: The transfer portal giveth and the transfer portal taketh away.
content:
The transfer portal giveth and the transfer portal taketh away.
UC Davis men's basketball star playmaker and second-leading scorer TY Johnson has entered the transfer portal, though Aggie head coach Jim Les hopes he will ultimately decide to finish his collegiate playing career with UCD.
"It's our new reality that players who have developed as TY has will attract attention and other schools will try to poach them," Les noted.
"It's become a wild, wild West scenario, with NIL (name, image and likeness payments) becoming a recruiting tool. That's actually been going on for a long time, but now it's legal."
A highly sought recruit out of DePaul College Prep in Chicago, Johnson spent his freshman year at Loyola Chicago, where he saw limited playing time.
Seeking a better opportunity, Johnson came to Davis two years ago and was an immediate fan favorite for his ability to score, dish out assists and key fast-breaks, along with an uncanny ability to elevate his game during critical moments.
"He's an awesome young man, an awesome player and he put in a lot of hard work to get where he is today," Les added.
"We're hoping that if he stays, we can springboard him into playing at the next level. He certainly has the skills, the work ethic and the mentality to succeed."
Johnson has just one year of eligibility left, whether at UC Davis or elsewhere, but a player who enters the transfer portal to test the waters still has the option to take his name out of the portal and remain with his current school.
Once a player's name has been placed in the portal, other schools are free to contact him.
Entering the transfer portal has become commonplace in college basketball, both men's and women's, with some schools experiencing multiple players in the portal and other schools relying heavily on the portal to rebuild their rosters.
UC Davis is no exception to that trend. While Les likes to bring in promising high school seniors and let them develop in the Davis system, he does on occasion use the portal to fill an immediate need.
The 2023-24 Aggie roster included transfers Kane Milling (Nevada), Pablo Tamba (Idaho State), Drew Carter (Colorado), Nico Rocak (UC Santa Barbara) and Johnson.
"We need to keep doing what we do, which is developing young players and offering them a great education and a great basketball experience," said the Aggie coach.
"But we have to respond to our needs, too, and sometimes that is in the portal."
In his first season at UCD, 2022-23, Johnson averaged 14.5 points a game, twice hitting 32 points in a single game. He led the Big West Conference in steals that year with 57.
He upped his game in the just-completed season, averaging 17.8 points a game, while leading the team in assists (104) and steals (58). He was also deadly from the foul line late in the game, helping to seal several wins with perfect free throw shooting down the stretch.
Johnson had 30 points each against Pacific, Hawaii and Long Beach State, 28 each against Pepperdine and Milwaukee, and 13 games in all with 20 points or more. He finished the season with 569 points and surpassed 1,000 points for his Aggie career on March 15 in a 68-65 win over Hawaii in the semifinals of the Big West Conference tournament.
Combined with Eli Pepper's 20.7 points per game, the two accounted for well over half of UCD's per-game scoring average of 71.2.
Pepper, the all-time leading scorer in Aggie history, has finished his eligibility.
"I think this is a really hard decision for him," Les said of Johnson.
"We're in regular communication, and in his heart, I think he doesn't want to leave Davis. He loves it here and is thriving, but for a variety of reasons, he feels like he needs to test the market.
"I still believe this is the best place for him, but we just have to see how it plays out. He knows how much we appreciate him as a player and as a person. He's on an upward trajectory and we'd love to have him finish that ride here."

author: Roche

Patients with HER2-low status may now be eligible for HER2-targeted treatment, which could significantly improve their outcome. 2
The VENTANA HER2 (4B5) test is the only approved companion diagnostic indicated as an aid in the assessment of HER2-low status in metastatic breast cancer patients.
TUCSON, Ariz., April 10, 2024 /PRNewswire/ -- Roche (SIX: RO, ROG; OTCQX: RHHBY) announced today the approval of the CE Mark for the VENTANA® HER2 (4B5) Rabbit Monoclonal Primary Antibody RxDx* to identify metastatic breast cancer patients with low HER2 expression for whom ENHERTU® (trastuzumab deruxtecan) may be considered as a targeted treatment. title: Changes in Enterprise delivery schedule
author: Enterprise staff
description: Deadlines and delivery schedules are changing at The Davis Enterprise, beginning May 10. That will be the last day for Friday publication. After that date, The Enterprise will publish two
content:
Deadlines and delivery schedules are changing at The Davis Enterprise, beginning May 10. That will be the last day for Friday publication.
After that date, The Enterprise will publish two days a week, Wednesdays and Sundays. Online content will continue to be updated daily.
'As our readers continue to migrate online, we need to stay flexible to reach them on the platforms where they engaging with the news,' said editor Sebastian Oñate. 'By consolidating delivery into two days, we can free up more resources for real-time newsgathering, as well as more in-depth reporting on the stories that matter to Davis residents.'

title: Locals push CalCare bill
author: Monica Stark
description: As too many are left behind in the current healthcare system despite paying exorbitant costs compared to other countries, the U.S. is still one of the few economically wealthy countries
content:
As too many are left behind in the current healthcare system despite paying exorbitant costs compared to other countries, the U.S. is still one of the few economically wealthy countries without a universal healthcare system.
California Assemblymember Ash Kalra (D-San José), with the support of California Nurses Association, introduced Assembly Bill 2200, the California Guaranteed Health Care for All Act which would 'enact a comprehensive framework of governance, benefits, program standards, and health care cost controls for a single-payer health care coverage system in California.' Advocates say its will allow California to 'begin consolidating existing healthcare programs, obtaining necessary federal waivers, and determining public financing.'

title: Social Services Commission reviews its scope amid mergers
author: Rebecca Wasik
description: Several of the advisory commissions in the city of Davis are set to merge with other commissions later this summer. One commission that will not be changed is the city's
content:
Several of the advisory commissions in the city of Davis are set to merge with other commissions later this summer. One commission that will not be changed is the city's Social Services Commission.
On Monday evening, the Social Services Commission met with Vice Mayor Bapu Vaitla, Assistant City Manager Kelly Stachowicz and Director of Social Services and Housing Dana Bailey to consider the City Council subcommittee's proposed scope for the commission.

title: Opera House hits a home run
author: Jennifer Goldman
description: It's another home run for the Woodland Opera House as they present 'Damn Yankees,' written by Richard Adler and Jerry Ross with book by George Abbot and Douglas Wallop.
content:

The musical is set in the mid-1950s when Americans were obsessed with baseball. The aging Joe Boyd (Nathan Lacy) expresses that he would sell his soul for his favorite team, the Washington Senators, to finally beat the Yankees and win the league pennant championship.

title: College athletes deserve compensation
author: Rich Rifkin
description: College sports are more equitable now than ever before. Rule changes that allow players generating billions of dollars for their schools, coaches and administrators to get a piece of the
content:
College sports are more equitable now than ever before. Rule changes that allow players generating billions of dollars for their schools, coaches and administrators to get a piece of the pie are long overdue. Letting a student transfer to another school and play right away is right.
But not everyone likes equity or values what is fair.

title: Davis Farm to School: Land acknowledgment and indigenous gardens
author: Lorie Hammond
description: We should take a moment to acknowledge the land on which we are gathered. For thousands of years, this land has been the home of Patwin people. Today, there are
content:
We should take a moment to acknowledge the land on which we are gathered. For thousands of years, this land has been the home of Patwin people. Today, there are three federally recognized Patwin tribes: Cachil Dehe Band of Wintun Indians of the Colusa Indian Community, Kletsel Dehe Band of Wintun Indians, and Yocha Dehe Wintun Nation.
The Patwin people have remained committed to the stewardship of this land over many centuries. It has been cherished and protected, as elders have instructed the young through generations. We are honored and grateful to be here today on their traditional lands.

title: Former state schools chief Delaine Eastin dead at 76
author: Enterprise staff

content:
Delaine Eastin — a UC Davis graduate and longtime Davis resident who served two terms as state superintendent of public instruction — died Wednesday in Davis, according to a statement from her representatives. She was 76.
'With heavy hearts, we are saddened to report that the Honorable Delaine Eastin died peacefully this evening surrounded by loved ones,' the statement said.

title: Bob Dunning: Water under the bridge
author: Bob Dunning
description: A few weeks ago, my daughter Maev and I were sitting next to each other on an Alaska Airlines flight to San Francisco when a kind flight attendant asked us
content:

I requested what I usually do on the rare times that I fly — black coffee — but for some reason, Alaska Airlines didn't have coffee of any kind available that day and refueling in midair was not an option.

title: Terra Drone, Unifly, and Aloft Technologies Launch UTM Development for AAM Targeting Global Markets
author: Terra Drone Corporation
description: World's first collaboration by multiple UTM leaders aims to enable AAMs to take off around the globe
content:
World's first collaboration by multiple UTM leaders aims to enable AAMs to take off around the globe
TOKYO, April 24, 2024 /PRNewswire/ -- Terra Drone Corporation, a leading drone and Advanced Air Mobility (AAM) technology provider headquartered in Japan, has announced the launch of joint development with its Group companies Unifly NV ("Unifly") and Aloft Technologies Inc. ("Aloft") focused on UAS Traffic Management (UTM) (1) for AAMs targeting global markets. Terra Drone has been making strides in its pioneering UTM business via strategic investments in Unifly, a leading UTM technology provider based in Belgium, and Aloft, which has the top UTM market share in the U.S. This collaboration marks the world's first-ever (2) joint UTM development for AAMs by multiple companies with extensive track records in UTM implementation and operation. The three companies made the announcement at the prominent uncrewed system and robotics expo XPONENTIAL 2024 in San Diego.

title: Day of remembrance set for Karim Abou Najm
author: Monica Stark
description: Taken too soon, Karim Abou Najm, the computer scientist just shy of six weeks from graduating from UC Davis with honors, was working on software to help the hearing impaired
content:
Taken too soon, Karim Abou Najm, the computer scientist just shy of six weeks from graduating from UC Davis with honors, was working on software to help the hearing impaired in noisy environments.
He was returning to his family home from an undergraduate award ceremony when slain on April 29, 2023, in Sycamore Park, the second victim in a series of stabbings that shook the town and brought grief to loved ones.

title: DMTC presents 'Into the Woods'
author: Special to The Enterprise
description: Davis Musical Theatre Company (DMTC) presents 'Into the Woods' (Underwritten by Sharon Joyce) from Friday, April 26, through Sunday, May 19, at the Jean Henderson Performing Arts Center, 607 Pena
content:
Davis Musical Theatre Company (DMTC) presents ' Into the Woods' (Underwritten by Sharon Joyce) from Friday, April 26, through Sunday, May 19, at the Jean Henderson Performing Arts Center, 607 Pena Drive, No. 10, in Davis.
An ambivalent Cinderella? A bloodthirsty Little Red Riding hood? A Prince Charming with a roving eye? They're all among the cockeyed characters in James Lapine and Stephen Sondheim's fractured fairy tale centered around a childless baker and his wife whose only wish is to lift the family curse and live happily ever after. Thus, what begins as a lively irreverent fantasy becomes a moving lesson about community responsibility and the stories we tell our children. In addition to the stories, we have the music of Stephen Sondheim (who passed away in 2021) an American composer and lyricist. He is regarded as one of the most important figures in 20th-century musical theater and is credited with reinventing the American musical.

title: Special UCD exhibition showcases traditional Jiangnan Style design
author: Michael G. French
description: The UC Davis Design Museum examines the vibrant fusion of traditional yet innovative designs in the Chinese Jiangnan style as part of a special installation. "Tradition Meets Modernization: The Wisdom
content:
The UC Davis Design Museum examines the vibrant fusion of traditional yet innovative designs in the Chinese Jiangnan style as part of a special installation. "Tradition Meets Modernization: The Wisdom of Livelihood and Design in Jiangnan Style" will be on exhibition April 30 through May 3 only.
Showcasing the unique characters in the Jiangnan style, which was developed over centuries in the Southern Yangtze Delta area, this exhibition interprets the wisdom of livelihood through integrating Chinese traditional material culture and contemporary design innovations.

content:

title: Dan Walters: Charter school battles intensify as education finances get squeezed
author: Linda Du Bois
description: California's public schools, with nearly 6 million students, are feeling the financial impacts of a quintuple whammy.
content:
California's public schools, with nearly 6 million students, are feeling the financial impacts of a quintuple whammy.
Billions of federal dollars to cushion the impacts of COVID-19 have been exhausted, school closures during the pandemic magnified declines in enrollment, chronic absenteeism has worsened, inflation is increasing operating costs, and the state budget is plagued by a huge deficit.

title: Letter: Sun powers Odd Fellows
author: Letter to the Editor
description: The Davis Odd Fellows Hall may look like another ordinary building on Second Street in downtown Davis, but it is concealing a powerhouse of energy. Literally.
content:
The Davis Odd Fellows Hall may look like another ordinary building on Second Street in downtown Davis, but it is concealing a powerhouse of energy. Literally.
Starting on Tuesday, April 2, the city of Davis and PG&E approved turning on a solar system that will generate 69,000 kilowatt hours per year for the Davis lodge, offsetting the 69 megawatt hours currently drawn from the California energy grid on an annual basis.

title: Wineaux: The Impossibility of Keeping up with the world of wine
author: Linda Du Bois
description: The most frequent question I'm asked: 'Do you know (insert name) wine/winery?' Ninety percent of the time my answer is a chagrined 'no.'
content:
The most frequent question I'm asked: 'Do you know (insert name) wine/winery?' Ninety percent of the time my answer is a chagrined 'no.'
I can't even begin to keep track of the hundreds of wineries in Northern California, much less in the rest of the state, country, world. Besides the sheer numbers, part of the reason is that I don't travel much, not even to nearby wine-rich areas like Sonoma, much less further places like Columbia Gorge in Oregon/Washington, now home to so many tiny, intriguing wineries (like The Color Collector).

title: Photography program set for May 20
author: Anna Tomé Granado Petersen
description: The Woodland Camera Forum camera club will host a free public program on photography on Monday evening, May 20, at 7 p.m. The location is Norton Hall, 70 Cottonwood St.
content:
The Woodland Camera Forum camera club will host a free public program on photography on Monday evening, May 20, at 7 p.m. The location is Norton Hall, 70 Cottonwood St. in Woodland.
The program is 'Realism\Fantasy,' by Lucille and Gert van Ommering. The van Ommerings are talented photographers from Gold River. Both have significantly stepped up their photography after their retirement from busy careers and are involved with Viewpoint Gallery, Sierra Camera Club, Gold Rush Chapter, Rancho Cordova Arts and Yolo Arts among others, entering a variety of exhibits and competitions and garnering a nice range of local awards.
They will offer up a sneak preview of their two-person photography exhibit that will be shown at the Mills Station Art and Culture Center (MACC) in Rancho Cordova in July 2024, occupying the entire second floor of the facility.
The exhibit is titled 'Realism\Fantasy' with Lucille presenting exquisite renderings of real scenes from travels near and far, while Gert focuses on seriously manipulated, constructed, strange and abstract representations of just about anything.
Woodland Camera Forum members can offer constructive critique on the 60-image show as it is still being assembled, and are of course invited to come view the final show in Rancho Cordova in July.

title: Dan Walters: Lagging revenue continues to drive California budget deficit
author: Dan Walters
description: As the June 15 constitutional deadline for enacting a 2024-25 state budget approaches, the good news for Gov. Gavin Newsom is that all-important income tax revenues in April slightly exceeded
content:
As the June 15 constitutional deadline for enacting a 2024-25 state budget approaches, the good news for Gov. Gavin Newsom is that all-important income tax revenues in April slightly exceeded the administration's $16.3 billion assumption.
Even so, the bad news is that overall revenues from income, sales and corporate taxes are still running $6 billion behind what Newsom's January budget projected for the current fiscal year, meaning that cumulative deficit will be substantially more than the $38 billion Newsom's proposed budget assumed.

title: Trustees hear stats on disabled students
author: Monica Stark
description: While all of the districts and the state overall have experienced increases in their population of students with disabilities over the five year period, DJUSD's rate of increase in the
content:
While all of the districts and the state overall have experienced increases in their population of students with disabilities over the five year period, DJUSD's rate of increase in the percentage of students with disabilities is the highest of their peer districts, according to a report from WestEd, a nonprofit focused on educational research.
Davis Joint Unified School District trustees heard these findings at Thursday's Board of Education meeting, which further showed changes in the DJUSD enrollment rate for students with disabilities has increased while the total student enrollment has had an overall cumulative decrease. Specifically, from FY 2018 through FY 2021 the district's total enrollment decreased by 4.6% and the enrollment for students with disabilities increased significantly higher at 14.9%.

title: Helping You Get The Most out of Your Prescription Drug Benefits
description: (StatePoint) The health care system can feel uncoordinated and costly. One in 10 U.S. adults ration medication because they can't afford their prescriptions, according to the Centers for Disease Control
content:
(StatePoint) The health care system can feel uncoordinated and costly. One in 10 U.S. adults ration medication because they can't afford their prescriptions, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. In fact, the more a patient must pay at the counter, the more likely they are to abandon their treatment. Other Americans simply lack convenient access to primary care providers and pharmacies, and go undertreated as a result.
Pharmacy services companies exist to fill these gaps in care. Because these companies sit in the middle of the health care delivery system, they have the unique ability to spot and solve problems across the supply chain to drive affordability and deliver improved clinical outcomes.

title: UC union votes to strike after UCLA unrest
author: Monica Stark
description: In the wake of on campus violence at UCLA between pro-Palestinian demonstrators and counter-protesters, the executive board of UAW 4811, which represents 48,000 workers at 11 University of California campuses,
content:
In the wake of on campus violence at UCLA between pro-Palestinian demonstrators and counter-protesters, the executive board of UAW 4811, which represents 48,000 workers at 11 University of California campuses, including UC Davis, announced to its members on Wednesday in a letter obtained by the Enterprise that it voted to hold a strike authorization vote as early as next week to give the board authority to call a strike.
The board letter cited 'counter-protesters attacking the Palestine Solidarity encampment at UCLA, hitting protesters with sticks, spraying them with bear spray, and pelting them with bottles and fireworks.'

title: UU Church of Davis welcomes new minister
author: Special to The Enterprise
description: In a joyous celebration on April 28, the congregation of the Unitarian Universalist Church of Davis welcomed its new minister, the Rev. Angeline C. Jackson. Her selection caps an interim
content:
In a joyous celebration on April 28, the congregation of the Unitarian Universalist Church of Davis welcomed its new minister, the Rev. Angeline C. Jackson. Her selection caps an interim ministry by the Rev. Connie Simon following the retirement of longtime senior minister the Rev. Elizabeth Banks in 2022.
First organized in 1954 as a small group of liberal-minded parents seeking meaningful religious education for their children, today UUCD is a vibrant community with over 300 congregants from both Yolo and Solano counties. The church provides children, youth, young adults, and adults an opportunity to explore, reflect, and learn in a nurturing spiritual community. UUCD is proudly committed to social justice and environmental sustainability.

title: Phased approach to improving animal services seems to be working
author: Janis Rosenberg-Stamm
description: Yolo County residents and lifelong animal activists have been tirelessly advocating to improve animal services for many years. Personally, I've dedicated 15 years to this cause, and the discussion about
content:
Yolo County residents and lifelong animal activists have been tirelessly advocating to improve animal services for many years. Personally, I've dedicated 15 years to this cause, and the discussion about our dilapidated Yolo County Animal Services building and lack of services predates my involvement.
In the past, it was a struggle with elected officials who, at the time, were weary of us "crazy animal" people. Cost and lack of interest were always the hurdles to overcome. While we may have different priorities in what needs to be done and when, the end goal is the same: Yolo County needs and deserves a new, state-of-the-art building that will promote adoptions, save lives and offer the services this county desperately needs.

title: Letter: Keep the terms straight
author: Letter to the Editor
description: As a Jew who has opposed the Israeli occupation of Gaza and the West Bank for many decades, I find it disturbing that any criticism of Israeli policies and actions
content:
As a Jew who has opposed the Israeli occupation of Gaza and the West Bank for many decades, I find it disturbing that any criticism of Israeli policies and actions is being labeled 'antisemitic.' Our community is experiencing real instances of antisemitism and we must speak out against such words and actions, but expressing solidarity with the Palestinian people whose lives are being destroyed is not antisemitic.
In fact, using the charge of antisemitism against criticism of the state of Israel for its actions only weakens the meaning of the term, so that real instances of antisemitism may be lost in the rhetoric and taken less seriously than they should be.

title: Commentary: Everybody look what's going down
author: Jessie Drew
description: I grew up in a blue-collar town near a major metropolitan area that in the mid-1960s was in a county deemed one of the most patriotic in the USA. As
content:
I grew up in a blue-collar town near a major metropolitan area that in the mid-1960s was in a county deemed one of the most patriotic in the USA. As a pre-teen I was part of a group of patriotic youths who, on Friday evenings, used the school gym as a 'battleship' to be trained as sailors and soldiers by ex-military dads and volunteers.
My cohort was raised to honor the bravery of those who fought to defeat fascism on the battlefields and seas of Europe and Asia, and we were prepared to fight in similar wars for freedom and justice. In the schools the 'Diary of Anne Frank' was required reading, and popular entertainment like 'Hogan's Heroes' and 'Stalag 17' were integral parts of our outlook. We were raised to be anti-fascist! We knew of a place called 'Vietnam' where we would probably be headed as soon as we were old enough to go.

title: The view from the dugout
author: Mike Trask
description: Standing on the top step of the dugout was a towering figure, in tennis shoes, team hoodie and a bag of candy. He greets his teammates and dishes out hand
content:
Standing on the top step of the dugout was a towering figure, in tennis shoes, team hoodie and a bag of candy. He greets his teammates and dishes out hand fulls of pink, red and yellow sweet treats.
I was trying to figure out where this happy go-lucky fellow fits into the High Wheelers team. Was he the team equipment manager, assistant coach or, my first thought, an injured High Wheeler player?
All were wrong, it turns out this was Cameron Repetti not only a High Wheeler player but the opening-day starter. Repetti, a 23-year-old righty, pitched the night before. So why the relaxed appearance?
You see, having pitched the previous day there was zero chance he would appear Wednesday (due time needed to recover, starting pitchers usually will get four days of rest before their next start). This is a rare and glorious day for a minor league ball player.
The High Wheelers play a 96-game schedule in 111 days and the grind for the everyday players can be relentless. But the starting pitcher has this unique opportunity to get a break.
However, despite being a mostly stress-free day, his job was far from done. During pregame, he still gets in his daily throwing, lifting and cardio done. Once the game begins, in addition to keeping the energy high with candy, Repetti was snagging foul balls, gathering elbow guards, providing scouting info and being the first one to greet the players coming in from a defensive inning.
Repetti attended Cypress High School, where his stellar career garnered All-American recognition. Last season he pitched at Georgia Gwinnett College, going 12-1 with 89 strikeouts and only 16 walks. Soon after graduation, he signed with the Billings Mustangs of the Pioneer League. He had a great season and finished 6-1.
Now that he's in Norther California, Repetti is enthused for what comes next. "I am excited to come out to Yolo County,' he said. 'I am pumped up to stay in the great state of California and can't wait to get to work."

content:
The Sacramento-Yolo Mosquito & Vector Control District, in partnership with the County of Yolo, announced today that the first signs of West Nile Virus (WNV) activity have been detected in Yolo County. A House Finch, found dead near Jack Slaven Park in southeast Woodland, tested positive for the virus. Concurrently, WNV activity is gradually increasing in Sacramento County, with more mosquito samples and dead birds testing positive today.
'As the weather gets warmer, WNV activity will steadily increase,' said Gary Goodman, District Manager. 'This is a cause for concern, especially with summer around the corner and the hottest months of the year approaching, when activity typically intensifies.'

(NewsUSA) - I almost died shortly before Father's Day in 2012, saved, ultimately, by my father. You might say I found him the night I almost lost my life.
He had died nearly thirty years before, but he was with me in the darkest moments of a harrowing, night-long ordeal being stranded at sea off the Bahamas in the midst of a violent storm. Through those endless rain-swept and wind-ravaged hours, my thoughts turned to him.

title: Explorit: Blasting off with Sally Ride
author: Sara Thompson
description: Sally Ride was born on May 26, 1951, in Los Angeles. She was the oldest of two children born to her parents. In school she excelled at science and sports,
content:
Sally Ride was born on May 26, 1951, in Los Angeles. She was the oldest of two children born to her parents. In school she excelled at science and sports, especially tennis. By the end of high school, she knew she wanted to be an astrophysicist.
She began her college journey in Pennsylvania, but after a few semesters, homesickness took over and she transferred to UCLA. She continued to play collegiate tennis and won several championships and titles, but decided that a professional career in tennis was not right for her.

title: Commentary: Where will lithium lead?
author: Silvia Paz
description: California is at a policy and fiscal crossroads. It must decide whether to rewrite the extraction business model to benefit impacted communities, or to continue with the traditional model that
content:
California is at a policy and fiscal crossroads. It must decide whether to rewrite the extraction business model to benefit impacted communities, or to continue with the traditional model that causes unmitigated environmental and economic injustices.
The Salton Sea region is facing economic pressure to become a substantial domestic supplier of lithium, placing greater challenges on lower-income communities that already face significant disparities — yet contribute so much to the prosperity and quality of life of others. Without meaningful investment, these communities will fall further behind as their needs are sidelined in the rush for lithium development.

title: View From the Dugout: The tools of ignorance
author: Mike Trask
description: Watching the High Wheelers' two catchers go about their daily routine on game day made me wonder if any other position in pro sports works as hard as a professional
content:
Watching the High Wheelers' two catchers go about their daily routine on game day made me wonder if any other position in pro sports works as hard as a professional catcher.
Football players wear a similar amount of protective gear as catchers, but they play only once a week in the fall. The High Wheelers play six days a week in the summer heat.
Hockey goalies get beat up pretty badly and wear tons of gear. But again they only play 2-3 games a week and play in a refrigerated building. That beats playing on the dirt in 100° weather.
I quickly realized as I hid in the shade, to avoid the scorching sun, that I was pretty biased and this exercise was too subjective. Regardless, I was impressed watching Angel Mendoza and Mason Minzey put in seven hour days at the ball park on a daily basis.
On game day they arrive three hours before first pitch. They stretch, get loose and need to be available to catch any of the pitchers' bullpen sessions. They will take their swings in the cage and get their offensive work in.
Next they go to the clubhouse to take a break, (remember they still have a three hour game to play), and they watch film on opposing batter and pitchers.
About forty minutes before game time Mendoza is working on defensive drills with pitching coach and former big leaguer Jerome Williams. Minzey is back in the cage to take a few more swings. They play catch again and Mendoza, today's starting catcher, stays in the bullpen to get the starting pitcher ready.
Starting lineups are announced, the National Anthem is played, and it is finally time to play ball.
Mendoza jogs to the dugout in full catcher's gear. The gear fits better at this level. Unlike in Little League, I rarely see these guys fumbling around with their shin guard straps that come unhooked constantly and oversized chest protectors that are so big they sag to the ground. When asked about wearing the gear Mendoza said, "It is not just protective gear, but like a suit of armor and makes me feel ready to go to battle."

title: Tom Elias: Pot lounges? Why expand a destructive business?
author: Linda Du Bois
description: Since California voters legalized cannabis via a 2016 ballot initiative, the weed has evolved into something like a normal business. It's complete with webcasts on how to operate efficiently, disputes
content:
Since California voters legalized cannabis via a 2016 ballot initiative, the weed has evolved into something like a normal business. It's complete with webcasts on how to operate efficiently, disputes over where to place stores and gripes about black marketeers siphoning off too much of the multi-billion-dollar take.
Now the state Assembly has decided the marijuana trade, with retail outlets in almost every corner of the state, is not yet big enough. The lower legislative house voted by a huge margin (49-4, with almost half its members not voting) to expand the business even farther by allowing Amsterdam-style lounges that could serve food and drinks along with varieties of the weed.

title: Letter: Looking back
author: Letter to The Editor
description: As a former commissioner and chair of the now disbanded Utilities Commission I wish to comment.
content:
As a former commissioner and chair of the now disbanded Utilities Commission I wish to comment.
The Utilities Commission urged the Davis Public Works Department to search out and secure ways to build resilience and increase environmentally sustainable practices in the city's utilities. A battery energy storage system at the wastewater treatment plant was proposed and will achieve those goals. I know former commissioners, if they had been there at the City Council meeting that approved the project, would enthusiastically have applauded this effort. And it was achieved by significantly offsetting the steep cost with tax credits and a grant, reducing the price from $3.4 million to $500,000, thanks to city staff.

description: Fusion power, the Holy Grail of nuclear energy for decades, may finally be within our grasp.
content:

In Devens, Mass., CFS says it will be ready to ship its first devices in the early 2030s.

title: Letter: Gems at the library
author: Letter to The Editor
description: One reason to go to the monthly Friends of the Library book sale is that one is virtually assured of finding something wonderful one had never known about. At the
content:
One reason to go to the monthly Friends of the Library book sale is that one is virtually assured of finding something wonderful one had never known about. At the June sale I found a somewhat battered copy of "Palestine at the Crossroads" by Ladislas Farago (1937).
It is a picturesque and picaresque account of several weeks in Mandatory Palestine by a young investigative journalist in 1935. He dodged sniper bullets and met, among others, Haj Amin al-Husseini, the Grand Mufti of Jerusalem. and the recently-installed Emir Abdullah of what was then called Transjordan.

title: Letter: Nuclear power
author: Letter to the Editor
description: John Mott Smith's Enterprise column this week on the history of climate failure was excellent! It made me think that the most important 'tipping point' is tipping enough people to
content:
John Mott Smith's Enterprise column this week on the history of climate failure was excellent! It made me think that the most important 'tipping point' is tipping enough people to the understanding of fossil fuel's effect on warming the planet. If there were an enlightened majority we could quickly plan the way to stop using fossil fuels including natural gas, develop habits of efficiency and substitute clean nuclear power.
We quickly built over 100 nuclear power plants in the 1970s-80s Most of them are still quietly producing almost 20% of our power. They now supply 50% of our CO2-free electricity. Some people are surprised to learn that no one in the US has ever died from nukes (www.ourworldindata). 645 people in Arizona died from lengthy heat waves in 2023.

title: Yolo County's placard system enhances food safety and public health
author: Special to the Enterprise
description: The Yolo County Department of Community Services' Environmental Health Division held its inaugural Food Safety Forum on June 10, which was attended by dozens of food industry stakeholders, academics, non-profit
content:
The Yolo County Department of Community Services' Environmental Health Division held its inaugural Food Safety Forum on June 10, which was attended by dozens of food industry stakeholders, academics, non-profit organizations, and residents. The forum provided updates on how the Environmental Health Division, in collaboration with its partners, is working to protect and enhance residents' quality of life by identifying, assessing, mitigating and preventing environmental hazards.
To protect residents, Yolo County implemented a placard system in July 2017. This system, praised by residents and business owners alike for its simplicity and effectiveness at the recent forum, uses different colors to make safety inspection results easily identifiable and to highlight an establishment's level of accountability for patrons' wellbeing. The placards are posted in clear view of patrons entering a food facility. Inspection reports are accessible online at www.YoloCounty.org/InspectionReports or by scanning a QR code on the placards.

content:

In the video, filmed by drag performer Marina Del Rey (real name: Mark Imaizumi), Bourne said Alohilani should not expose kids to 'cross-dressers' and said she had paid $3,000 so she 'can believe in biological reality. I am a real woman.' She called the drag queens 'fake' and said the hotel wasn't providing a safe environment for her son.

title: Commentary: Tell the whole story
author: David Siegel
description: Many decades ago, I was editor-in-chief of my high school newspaper. I and many other high school editors in the New York area attended conferences at the Columbia School of
content:
Many decades ago, I was editor-in-chief of my high school newspaper. I and many other high school editors in the New York area attended conferences at the Columbia School of Journalism.
We were taught that an effort should be made to make news articles as objective as possible and to rigorously check information: who, what, where, when, why and how. Both sides of issues must be presented to the reader. I am concerned that a recent article in The Davis Enterprise violates these principles of journalism.

content:
It was a muggy Tuesday morning, and out of the classroom doors at Birch Lane, pairs of seniors and students needing extra help reading enjoyed each other's company over their favorite books.

content:

As director of the UC Student and Policy Center (1115 11th St.), Baker will lead Universitywide public programming and outreach in the heart of Sacramento, including high-profile speakers, debates, and briefings that will engage elected officials, lawmakers, community groups, and thought leaders on timely national and state policy issues. In recent months, the center has hosted conversations with California Lieutenant Governor Eleni Kounalakis and President pro Tempore of the California State Senate Toni Atkins as part of its 2024 California Leaders Speaker Series.

title: Get tickets for Acme's summer production
author: Special to The Enterprise
description: Tickets for Acme Theatre Company's summer show, 'Marian: Or The True Tale of Robin Hood,' are now on sale!
content:
Tickets for Acme Theatre Company's summer show, 'Marian: Or The True Tale of Robin Hood,' are now on sale!
A gender-bending, patriarchy-smashing, hilarious new take on the classic tale. Here, Robin Hood is (and has always been) Maid Marian in disguise, and leads a motley group of Merry Men (few of whom are actually men) against the greedy Prince John.
As the poor get poorer and the rich get richer, who will stand for the vulnerable if not Robin? What is the cost of revealing your true self in a time of trouble?
Modern concerns and romantic entanglements clash on the battlefield and on the ramparts of Nottingham Castle in this play about selfishness, selflessness, love deferred and the fight. Always the fight. The fight must go on.
The show runs July 26 to Aug. 4 at the Wyatt Pavilion Theater on the UC Davis Campus, Old Davis Road.
Times are 7 p.m. on Fridays and Saturdays, July 26, July 27, Aug. 2 and Aug. 3; and 2 p.m. on Sundays, July 28 and Aug. 4.
Tickets for Friday and Saturday shows are $10 for students and seniors, $15 general. On Sunday matinees, audience members are invited to pay what they choose. Masks are required at Sunday performances.

content:
SACRAMENTO — UC Davis Health has launched a new program that monitors patients with high blood pressure at home. To support this initiative, the health system is working with Best Buy Health 's care-at-home platform, Current Health.
Patients will use connected devices including blood pressure cuffs and scales. Readings from the devices will be sent to the Current Health platform and also transferred to the patient's UC Davis Health electronic medical chart. All readings sent from the patient's home can be accessed by the UC Davis Health Connected Care Center in real time.

title: Commentary: Reflections on Independence Day 2024
author: Jesse Drew
description: I write this on the Fourth of July, contemplating the possible coronation of King Trump in light of the Supreme Court regranting the divine right of kings to our executive
content:
I write this on the Fourth of July, contemplating the possible coronation of King Trump in light of the Supreme Court regranting the divine right of kings to our executive leadership.
Nevertheless, on this Independence Day, I remain in great admiration for our Declaration of Independence, a document with great flaws and contradictions but also with revolutionary ideas and inspirations. title: Street Beat: Bruxie's makes us feel at home
author: Karen Levy
description: I have always believed that the tone of most businesses is set by whoever is at the top, and my theory was proven correct when Bruxie's manager, Sonia Barrera, greeted
content:
I have always believed that the tone of most businesses is set by whoever is at the top, and my theory was proven correct when Bruxie's manager, Sonia Barrera, greeted me with a smile and a handshake as we sat down to talk on a surprisingly cool Tuesday morning.
I was already impressed that she had arrived well before it was time to open, doing what a good manager does which is step in when her employees, many of whom are students, have gone home for vacation. Not surprising, Sonia began the conversation by sharing that the owner, Kevin Massie, is 'kind and really sweet,' and 'doesn't try to micromanage and boss' his employees but rather educates. 'He talks to customers' and even 'busses tables,' she continued, before telling me that she's also 'big on making sure customers are happy' because when you go to a restaurant, 'you want to be treated well.'

title: Commentary: History teaches how to fight antisemitism
author: William W. Hagen
description: Antisemitism has sung many tunes in willingly open or gullible ears. But its keynotes are fear and resentment. Historically, it often arose from the mysterious thought that the children of
content:
Antisemitism has sung many tunes in willingly open or gullible ears. But its keynotes are fear and resentment. Historically, it often arose from the mysterious thought that the children of Israel were, collectively, a negative and even dangerous presence. Such fear had primordial roots, but took long-lasting anti-Jewish shape in early Christian attitudes, transmuting later into modern prejudices.
It now slumbers in Western culture, waking now and then to foment small or big trouble. The resentment arises in hostile minds from bafflement that a numerically weak and historically persecuted people should, as a group, flourish materially and culturally – and, seemingly, possess power inimical to the aggrieved antisemite.

title: Everyday Ways to Nurture Your Skin This Summer: 4 simple habits to support healthy skin
description: (Family Features) Good skin care doesn't have to mean intensive routines or expensive moisturizers – it can be as easy as adopting everyday habits that nurture your skin from the
content:
(Family Features) Good skin care doesn't have to mean intensive routines or expensive moisturizers – it can be as easy as adopting everyday habits that nurture your skin from the inside out. Keeping your skin healthy and glowing begins with protecting it from harmful ultraviolet (UV) rays and eating and drinking healthy foods and beverages.
With an important role in maintaining overall well-being, it's reassuring to know skin health may be supported with healthy, everyday foods including fresh, juicy grapes. In fact, emerging research suggests consuming grapes may help protect healthy skin even when exposed to UV light, which is known to be damaging. A study published in the journal 'Antioxidants,' in which people consumed 2 1/4 cups of grapes every day for two weeks, showed increased resistance to sunburn and reduced markers of UV damage at the cellular level.

title: Biden steps down as Democratic nominee
author: Enterprise staff
description: President Joe Biden announced Sunday on social media that he will step aside as the Democratic presidential nominee, ending weeks of speculation by the public and Democratic officials who urged
content:
President Joe Biden announced Sunday on social media that he will step aside as the Democratic presidential nominee, ending weeks of speculation by the public and Democratic officials who urged him to leave the race after a rocky first debate against former President Donald Trump.
'My fellow Democrats, I have decided not to accept the nomination and to focus all my energies on my duties as president for the remainder of my term,' he announced online.
In the same statement he backed former Vice President Kamala Harris to take the torch for the Democratic Party. 'My very first decision as the party nominee in 2020 was to pick Kamala Harris as my Vice President,' he said. 'And it's been the best decision I've made. Today I want to offer my full support and endorsement for Kamala to be the nominee of our party this year.' Harris is a former California senator
In addition to Harris, other Democrats, including California Gov. Gavin Newsom, could enter the race.
Former President Barak Obama was quick to praise Biden's record. 'Joe Biden has been one of America's most consequential presidents, as well as a dear friend and partner to me,' he said. 'Today, we've also been reminded — again — that he's a patriot of the highest order.' Biden served as vice president in Obama's administration.
Rep. Mike Thompson, D-St. Helena, also had thanks for Biden. "From the Senate to the White House, President Biden has selflessly dedicated his life to serving our country,' Thompson said. 'And nowhere is his ability to govern more apparent than in his tremendous successes as President. ... To President Biden: Thank you. The American people are better off because of your steadfast and honest leadership, and we owe you a debt of gratitude for your decades of service to our country."
Biden becomes the first sitting president to forgo running for re-election since Lyndon Johnson during the Vietnam War in 1968.

title: How to bring optimistic content to your social media feeds
author: Brandpoint
description: (BPT) - For many Gen Z-ers, scrolling on social media has become a primary source of entertainment and a tool for staying connected. In fact, the majority of Gen Z
content:
(BPT) - For many Gen Z-ers, scrolling on social media has become a primary source of entertainment and a tool for staying connected. In fact, the majority of Gen Z Americans report going on at least one social media platform each day. Reasons for turning to social media include combatting boredom (66%), the desire to laugh or smile (59%) or to see what's happening in the world (49%).
However, often, when scrolling, the content isn't necessarily what you were looking for — or worse, it causes stress or anxiety. In fact, over half of Gen-Zers (53%) said they are frustrated because what they see on their social media feeds doesn't match what they want to see and just as many (54%) believe they have either "some," "little," or "no control at all" over the content that pops up on their feeds.

title: 10 expert payment tips for a safe summer vacation
author: Brandpoint
description: (BPT) - This summer, people are traveling and spending more money than ever. According to the Mastercard Economics Institute's Travel Trends 2024 report, an annual industry deep dive across 74
content:
(BPT) - This summer, people are traveling and spending more money than ever. According to the Mastercard Economics Institute's Travel Trends 2024 report, an annual industry deep dive across 74 markets, there are a few key trends:
American wanderlust: A record-breaking 15.9 million Americans jetted off internationally in the first quarter of 2024 alone. For example, Japan welcomed over 3 million passenger arrivals in March 2024.
Global spending spree: The cruise and airline industries are experiencing a windfall, with nine out of the last 10 record-setting spending days occurring in 2024.
Taking much-deserved PTO: Tourists are savoring their getaways, extending their stays by an average of one extra day compared to pre-pandemic times. This trend is particularly strong for budget-friendly destinations.

title: Gig workers remain contractors
author: Levi Sumagaysay
description: In a major victory for gig-work companies, the California Supreme Court on Thursday upheld a voter-approved law that allows Uber and other app makers to treat their drivers and delivery
content:
In a major victory for gig-work companies, the California Supreme Court on Thursday upheld a voter-approved law that allows Uber and other app makers to treat their drivers and delivery workers as independent contractors instead of employees.
The decision on Proposition 22 was unanimous. Approved by 58% of California voters in 2020 and enacted the same year, Prop. 22 gave app-based gig workers some benefits but not full worker protections because the ballot initiative — which gig companies spent more than $200 million to pass — ensures they are not considered employees.

title: If Californians vote to ban forced labor this fall, will prisoners get a raise?
author: Shaanth Nanguneri
description: Californians in the November election will vote on a ballot measure that would change the state Constitution to ban the practice of forced labor in jails and prisons, a proposal
content:
Californians in the November election will vote on a ballot measure that would change the state Constitution to ban the practice of forced labor in jails and prisons, a proposal advocates say would wipe out a legacy of enslavement that dates to the 19th century.

title: Back-to-School Essential: Protection Against Meningitis
author: Amy Pisani
description: (Amy Pisani) - The summer heat still lingers, but parents and caregivers have embarked on the annual ritual of preparing children for the school year ahead. Store shelves overflow with
content:
(Amy Pisani) - The summer heat still lingers, but parents and caregivers have embarked on the annual ritual of preparing children for the school year ahead. Store shelves overflow with school supplies, and dorm décor, a clear sign of this busy season. Amidst the hustle, one crucial task often gets overlooked: ensuring children are up to date on their recommended immunizations. This is especially vital for students heading to college or living in group settings, where reminders or school-entry vaccination requirements may be lacking.
Meningococcal meningitis is a serious bacterial infection that can cause inflammation of the brain and spinal cord. While many parents have heard of this disease, they may not fully understand the risks. It spreads easily through respiratory droplets, like those produced when coughing or sneezing, and close contact, such as kissing or sharing drinks, e-cigs, vapes and utensils.

title: Commentary: Bombs bursting in air

content:
Responding to the announcer's familiar, 'ladies and gentlemen, boys and girls, please rise for our national anthem,' I stood at a recent baseball game, but Francis Scott Key's lyrics transported me from the cheerful families around me to distant families, similarly innocent and civilian, besieged in Ukraine and Gaza.
Two centuries have passed since Key scribbled his impromptu poem on the back of an envelope amidst a war the United States had declared on Britain.
